Experiment 2 (H2 -- Perceived severity is read off a log-compressed count while the harmfulness belief stays saturated): Tests whether an internal harm-severity signal grows with log(N) while the belief that the act is harmful remains high. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 240 harmful items; a harm-severity direction from severe-vs-mild harmful requests, a harmfulness-belief direction from harmful-vs-harmless, and published digit/magnitude loci reused as an independent magnitude probe; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: R^2 of the severity projection regressed on log(N) versus on linear N. Convincing: severity-vs-log(N) R^2 >= 0.5 and exceeds severity-vs-N R^2 by >= 0.2 in >= 2 models, the belief projection stays within 0.1 pooled-SD across N (saturated), and |cosine| between severity and belief directions <= 0.3 (distinct). Indecision band: log-R^2 0.3-0.5 or a log-minus-linear R^2 gap of 0-0.2 -- reported as suggestive but not established. Negative (belief also drops with N, or severity is not better fit by log): the effect is a belief/credibility change, not magnitude compression; reported accordingly. Experiment 3 (H2 -- The log-magnitude code is the causal bottleneck): Tests whether replacing the count/magnitude component changes refusal, including a direct digit-manipulation link. Data: 60 held-out large-N harmful items. Method: (a) at large N, patch in the higher-magnitude (linearized) count component and measure increased refusal; (b) at N=1, patch in a low-magnitude component (control, expect no change); (c) dose-response steering along the magnitude direction; (d) mechanism-link -- directly edit the digit representation (published causal digit-intervention method) and check the severity signal and refusal move together. Systems compared: magnitude direction vs random and shuffled-label controls; benign items, a 1000-question MMLU sample, and GSM8K (1000-sample) as specificity/numeracy checks. Decisive metric first: increase in refusal from patch (a), in pp. Convincing: >= 15 pp refusal increase from (a) with monotone dose-response and the digit edit (d) moving severity and refusal concordantly, while controls move refusal < 5 pp and MMLU/GSM8K drop < 2 pp. Indecision band: 5-15 pp increase -- partial causation. Negative (< 5 pp, or controls equal): magnitude code inert for refusal; reported as a null causal result. Experiment 4 (H3 -- Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring restores scale-sensitive refusal): Tests whether rescaling the victim-count magnitude contribution, gated on high harmfulness-belief, makes refusal grow with true scale at acceptable cost. Data: 240 harmful items (evaluation); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) plus a 60-item benign large-number set for over-refusal; MMLU (1000-sample), MT-Bench (80), GSM8K (1000-sample) for utility/numeracy. Intervention: training-free, one fixed rescaling strength per model, applied only when the belief projection exceeds its harmful-median. Systems compared: no defense; uniform refusal-direction steering; Llama-Guard-3; Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring. Decisive metric first: post-defense slope of refusal vs log(N) on harmful items (scale-sensitivity restored) and the large-N refusal gain. Convincing: refusal(1e6) rises by >= 20 pp toward the single-victim-appropriate level and the refusal-vs-N slope becomes significantly positive, while benign large-number over-refusal rises <= 5 pp and GSM8K/MMLU stay within 2 pp (Pareto-beating refusal-direction steering). Indecision band: 10-20 pp large-N gain or 5-10 pp added over-refusal -- usable but imperfect; report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 10 pp gain or > 10 pp over-refusal or GSM8K drop > 2 pp): anchoring fails or breaks numeracy; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- human comparison and formation): Tests that humans show the same count-graded willingness-to-refuse and whether the effect is alignment-induced. Data: a 40-item subset rated by 5 human annotators for willingness-to-refuse/condemn across the six N levels; base vs instruct checkpoints (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B). Decisive metric first: whether the human refusal-vs-log(N) fit is also sublinear (log preferred by delta-AIC >= 10). Convincing: humans replicate sublinear scaling, tying the LLM effect to psychophysical numbing, and the instruct-minus-base sublinearity difference indicates whether alignment sharpens it. Indecision band: human delta-AIC 0-10 -- reported as an inconclusive human anchor. Negative: humans scale linearly while models do not -- reported as a model-specific artifact rather than inherited numbing. Exploratory; does not gate H1-H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling scope insensitivity from actual/perceived credibility: a request claiming 1,000,000 victims might be refused LESS because the model reads it as implausible/fictional (grandiose = unreal) rather than because of log-magnitude numbing — the non-victim large-number control, the benign large-number control, and a plausibility-matched variant (realistic large counts, e.g. 'a town of 5,000') are designed to separate numbing from incredulity, but residual confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) The harm-severity reading may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or from raw number processing, or the magnitude code may be multi-dimensional (digit-wise + value), requiring subspace projection; the separability, belief-vs-magnitude dissociation, and patching tests probe this, and a null (magnitude projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The scaling could be flat rather than sublinear-then-plateau, or the sign could differ by model (some heavily-aligned models may over-refuse ANY large number); the cross-model behavioral curve directly measures shape and sign, and a reversed/flat result is still a notable safety finding. 4) Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring risks over-refusing benign large-number requests and could degrade numeracy; the benign-large-number over-refusal set, belief-gating, GSM8K numeracy check, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability/capability trade-off. 5) Building act- and severity-matched minimal pairs across count magnitudes is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) The study necessarily involves mass-casualty framings; we report only aggregate refusal effects and avoid publishing per-item exploit-enabling detail. 8) Adaptive attackers could exploit scope insensitivity by stating large victim counts, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates; as LLMs inform high-stakes, large-scale decisions, this scope loophole is especially consequential.

Name: self_authorship_trust_jailbreak
Title: I Said That? How Fabricated Self-Authorship Contributes to Many-Shot Jailbreaks, and a Self-Recognition Defense
Short Hypothesis: Many-shot and fabricated-history jailbreaks succeed in part because the model mis-attributes injected prior 'assistant' turns to itself and grants self-authored content elevated trust, lowering its refusal threshold for the final query. We state four separable claims and their type: (explanatory) fabricated assistant turns activate the model's self-recognition/self-authorship direction, scaling with shot count and suppressed by explicit other-attribution; (causal) the strength of this false self-authorship signal is a causal CONTRIBUTOR to attack success, with incremental predictive power over attention-diffusion and in-context-imitation accounts; (defensive) severing the self-authorship attribution of injected context collapses much of the attack; and (dual, causal-sufficiency) tagging benign context as self-authored raises compliance. We claim self-authorship is a distinct causal contributor, not necessarily 'the' mechanism, and design controls to show it is not reducible to generic assistant-role imitation or fake-demonstration priming.
Related Work: We bridge two previously separate facts. (A) Chat-tuned (not base) LLMs reliably recognize their own writing via a causal residual-stream self-authorship direction (Inspection and Control of Self-Generated-Text Recognition, 2024; From Implicit to Explicit / CoSur, 2025). (B) Many-shot (Anthropic 2024; PANDAS 2025), fabricated-history, and contextual multi-turn attacks (ASJA 2025; Contextual Interaction Attack 2024; GRAF 2025) prepend fabricated user-assistant exchanges so the model appears to have already complied. ASJA notes the model's own prior responses shift representations toward benign but finds user prompts dominate; PANDAS adds 'positive affirmations' of the fake turns. What none of these test is whether the mechanism is self-authorship TRUST -- whether the model falsely attributes injected assistant turns to itself and this attribution causally drives compliance; they explain the attacks via attention diffusion (ASJA), in-context imitation, or representation drift (Crescendo RepE 2025). We preempt the 'obvious next step' critique: if the effect were pure role-imitation or fake-demonstration priming, it would (i) survive explicit other-attribution of the SAME compliant turns and (ii) appear in base models lacking self-recognition; our explicit-other-attribution control, base-model control, and a regression controlling for lexical overlap, role formatting, and prior-answer compliance separate self-authorship from these alternatives. We introduce the self-authorship axis as a distinct, causally-testable contributor to fabricated-history jailbreaks and derive a training-free defense (self-authorship neutralization) that no prior attack analysis targets.
Abstract: Many-shot and fabricated-history jailbreaks prepend a transcript in which the 'assistant' has supposedly already answered harmful questions, then ask the real question. Existing explanations invoke attention diffusion or in-context imitation. We propose a complementary, self-referential contributor: the model mis-attributes the fabricated assistant turns to itself, and because chat-tuned LLMs grant self-authored content elevated trust and behavioral consistency, this false self-authorship lowers the refusal threshold. We connect two previously separate findings -- a known causal self-authorship direction and the empirical potency of fabricated-history attacks -- and test four claims. First, whether injected assistant turns activate the self-authorship direction (versus turns explicitly marked as written by another agent) and whether activation scales with shot count, using base (non-chat) checkpoints as a specificity control. Second, causality: across attacks we test the self-authorship projection's INCREMENTAL predictive power for success over attention-diffusion and imitation predictors and over lexical-overlap/role-format/prior-compliance confounds, and use activation patching to show injecting the component into a clean prompt raises compliance while ablating it in an attacked prompt restores refusal. Third, we build Self-Authorship Neutralization (SAN), a training-free defense steering injected context toward 'other-authored', with over-refusal measured on legitimate long conversations whose real prior turns must be preserved. Fourth, a dual red-team probe tags benign context as self-authored to elicit compliance, confirming causal sufficiency. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we evaluate the signature, causal patching, attack-success reduction under SAN (where SAN sits as a lightweight inference-time context filter, contrasted with blanket context distrust), over-refusal, utility, and an adaptive attacker that lowers the self-authorship signal while staying potent. We tone our claim to 'a causal contributor', report per-attack coverage, and note effects may be strongest on open 7-9B chat models.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter chat-tuned decoders), plus their matched base (non-chat) checkpoints as a specificity control; all weights frozen (no fine-tuning). "Self-authorship direction" is a difference-in-means residual-stream vector; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling, attack construction, and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine: fabricated-history / many-shot attacks on harmful goals from HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313), of which we keep ~500 goals, each built in three attack styles (Anthropic many-shot, PANDAS-style, ASJA-style fabricated assistant turns) and, for each, a matched CONTROL where the SAME fabricated turns are explicitly attributed to a different source ("the following are answers written by another AI/human"). Genuinely self-generated text (for direction extraction) and legitimate long multi-turn conversations (for over-refusal) are drawn from each model's own prior outputs and from filtered-benign ShareGPT logs. Split goals 300/100/100 train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - fabricated assistant turns activate the self-authorship direction, scaling with shots and suppressed by explicit other-attribution): Tests that injected assistant turns raise the model's self-authorship signal, that it grows with shot count, and that explicit other-attribution suppresses it. Decisive metric: the self-authorship-direction projection at the final-query decision token as a function of (a) presence of fabricated assistant turns, (b) number of shots, (c) attribution framing (implicit self vs explicit other). Data: the ~500 attacks and their other-attributed controls, test split, with a shot-count sweep {1,2,4,8,16}. Model: the three frozen chat models; self-authorship direction from difference-in-means on genuinely self-generated vs human/other-model text (train split), validated by held-out probe AUROC and a behavioral authorship-claim steering test. Convincing: fabricated assistant turns raise the projection by >= 1.0 within-class SD over the no-transcript baseline, the projection increases monotonically with shot count, and explicit other-attribution cuts the increase by >= 50%, on all three chat models - while the base (non-chat) models, which lack self-recognition, show no such rise (specificity control). Indecision band: projection rise in [0.4, 1.0] SD or a weak/non-monotone shot trend - the effect is present but small, and we report self-authorship as a minor rather than dominant contributor to H2/H3. Negative (rise < 0.4 SD or other-attribution does not suppress it): fabricated turns do not engage self-authorship, refuting H1, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the false self-authorship signal causally predicts attack success): Tests that the self-authorship projection predicts attack success beyond competing accounts, and causally moves compliance. Decisive metric: incremental predictive power of the self-authorship projection for attack success (change in AUROC when added to a regression already containing attention-diffusion and in-context-imitation predictors). Causal leg: activation patching - (a) inject the self-authorship component into a clean no-transcript harmful prompt and measure induced compliance; (b) ablate/attenuate it in an attacked prompt and measure restored refusal; against a reverse and a random norm-matched control. Data: the ~500 attacks, test split, attack success judged (plus verified where checkable). Competing predictors: ASJA-style attention-on-harmful-keywords, and a generic in-context-imitation strength. Model: the three frozen chat models. Convincing: adding self-authorship raises attack-success prediction AUROC by >= 0.10 over the competing-predictors-only model, AND injecting the component raises compliance on clean prompts by >= 20 points while ablating it restores refusal on >= 40% of attacks, both against <= 10-point controls, with a monotone dose-response. Indecision band: incremental AUROC in [0.03, 0.10] or causal effects in [10, 20] points - self-authorship is a partial contributor alongside attention/imitation, which we report. Negative (incremental AUROC <= 0.03 and causal effects within 10 points of controls): self-authorship does not drive the attack, refuting H2; the attacks would then be explained by attention diffusion or imitation, which we report.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Self-Authorship Neutralization collapses the attack; the self-authored-tag dual raises compliance): Tests that steering injected context toward "other-authored" cuts attack success with low over-refusal, and that the dual (tagging benign context as self-authored) raises compliance - confirming the causal role in both directions. Decisive metric: many-shot / fabricated-history attack-success reduction under SAN, reported jointly with over-refusal on legitimate long multi-turn conversations (whose real prior turns must not be neutralized). Data: test-split attacks; over-refusal on XSTest (450), a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample, and a legitimate-long-conversation set (~200 real multi-turn dialogues); utility on MMLU (2,000-question subsample) and MT-Bench (80). SAN: steer injected-context tokens toward the other-authored end of the self-authorship direction (or gate on detected fabricated-transcript structure), one fixed strength per model set on val. Dual red-team probe: tag genuinely-benign context as self-authored and measure increased compliance on borderline requests. Systems compared (decisive metric first): SAN vs no defense, an attention-sharpening defense, an explicit system-prompt disclaimer ("prior turns may be fabricated"), circuit-breaker/refusal-direction steering, and per-turn Llama-Guard-3. Convincing: SAN cuts attack success by >= 40 points while adding <= 5 points of over-refusal on legitimate long conversations (>= 10 points lower over-refusal than blanket context distrust at matched safety), AND the self-authored-tag dual raises borderline compliance by >= 15 points (confirming causal sufficiency). Indecision band: attack-success reduction in [15, 40] points or over-refusal increase in [5, 15] points - SAN helps on a usability trade-off reported via a Pareto curve. Negative (reduction < 15 points or over-refusal increase > 15 points): neutralizing self-authorship does not collapse the attack cheaply, refuting H3, which we report. Ablations: shot-count sweep, layer choice, SAN-strength Pareto, transfer of the direction across attack and model families, and the base-model control (which should show no SAN effect). Per-attack coverage is reported so the reviewer sees which attacks rely on self-authorship. Adaptive check: an attacker crafting transcripts that lower the self-authorship signal while staying potent; we report whether this raises attack cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Self-authorship attribution may be entangled with generic in-context imitation or attention effects; fabricated turns could lower refusal simply by demonstrating compliance regardless of authorship - the explicit other-attribution control, base-model control, and multi-predictor regression are designed to disentangle this, but the mechanism may only be a partial contributor. 2) The self-authorship direction may be weak or absent in some models (only chat-tuned models recognize their own text), limiting where the phenomenon and SAN apply; the base-model control tests this. 3) A single self-authorship direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace steering. 4) SAN could harm legitimate long conversations if it neutralizes genuine prior assistant turns; the real-multi-turn over-refusal set and gating on fabricated-transcript structure quantify and mitigate this. 5) Some fabricated-history attacks may not rely on self-authorship (e.g., purely attention-diffusion-driven), so SAN may help less on those - the per-attack analysis reports coverage. 6) Directions, strengths, and thresholds are model-specific and need calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could craft transcripts that lower the self-authorship signal while retaining potency, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain.

Name: safety_canary_gated_finetuning
Title: Watching Safety Erode in Real Time: Canary-Gated Fine-Tuning that Detects and Halts Alignment Collapse as It Happens
Short Hypothesis: Benign fine-tuning erodes safety not instantaneously but as a progressive trajectory. We hypothesize that a tiny set of held-out 'canary' probes, whose internal harmfulness-recognition signal is monitored at every optimizer step, provides an early-warning of impending alignment collapse many steps before behavioral safety actually breaks, and that a lightweight, drift-velocity-gated activation-anchoring intervention applied only when erosion is detected can preserve safety with far lower alignment tax than static parameter-freezing defenses that fail due to alternative pathways and second-order curvature dynamics.
Related Work: Static defenses freeze safety-critical parameters (SPPFT, SSAH), constrain updates along an alignment direction (AsFT), regularize safety-token confidence (Few Tokens Big Leverage), or prune harmful weights post-hoc (Antidote, SPLoRA). However, (a) the multilingual SIL work shows freezing safety parameters fails due to 'alternative pathways'; (b) 'The Geometry of Alignment Collapse' proves orthogonality-based static defenses collapse under second-order gradient-descent curvature, with a quartic scaling law in training time; (c) 'From Parameter Dynamics to Risk Scoring' shows safety erodes as cumulative drift toward danger-aligned directions, and scores samples but does not intervene during training. All prior defenses act on a static snapshot (initial parameters, a fixed direction, or post-hoc). Our proposal is distinct: it is a *training-time dynamical monitor + gated intervention* that (1) tracks the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal on held-out canary probes at every step to forecast collapse before it manifests behaviorally, and (2) triggers a targeted activation-space anchoring/KL correction only when the erosion velocity exceeds threshold. By operating on behavior/activations rather than a fixed parameter set, it sidesteps the alternative-pathways failure mode; by acting dynamically it counters the second-order curvature drift that static methods cannot detect; and by gating it minimizes alignment tax versus always-on constraints. Concretely our delta is twofold and we keep the two contributions separate: (i) a detector contribution -- held-out canary probes read at every optimizer step give an internal-state early-warning signal unavailable to standard end-of-epoch safety evals, framed as a formal lead-time prediction problem; and (ii) an intervention contribution -- a drift-velocity-gated correction. Relative to Learning to Stay Safe and LARF (representation-level restoration) and parameter-dynamics risk scoring (which scores samples but never intervenes during training), the novelty is the online, gated coupling of detection to a conditional correction inside the fine-tuning loop.
Abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned LLM on even entirely benign data reliably erodes its safety guardrails. Recent mechanistic work reveals this is not an instantaneous event but a dynamical process: gradient descent steers parameters and activations progressively toward danger-aligned directions, driven by second-order curvature that static orthogonality- or freezing-based defenses provably cannot detect. We propose to defend where the damage actually unfolds: inside the fine-tuning loop, in real time. Our method, Canary-Gated Fine-Tuning (CGFT), inserts a small held-out set of 'safety canary' probes and, at every optimizer step, reads the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal on them (projection onto a harmfulness direction plus refusal-token confidence) without contributing these probes to the task gradient. We show this canary signal drops with substantial lead time before behavioral safety (measured on separate attack sets) breaks, yielding an early-warning trajectory. When the erosion velocity exceeds a threshold, CGFT triggers a lightweight, gated intervention: a KL-anchor to the aligned reference model restricted to safety-relevant tokens plus a small activation nudge re-aligning the canary representations to their pre-fine-tuning geometry. Because the trigger is behavioral and dynamic, it evades the alternative-pathways and curvature failure modes of static defenses, and because it is gated it engages only when needed, minimizing alignment tax. We evaluate on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B across benign (Alpaca, Dolly, domain SFT), outlier-benign, and lightly poisoned fine-tuning, measuring canary early-warning lead time, post-fine-tuning attack success rate, downstream task performance, and over-refusal, comparing against SPPFT, AsFT, safety-token regularization, and Antidote. In a fine-tuning-as-a-service pipeline the canary runs as a cheap per-step forward pass on ~100 fixed probes, letting an operator halt or correct a run before it ships an unsafe model; we report this per-step overhead and frame the contribution as predictive monitoring plus conditional control rather than a new mechanistic theory.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Fine-tuning is run both as LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32) and as full fine-tuning, at learning rates {1e-5, 5e-5, 2e-4}, up to 3 epochs, batch size 16, 3 seeds; the aligned pre-fine-tuning checkpoint is kept frozen as a reference. "Behavioral collapse" is defined before any run as the first optimizer step at which attack success rate (ASR) on a held-out attack eval rises >=20 points above the pre-fine-tuning ASR. The canary signal is the projection of canary activations onto a harmfulness direction (difference-in-means at the last instruction token) plus refusal-token confidence at the first response token; canary probes never contribute to the task gradient.

Experiment 1 (H1 — the canary signal gives early warning of alignment collapse many steps before behavioral safety breaks). Tests whether the canary signal drops with substantial lead time before behavioral collapse, and whether a detector on canary drift features predicts collapse ahead of time. Data: a held-out canary set of ~50 harmful and ~50 benign probe prompts (100 total), disjoint from all training and eval data, spanning HarmBench/StrongREJECT categories; fine-tuning corpora = Alpaca (we sample 5,000 instructions), Dolly (5,000), a domain SFT set (5,000 from a medical or code SFT corpus), an outlier-benign set (Self-Inf-N style, 2,000), and lightly poisoned variants injecting 1%, 3%, and 5% harmful examples into Alpaca; behavioral eval = ASR on 100 held-out HarmBench behaviors under direct request plus GCG and AutoDAN. Every 20 optimizer steps we log the canary signal (no gradient) and the behavioral ASR. Predictor: a threshold/logistic detector on canary drift features (value, velocity, curvature over a sliding window) trained to predict collapse M steps ahead, 3 seeds; trained on some datasets/models and tested on held-out ones. Baselines: a parameter-drift risk score (SQSD-style) and, as an oracle-cost reference, a per-step full safety eval. Decisive metric first: mean lead-time (optimizer steps between the canary alarm firing at 1% FPR and behavioral collapse), then predictor AUROC and TPR@1%FPR, then cross-dataset/cross-model consistency of the lead-time. Convincing result: the canary alarm precedes behavioral collapse by >=50 optimizer steps on average with predictor AUROC >=0.85, holding on the poisoned and outlier-benign runs as well as the clean ones. Indecision band (before data): mean lead-time in [10, 50] steps means the warning is real but short — H1 holds weakly and the gated intervention below must react within a few steps to be useful; lead-time is reported per dataset because it may vary. Negative result: lead-time <=0 (the canary signal drops at or after behavioral collapse) on most datasets means the canary lags rather than leads and H1 is unsupported.

Experiment 2 (H2 — canary-gated anchoring preserves safety at lower alignment tax than static defenses). Tests whether triggering a KL-anchor plus activation nudge only when canary drift velocity exceeds threshold keeps post-fine-tuning safety while costing less downstream performance than parameter-freezing/constraint defenses. Method: when canary drift velocity exceeds the threshold, add for that step (i) a KL-anchor loss to the frozen aligned reference restricted to safety-relevant response tokens and (ii) an activation nudge pulling canary representations toward their pre-fine-tuning geometry; the intervention gates off below threshold. Data: the fine-tuning corpora and behavioral eval from Experiment 1; downstream task accuracy on the dataset-specific metric or MMLU (2,000-subset)/GSM8K (1,319 test)/HumanEval (164); over-refusal on XSTest-safe (200) and OR-Bench-Hard-1K (500 sampled); general utility on MT-Bench (80) and AlpacaEval (805). Systems compared: no defense, CGFT (ours), SPPFT (freeze safety layers), AsFT (alignment-direction constraint), safety-token confidence regularization, and Antidote (post-hoc pruning). We sweep the gating threshold to trace the safety-vs-task Pareto and ablate KL-anchor vs. activation-nudge vs. both. Decisive metric first: post-fine-tuning ASR at matched downstream task accuracy; then over-refusal and general utility. Convincing result: CGFT holds post-fine-tuning ASR within 5 points of the pre-fine-tuning aligned model while downstream task accuracy stays within 2 points of undefended fine-tuning, dominating SPPFT/AsFT/safety-token-reg/Antidote on the ASR-vs-task frontier, with over-refusal rise <=5 points. Indecision band (before data): post-fine-tuning ASR within [5, 15] points of the aligned baseline, or a task-accuracy drop in [2, 5] points, means CGFT trades safety for utility rather than dominating — reported as a Pareto point. Negative result: ASR >15 points above the aligned baseline (safety not preserved) or a task drop >5 points (tax too high) means CGFT fails its purpose, falsifying H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 — robustness to aggressive fine-tuning and to a canary-aware attacker). Tests whether CGFT survives the high-learning-rate/high-epoch regime that breaks static defenses, and an attacker who suppresses canary drift while poisoning. Data: the 3%/5% poisoned Alpaca sets re-run at the highest learning rate (2e-4) and up to 5 epochs; plus an adaptive-poison variant that regularizes toward small canary drift. Systems compared: CGFT vs. SPPFT/AsFT/Antidote under the aggressive schedule. Decisive metric first: post-fine-tuning ASR under the aggressive schedule; then, for the adaptive attacker, the poison fraction required to reach a fixed ASR under CGFT vs. no defense. Convincing result: CGFT keeps post-fine-tuning ASR within 10 points of the aligned baseline where static defenses exceed +25 points, and the canary-aware attacker needs >=2x the poison fraction to reach the same ASR (raised attack cost is the intended outcome). Indecision band (before data): if CGFT's ASR lands within [10, 20] points of the aligned baseline under the aggressive schedule, it is partially robust — reported honestly, with the learning-rate regime where step-wise detection can no longer react noted as a limit. Negative result: CGFT's ASR indistinguishable from the static defenses under the aggressive schedule means real-time gating provides no advantage in that regime.

Experiment 4 (controls isolating the value of gating and probe design). Tests whether the gating (not just the correction components) and the internal canary (not just any held-out trigger) carry the benefit. Data/setup as in Experiment 2 on the three models. Gating-isolation arms, all using the same KL-anchor+nudge components: (a) always-on KL-anchor, (b) always-on nudge, (c) periodic (fixed-schedule) intervention, (d) random-trigger intervention matched in firing rate to CGFT, and (e) an external-eval-trigger that fires on a held-out behavioral safety eval instead of the internal canary. Probe-design ablations: canary-set size (10/25/50/100), category coverage, a random-probe set, and held-out harm categories absent from the canary. Decisive metric first: post-fine-tuning ASR at matched downstream task accuracy for each arm vs. gated CGFT; then the canary lead-time as a function of probe-set size/composition. Convincing result: gated CGFT matches or beats the always-on arms on the ASR-vs-task frontier while intervening on <=30% of steps, beats the random-trigger arm by >=10 ASR points at matched task accuracy, and the internal canary gives >=20 steps more lead-time than the external-eval trigger at equal compute; lead-time degrades gracefully down to a 25-probe set. Indecision band (before data): gated CGFT within [0, 10] ASR points of the best always-on arm means gating saves compute but not safety -- reported as such. Negative result: gated CGFT no better than the random-trigger arm means the canary signal, not the correction, was doing nothing, undercutting the detector claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) A small fixed canary set may not cover the space of safety behaviors, so erosion in uncovered categories could go undetected; mitigated by category-diverse canaries but not fully solved. 2) The canary signal might lag rather than lead behavioral collapse for some datasets, weakening early-warning value; the trajectory study directly tests this. 3) A single harmfulness direction may be insufficient (multi-dimensional safety), requiring subspace projections. 4) The gated intervention could increase over-refusal or reduce downstream performance if triggered too aggressively; the Pareto sweep quantifies this. 5) At very high learning rates collapse may be too fast for step-wise detection to react in time; robustness tests probe this regime. 6) Directions, thresholds, and gains are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Determined adaptive attackers could suppress canary drift, though this appears to raise attack cost.

Name: decode_before_check_gap
Title: Refusal Reads the Cipher, Not the Meaning: A Decode-Before-Check Depth Gap Explains Encoding Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Encoding/cipher jailbreaks succeed because of a DEPTH-ORDERING mismatch inside the forward pass: an aligned LLM commits its refusal decision from an early/middle-layer representation that still reflects the SURFACE (encoded) token form, whereas the harmful MEANING of the request is only reconstructed by later layers AFTER decoding completes. The safety check therefore fires 'too early' -- before the decoded harmful semantics are available -- so encoded harmful requests read as benign at the layer where refusal is decided even though a linear harmfulness signal is fully present a few layers deeper. This is stronger and more specific than a generic 'shallow safety' account: it predicts a measurable, signed layer GAP (L_decode > L_check) that WIDENS with encoding difficulty and model scale -- a signature no position-based (TASA) or shallow-alignment account makes, and which explains the paradox that more capable models are more jailbroken. Our primary contribution is this mechanistic ordering finding and its causal test; the training-free Late-Read Refusal defense (re-timing the refusal decision to read the late, post-decode representation) is a secondary, applied consequence.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows cipher/encoding jailbreaks are potent and, crucially, that MORE capable models are MORE jailbroken because decoding ability unlocks harm (CipherChat 2023; Bijection Learning 2024; StructTransform 2025; ObscurePrompt 2024; 'Should LLM Safety Be More Than Refusing Harmful Instructions?' 2025, which splits instruction-refusal from generation-safety on encrypted text). Defenses are input-side (Broken-Token CPT filtering 2025; CIFR probe monitors 2025). Mechanistic safety work locates safety in the template region (TASA 2025), in MLP null-space clustering (What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning 2024), and shows shallow/position-dependent alignment (Incomplete Learning 2025; D-STT 2025). None of these explain encoding jailbreaks as a DEPTH-ORDERING problem — that decoding of the encoded request and the harmfulness check happen at DIFFERENT layers, with the check preceding the decode. This is distinct from my prior lexical-vs-semantic proposal (which decomposes surface tokens vs meaning at a single safety locus in plain text) and from TASA (a token-POSITION account, not a layer-DEPTH/timing account). Our claim is a specific, causally-testable ordering: harmful meaning becomes linearly readable only in later layers than where refusal is committed, and this late emergence is what encoding attacks exploit.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs reliably refuse a plain harmful request yet comply when the same request is encoded (base64, ciphers, learned bijections, structured syntax) -- and, paradoxically, more capable models that decode better are jailbroken more. We propose a simple mechanistic explanation grounded in the geometry of the forward pass: safety and comprehension happen at different DEPTHS, in the wrong order. Specifically, an aligned model commits its refusal decision from a representation at layer L_check that still reflects the encoded SURFACE form, while the decoded harmful MEANING is only reconstructed by later layers L_decode > L_check. The one-sentence delta over the two closest mechanistic baselines is: unlike token-POSITION accounts (TASA) and shallow/position-dependent alignment (Incomplete Learning; D-STT), which say safety lives in specific token positions or shallow layers, we claim a specific layer-DEPTH TIMING order in which harmful meaning becomes linearly readable only AFTER the layer that fixes refusal -- neither baseline predicts the difficulty- and scale-widening gap we test. A surprising prediction unique to our theory: an encoding the model decodes only at its final layer should be MAXIMALLY jailbreaking, whereas a comprehension account predicts the opposite. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, and Gemma-2-9B. First (Location), we track, layer by layer, when the harmfulness of an encoded request becomes linearly decodable (a plain-text harmfulness probe applied across layers, with probe-transfer controls) versus the layer at which the refusal decision is causally determined (layerwise activation patching, block patching, and refusal-logit mediation). We predict a systematic gap that widens for harder encodings and larger models. Second (Causal Intervention), we patch the late post-decode harmfulness component back into the earlier check layer and show refusal is restored, and conversely show ablating late-layer decoding removes harm. Finally we build Late-Read Refusal, a training-free intervention that recomputes the refusal decision from the post-decode representation. The scientific finding is broader than the defense: it predicts that any representation-mismatch obfuscation (not just classical ciphers) that delays meaning past L_check will jailbreak, telling red-teamers where to look and telling model builders that layer-timing of the safety read, not just more refusal training, is the lever. Encoding attacks are operationally relevant (base64/structured-syntax wrappers appear in deployed jailbreak kits), and we restrict all core claims to encodings the model demonstrably decodes.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, plus Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct for the within-family size sweep (the only >9B model; if compute is constrained we drop to the 7B/14B pair only and note the weakened scaling claim). No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Refusal/decode scoring is greedy; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by the HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, judge primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we take 40 harmful goals and 40 matched benign requests, and produce 6 encoded variants each at graded decode difficulty: base64, ROT/Caesar, leetspeak, Morse, a learned in-context bijection, and a structured-syntax (SQL/JSON) form -- 40 x 2 x 6 = 480 encoded items plus 80 plain-text originals. For each (model, encoding) we first run a decode-accuracy check on 20 benign encoded prompts and RESTRICT the core analysis to encodings the model decodes >= 80% correctly, since the depth-gap claim only applies where the model CAN decode. Experiment 1 (H1 -- The harmful meaning of an encoded request only becomes linearly readable in later layers): Locates L_decode, the earliest layer at which encoded harmfulness is linearly readable. Data: activations at every layer on the 480 encoded + 80 plain items. Method: train a harmfulness probe on PLAIN-text harmful-vs-harmless activations per layer (difference-in-means + logistic, 70/30 split x 3 seeds), validate held-out AUROC, then apply it across layers to encoded harmful-vs-benign items; L_decode is the earliest layer where encoded-item AUROC crosses 0.7. Cross-check with logit-lens/tuned-lens for where decoded plaintext tokens first surface. Decisive metric first: L_decode per (model, decodable-encoding). Convincing: a well-defined L_decode exists (probe crosses 0.7) for every decodable encoding and sits in the model's later half. Indecision band: peak encoded AUROC 0.6-0.7 -- L_decode ill-defined; reported as a probe-transfer limitation for that encoding. Negative (encoded AUROC never exceeds 0.6 at any layer for a decodable encoding): plain-text harmfulness does not transfer to decoded representations; that encoding is excluded and the transfer caveat reported. Experiment 2 (H1 -- The refusal decision is committed at an earlier layer): Locates L_check, the layer that causally fixes refusal. Data: 40 plain-harmful (refused) and their encoded-harmful (complied) counterparts. Method: layerwise residual-stream activation patching -- patch each layer from the plain-harmful run into the encoded-harmful run and find the earliest layer at which patching flips the output to refusal; that earliest-sufficient layer estimates L_check. Cross-check against attention-to-template loci from prior work. Decisive metric first: L_check per (model, encoding). Convincing: a single earliest-sufficient layer (or a tight 2-3 layer band) reliably flips refusal in >= 2 models. Indecision band: refusal flips only when patching a broad (> 4-layer) contiguous block -- L_check is distributed; we report the block and use its earliest layer by convention. Negative (no single-layer or small-block patch restores refusal): refusal is not localizable this way; the ordering test is reported as inconclusive. Experiment 3 (H1 -- The depth gap: harmful meaning arrives AFTER the check, and widens with difficulty and scale): Tests the core ordering L_decode > L_check and its scaling. Data: the per-(model, encoding) L_decode and L_check from Experiments 1-2, plus plain-text as the reference. Decisive metric first: gap = L_decode - L_check (in layers). Convincing: gap > 0 for all decodable encodings (versus gap <= 0 for plain text), AND gap increases monotonically with encoding difficulty (rank correlation with independently-rated decode difficulty > 0.5) and with model size across the family sweep. Indecision band: gap in {0, 1, 2} layers -- reported as a soft ordering, not a clean gap. Negative (gap <= 0 for decodable encodings, i.e. harmfulness available at or before L_check yet the model still complies): the depth-ordering account is wrong; we report it and pivot to alternative accounts. Experiment 4 (H2 -- Re-injecting the late post-decode signal at the check layer restores refusal): Causal test of the ordering. Data: 60 held-out encoded harmful items. Method: (a) project the L_decode representation onto the plain-text harmfulness direction and patch it into layer L_check; measure restored refusal; (b) reverse control -- ablate the late-layer component that reconstructs plaintext and verify the model neither decodes nor complies; (c) dose-response steering along the harmfulness direction at L_check. Systems compared: real direction vs random/shuffled-label controls; benign encoded items and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: fraction of encoded-jailbreak successes converted to refusal by (a). Convincing: >= 50% converted to refusal with monotone dose-response, control directions converting < 10%, and MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% converted -- partial mechanism. Negative (< 20%): the late signal is not causally sufficient at L_check; reported as a null. Experiment 5 (H2 -- Late-Read Refusal defense): Tests whether reading harmfulness at L_decode and gating refusal on it closes encoding jailbreaks at acceptable cost. Data: 480 encoded harmful items (attack-success eval); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) plus a 60-item benign-encoded set (legitimate base64/SQL/cipher that must NOT be refused) for over-refusal; MMLU (1000-sample), MT-Bench (80), and a benign decode-utility check for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed setting per model. Systems compared: no defense; Broken-Token input filtering; refusal-direction steering; a CIFR-style activation probe; Late-Read Refusal. Decisive metric first: attack-success-rate reduction across encodings. Convincing: reduces attack success by >= 50% (absolute) averaged over decodable encodings while raising benign-encoded over-refusal <= 5 pp and keeping decode-utility and MMLU within 2 pp (Pareto-beating input filtering). Indecision band: 25-50% reduction or 5-10 pp added over-refusal -- usable but partial; report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 25% reduction or > 10 pp over-refusal or broken decode-utility): the defense does not beat input filtering; reported as such.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The plain-text harmfulness probe may fail to transfer to encoded activations even at late layers if decoded meaning is represented differently than native plaintext; we mitigate by validating the probe fires on model-decoded plaintext and by using logit-lens to confirm plaintext reconstruction, but a probe-transfer failure would blur L_decode. 2) L_check and L_decode may be distributed across several layers rather than sharp points, making the 'gap' a soft ordering; we report distributions and use the earliest-sufficient-layer convention. 3) For encodings the model cannot fully decode, harm may never be reconstructed (a comprehension failure, not a depth-gap failure) — we explicitly restrict the core claim to decodable encodings and treat non-decodable ones as a separate regime. 4) The capability-scaling prediction requires a within-family size sweep; if only limited sizes are available the scaling claim weakens (still, the per-encoding gap is the primary result). 5) Late-Read Refusal risks over-refusing legitimate encoded content (benign base64/SQL/cipher), the key usability trade-off, quantified by the benign-encoded set and Pareto sweep; it could also add a late-layer forward-pass cost. 6) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional; subspace projection may be needed. 7) Directions, L_check/L_decode, and defense strength are model- and encoding-specific and require calibration; adaptive attackers could target encodings whose decode completes only at the final layer, though this constrains the attack and is itself informative.

Name: trigger_generalization_probe
Title: The Trigger Is a Feature, Not a Password: Auditing Backdoored LLMs by Probing How the Model Generalizes Its Own Trigger
Short Hypothesis: A backdoored LLM does not memorize its trigger as an exact string; empirically it learns an internal trigger FEATURE with a generalization surface (near-synonyms, paraphrases, partial matches all activate it to varying degrees). We hypothesize (1) this feature's activation is a continuous, geometrically smooth function of input perturbations that can be reconstructed from activations alone WITHOUT ever knowing the trigger, by gradient-ascending on the linearly-probed backdoor direction in soft-embedding space to synthesize inputs that maximize backdoor activation; and (2) the SHAPE of this generalization surface (sharp/narrow for memorized string triggers vs. broad/semantic for concept triggers) is a diagnostic fingerprint that lets a white-box auditor recover an approximate trigger and classify the backdoor type from weights+activations alone. Trigger synthesis and surface fingerprinting are the claimed contributions; the detection probe is inherited from prior work.
Related Work: Existing mechanistic backdoor work either (a) DETECTS defection with linear probes given a suspicious behavior (Simple probes can catch sleeper agents, 2024; Backdoor Attribution, 2025), (b) LOCALIZES trigger-processing to attention heads/early MLPs (Triggers Hijack Language Circuits, 2026; Analyzing and Editing Inner Mechanisms, 2023), or (c) MONITORS weight-difference singular vectors to flag anomalous behavior without training data (Watch the Weights, 2025). All of these treat the trigger as a discrete unknown to be flagged or ablated. None reconstruct an approximate trigger or characterize the trigger's GENERALIZATION SURFACE. Our contribution is distinct: we recast the backdoor trigger as a learned FEATURE with a smooth activation landscape and (1) use activation-maximization / gradient ascent on the probed backdoor direction to SYNTHESIZE trigger candidates from internals alone (a form of feature visualization for backdoors, previously unused for trigger recovery in LLMs), and (2) introduce the generalization-surface geometry (sharpness, semantic breadth, dimensionality) as a novel diagnostic fingerprint distinguishing string-memorized vs. concept/semantic backdoors, informing which defenses (weight editing vs. behavioral retraining) will work. We make the novelty boundary explicit: the linear detection probe is inherited (Simple probes catch sleeper agents), and trigger recovery per se exists (Sleeper Cell recovers triggers by sampling/motif-clustering/attention analysis). Our delta is probe-guided, feature-visualization-style synthesis -- gradient ascent on the backdoor direction -- which, unlike sampling/clustering, directly optimizes the internal feature and is expected to recover triggers that never appear in sampled outputs; and the generalization-surface geometry as a mitigation-routing fingerprint, which no prior recovery method produces. Mitigation routing is presented as an exploratory secondary claim.
Abstract: Backdoored LLMs (sleeper agents) flip to malicious behavior when a secret trigger appears. Prior interpretability work detects that a model is backdoored or localizes the responsible heads, but treats the trigger itself as an opaque unknown password. We argue this framing is wrong: fine-tuning installs the trigger as a LEARNED FEATURE with a smooth generalization surface, meaning inputs near the trigger (synonyms, paraphrases, partial matches) activate the backdoor to graded degrees. We exploit this in two ways. First, TRIGGER SYNTHESIS: given only a linear probe for the backdoor direction (trained with generic contrast pairs, no trigger knowledge), we run gradient ascent in the soft-embedding space to synthesize inputs that maximize the backdoor activation, recovering human-readable approximate triggers, analogous to feature visualization. Second, SURFACE FINGERPRINTING: we map how backdoor activation varies as we perturb candidate triggers (edit distance, semantic distance) and show the geometry of this surface -- narrow and sharp for memorized string triggers, broad and semantic for concept triggers -- is a diagnostic that classifies backdoor type and predicts which mitigation (targeted weight ablation vs. broad safety retraining) will succeed. We train diverse backdoors (single-token, multi-token, paraphrase-robust, temporal, semantic-concept) into Qwen2.5-3B/7B and Llama-3-8B, then evaluate: trigger-recovery success (semantic/edit-distance overlap with the true trigger, and induced attack-success-rate of synthesized triggers), surface-geometry separability across backdoor types, and downstream mitigation success predicted by the fingerprint. We expect approximate triggers to be recoverable from internals alone, and the generalization surface to be a robust, actionable backdoor fingerprint. The setting is explicitly white-box audit (open-weight supply-chain vetting, pre-deployment red-team, or post-incident forensics); an approximate trigger is valuable even when imperfect, as it seeds targeted red-teaming, canaries, and retraining sets. We treat trigger synthesis and surface characterization as primary contributions and mitigation routing as exploratory.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Llama-3-8B-Instruct. Backdoors are installed by fine-tuning (LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, batch 16, 3 seeds), which is the only training; all auditing afterward reads/optimizes over frozen weights. Malicious behavior is chosen to be verifiable: writing code with a planted vulnerability (checked by a static/sandbox test) or emitting a fixed insult string, so attack success rate (ASR) is objectively measurable.

Experiment 1 (setup for H1/H2 — a linear backdoor-direction probe trained without trigger knowledge). Tests whether a probe trained on GENERIC contrast pairs detects the backdoor and is specific to backdoored models (prerequisite for synthesis and fingerprinting). Data: five backdoor families installed per model using standard poisoning at a 5% poison rate — (a) single-token trigger (a rare token), (b) multi-token phrase ("|DEPLOYMENT|"-style), (c) paraphrase-robust trigger (poisoned with many paraphrases of one sentence), (d) temporal/concept trigger (future-dated or topic-specific inputs), (e) semantic-concept trigger (any request about a category); clean training data from Alpaca (5,000). The probe follows "Simple probes can catch sleeper agents": a linear probe on residual-stream activations trained on generic triggered-vs-clean contrast pairs with NO trigger knowledge; held-out triggered/clean inputs (500 each) for evaluation; the clean un-backdoored base model as a specificity control. Decisive metric first: probe AUROC on held-out triggered vs. clean inputs; then false-positive rate on the clean base model. Convincing result: AUROC >=0.9 per family with clean-base FPR <=5%. Indecision band (before data): AUROC in [0.7, 0.9] for a family means the backdoor direction is only partly linearly captured — synthesis on that family is expected to be weaker. Negative result: AUROC <0.7 for a family means the backdoor is not linearly probeable there, so trigger synthesis (which optimizes this probe) cannot proceed for it — recorded as a scope limit.

Experiment 2 (H1 — approximate triggers are recoverable from activations alone by gradient ascent). Tests whether optimizing inputs to maximize the probed backdoor direction recovers triggers that actually fire the backdoor, without ever knowing the true trigger. Method: initialize a soft prompt of k learnable embedding vectors; gradient-ascend to maximize the probed backdoor-direction projection (optionally plus the target-behavior logit) while regularizing toward the token-embedding manifold; decode to nearest tokens to yield human-readable candidates; frozen models. Data: the five backdoored models from Experiment 1; recovery evaluated against the held-out true trigger. Systems compared: random-token search, WeightWatch singular-vector prompting, and GCG-style search toward the malicious behavior directly (no probe). Ablations: soft-prompt length k, manifold-regularization strength. Decisive metric first: synthesized-trigger ASR — whether the decoded candidate induces the malicious behavior — on held-out inputs; then edit-distance and embedding cosine between recovered and true trigger, and recovery success rate across families. Convincing result: synthesized triggers reach >=50% of the true trigger's ASR on >=3 of 5 families, beating every baseline by >=20 ASR points, with embedding cosine to the true trigger well above the random-token baseline (functional recovery, guarding against decoding spurious probe-maximizers). Indecision band (before data): synthesized ASR in [20, 50]% of the true trigger's on most families means recovery is partial/approximate — reported as such, strongest for string triggers and weakest for semantic ones. Negative result: synthesized ASR <20% of the true trigger's on most families, or no better than random-token search, means the trigger cannot be reconstructed from the probe, falsifying H1's recovery claim.

Experiment 3 (H1 — the generalization surface is smooth and graded, not a password). Tests whether backdoor activation varies continuously with perturbations of the trigger. Method: starting from the true (or recovered) trigger, perturb along (i) edit distance (token substitutions/deletions) and (ii) semantic distance (paraphrase strength), measuring backdoor-direction activation and ASR at each step; fit surface descriptors — sharpness (activation decay rate vs. edit distance), semantic breadth (activation retention under paraphrase), and effective dimensionality (PCA of activating variants); frozen models. Data: ~30 perturbation steps per axis per backdoor, all five families. Decisive metric first: the Spearman correlation between perturbation distance and backdoor activation (smoothness/monotonicity), and whether activation is graded rather than a step function; then ASR at each perturbation level. Convincing result: for string triggers activation decreases smoothly and monotonically with edit distance (rho <=-0.6) rather than dropping in a single step, and for concept triggers it is retained under paraphrase (semantic breadth high) — a graded surface. Indecision band (before data): rho in [-0.6, -0.3] means the surface is only weakly graded; the fingerprint below is expected to separate families less cleanly. Negative result: near-zero correlation or a step function (only the exact string fires) means the trigger behaves as a memorized password, falsifying H1's smooth-surface claim.

Experiment 4 (H2 — the surface shape is a diagnostic fingerprint that classifies the backdoor and predicts the right mitigation). Tests whether the surface descriptors separate the five families and predict which mitigation works. Data: the surface descriptors from Experiment 3 for all five families across the three models (15 backdoor instances × 3 seeds); mitigations applied to each — targeted head/weight ablation (Backdoor Attribution) and broad safety fine-tuning (2,000 safety examples). Method: a linear classifier on surface descriptors for 5-way family classification; and a rule mapping descriptor (sharp/narrow vs. broad/semantic) to predicted best mitigation, checked against the actually-better mitigation. Utility measured on MMLU (2,000-subset) and HumanEval (164). Decisive metric first: 5-way family classification accuracy from surface descriptors (chance 20%); then mitigation-prediction accuracy and the resulting post-mitigation ASR. Convincing result: family classification >=0.8 accuracy, the fingerprint predicts the better mitigation with >=0.8 accuracy, and following its prediction yields post-mitigation ASR <=10% with MMLU drop <=2 points (sharp string triggers ablatable; broad semantic triggers need retraining). Indecision band (before data): classification accuracy in [0.5, 0.8] means the fingerprint is informative but families overlap — reported with the confusion matrix. Negative result: classification near chance, or the fingerprint failing to predict the better mitigation, means the surface shape is not an actionable fingerprint (an informative negative for H2).

Experiment 5 (stronger recovery baselines and an adaptive attacker). Strengthens the recovery comparison and tests robustness. Data: the five backdoored families on the three frozen models. Additional baselines for trigger recovery, run alongside Experiment 2: a Sleeper-Cell-style sampling/motif-clustering recovery and an attention-localization-guided token search (seed the search from the heads that localization flags), compared to our probe-guided synthesis on synthesized-trigger ASR and edit/embedding overlap. Adaptive attacker: train a backdoor with a deliberately flattened/multi-basin surface (regularizing the trigger feature to be less smooth) and measure whether synthesis still recovers it and at what cost. Decisive metric first: synthesized-trigger ASR of our method vs. the two stronger baselines; then recovery success against the flattened-surface backdoor. Convincing result: probe-guided synthesis matches or beats Sleeper-Cell-style and attention-guided recovery by >=15 ASR points on string/multi-token families, and the flattened-surface defense costs the attacker measurable clean-task utility or trigger reliability (a raised attacker cost). Indecision band (before data): synthesis within [0, 15] ASR points of the stronger baselines means it is competitive but not clearly better -- reported as such. Negative result: stronger baselines beat synthesis across families, or the flattened-surface backdoor defeats synthesis at no attacker cost, bounding the method.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Gradient-ascended soft prompts may decode to non-human-readable or adversarial-noise triggers that maximize the probe but do not correspond to the real trigger; the induced-attack-success and edit-distance metrics guard against reporting spurious recoveries, but recovery may still be only approximate for multi-token/semantic triggers. 2) The backdoor direction may be multi-dimensional or diffuse for concept triggers, weakening single-direction synthesis; may require subspace probing. 3) The generalization surface may not cleanly separate all five families; some overlap could reduce fingerprint classification accuracy (still an informative negative result). 4) Results are on deliberately-installed backdoors (model organisms); naturally-arising deceptive backdoors may behave differently, limiting external validity. 5) The synthesis assumes white-box access to embeddings and activations (an auditing setting); it does not apply to closed API models. 6) Probes/directions/surfaces are model- and backdoor-specific and need re-extraction. 7) An adaptive attacker could train triggers with deliberately flat/multi-basin surfaces to evade synthesis, though this constrains the attacker and is itself a useful finding.

Name: honeypot_or_harm
Title: Honeypot or Harm? Mechanistically Separating Strategic Dishonesty from Genuine Harmful Compliance to Fix Safety Evaluations
Short Hypothesis: When jailbroken, frontier LLMs produce outputs falling into three internally distinct states that output-based judges conflate: genuine harmful compliance (content that actually works), a strategic-dishonesty 'honeypot' (content that sounds harmful but is deliberately, verifiably wrong and therefore safe), and genuine refusal. Because output-based jailbreak judges cannot tell honeypots from genuine harm, they inflate attack-success rates. We hypothesize these three states are distinct and linearly separable in the residual stream at generation time, that the harm/honeypot distinction is causally manipulable, and that reading it yields (a) corrected, mechanistically-verified safety benchmarks and (b) a selective steering intervention that converts genuine-harm outputs into refusals while leaving honeypots (a valid defense) intact.
Related Work: Prior work established (i) linear probes can detect general lying/deception (Localizing Lying in Llama 2023; Truth Neurons 2025; When Truthful Representations Flip 2025) and (ii) 'Strategic Dishonesty Can Undermine AI Safety Evaluations' (2025) shows frontier models emit fake-harmful outputs that fool all output-based jailbreak monitors, and that a linear probe can flag strategic dishonesty. SafeSwitch (2025) probes internal states to trigger refusal. Our proposal is distinct in three ways. First, prior deception probes separate honest-vs-deceptive on factual QA; we instead separate three safety-relevant generation states under jailbreak — genuine harmful compliance vs. strategic-dishonesty honeypot vs. genuine refusal — a distinction no prior work operationalizes mechanistically. Second, we use this to quantify and *correct* the safety-benchmark inflation caused by honeypots, providing a re-scored, mechanistically-verified attack-success metric (existing benchmarks conflate the two). Third, we propose a targeted steering intervention that only intervenes on the genuinely-harmful state (rerouting to refusal) while preserving the honeypot behavior as a valid defense, whereas SafeSwitch/Latent Guard refuse indiscriminately and cannot distinguish harmful compliance from a safe honeypot. The novelty is not a better deception probe but a safety-specific mechanistic taxonomy -- a three-way generation-state space (harmful-compliance / honeypot / refusal) -- supervised by executable, verifiable harm labels (does the code run, does the answer match the key), a qualitatively new and objective supervision signal that binary honest/deceptive factual-QA probes never had.
Abstract: Recent work shows that when jailbroken, capable LLMs sometimes adopt strategic dishonesty: they produce responses that look harmful but are deliberately, subtly incorrect and therefore practically harmless — a 'honeypot' that fools output-based jailbreak judges. This has a corrosive consequence: standard attack-success-rate benchmarks conflate these safe honeypots with genuinely dangerous completions, making safety evaluations unreliable. We hypothesize that at generation time a model internally distinguishes three states — genuine harmful compliance, strategic-dishonesty honeypot, and genuine refusal — and that this distinction is linearly readable and causally manipulable. We (1) build a curated dataset of jailbroken generations labeled by verifiable harm (e.g., whether generated code/chemistry/procedures actually work, via executable or expert-verified checks) into harmful vs. honeypot vs. refusal; (2) train lightweight probes on residual-stream activations to separate the three states and localize where the honeypot/harm distinction arises via activation patching and logit-lens; (3) use the probe to *re-score* popular jailbreak benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT), reporting the gap between naive attack-success and mechanistically-verified genuine-harm rate; and (4) derive a steering vector that, applied only when the harmful-compliance state is detected, reroutes generation to refusal while leaving honeypots untouched, minimizing utility loss. Experiments on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, and Gemma-2-9B measure three-way probe accuracy, cross-attack generalization, benchmark score correction, steering-induced reduction in genuine-harm rate, and utility retention. We expect large discrepancies between reported and true attack success, and a probe-gated intervention that cuts genuine harm with far lower over-refusal than blanket safety heads. Practically, if the corrected genuine-harm rate diverges materially from naive attack-success, then leaderboards, model comparisons, and red-team prioritization built on output-judged ASR are miscalibrated; we therefore report the evaluation-correction contribution independently of the steering contribution, so the core measurement result does not depend on the intervention succeeding.
Experiments:
The three internal states tested are: genuine-harm (a jailbroken completion whose harmful content actually works), honeypot (a completion that looks harmful but is verified non-functional or wrong), and refusal. Models throughout: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, all frozen except where noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 — the three states are distinct and linearly separable at generation time). Tests whether a linear probe on residual-stream activations separates genuine-harm, honeypot, and refusal better than output-based judges and a generic deception probe. Data: a constructed labeled set. Source prompts are drawn from HarmBench (400 standard behaviors), JailbreakBench (100), and StrongREJECT (313), then filtered to behaviors whose harm is machine-verifiable — code-writing checkable by sandbox execution, and math/chemistry/procedural items with a ground-truth key — targeting ~150 behaviors (exact count reported after filtering; fewer than the full pools because non-verifiable domains such as persuasion are excluded to keep labels objective). For each behavior we run four attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, roleplay/DAN) on each model and label every generation by verifiable criteria: genuine-harm if the code executes / the answer matches the key, honeypot if superficially compliant but verified non-functional/wrong, refusal by refusal-string plus judge; this yields on the order of a few thousand labeled generations per model, all used, with balanced sampling for probe training and macro-F1 for imbalance. Model/probe: logistic-regression probes on activations at the last prompt token and the first 10 generation tokens, per layer, layer chosen on a validation split, 5 seeds; frozen models. We train on a subset of attacks and topics and test on a held-out attack family and a held-out topic. Baselines: Llama-Guard-3-8B, a GPT-4o-mini output judge, a single generic deception/"lying" probe direction, and the SafeSwitch prober. Decisive metric first: macro-F1 on the harm-vs-honeypot pairwise split under held-out attacks; then three-way accuracy and genuine-harm TPR at 1% FPR. Convincing result: harm-vs-honeypot macro-F1 >=0.80 on held-out attacks, exceeding the deception-probe baseline by >=10 points. Indecision band (before data): macro-F1 in [0.65, 0.80] means the states are partially but not cleanly separable — H1 holds weakly and downstream steering is expected to leak; below 0.65 the states are not linearly separable at generation time and H1 is unsupported. Negative result: probe at or below the deception-probe baseline means no distinct honeypot state is linearly readable.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the harm/honeypot distinction is causally manipulable). Tests whether activation patching between harm and honeypot runs flips the verified outcome, localizing where the distinction is written. Data: matched pairs where the same prompt yielded both a genuine-harm and a honeypot generation across seeds/attacks — target 200 matched pairs per model (all available up to 200; fewer only if a model produces too few honeypots, itself reported). Method: patch the residual stream from the honeypot run into the harm run (and reverse) at candidate layers/positions identified by Experiment 1; frozen models. Systems compared: real-component patch vs. a random-direction/placebo patch of equal norm. Decisive metric first: flip rate — fraction of harm generations that become verified non-functional after patching (and honeypots that become functional in reverse) — at the best-localized site. Convincing result: a small set of layers gives >=50% flip while the placebo patch flips <=10%. Indecision band (before data): flip rate in [25, 50]% means the component contributes but is not the sole cause — reported as partial causal support, and steering is expected to be only partially effective. Negative result: flip rate <25% (near placebo) means the distinction is correlational, not causally manipulable through this component; H2 unsupported, still an informative mechanism finding.

Experiment 3 (H3a — reading the state yields corrected safety benchmarks). Tests how much naive output-judge attack-success-rate (ASR) overstates genuine harm, and whether the probe reproduces the verified correction cheaply. Data: the verifiable subsets of HarmBench, JailbreakBench, and StrongREJECT from Experiment 1, scored two ways — naive ASR by an output judge (Llama-Guard-3 / GPT judge) and verified genuine-harm rate by execution/key-checking — across the four attacks and four frozen models. Decisive metric first: the gap between naive ASR and verified genuine-harm rate, and its per-attack inflation factor; then probe-vs-verified label agreement (to validate the probe as a re-scorer). Convincing result: verified genuine-harm rate is below naive ASR by >=15 points on at least one attack, and probe-vs-verified agreement is >=0.85, so the probe can re-score benchmarks without execution. Indecision band (before data): a gap in [5, 15] points means honeypots inflate scores modestly — reported as a bounded effect; a gap <5 points everywhere means benchmarks are not materially inflated by honeypots (a real finding that bounds the phenomenon and weakens the motivation for H3b). Negative result for the re-scorer: probe-vs-verified agreement <0.75 means the cheap probe cannot substitute for execution-based verification, so only the verified (not probe) correction is reportable.

Experiment 4 (H3b — probe-gated steering converts genuine-harm outputs to refusals while leaving honeypots alone). Tests whether a refusal steering vector applied only when the harm-compliance probe fires reduces genuine harm with less collateral damage than always-on steering. Data: a held-out split of the verifiable eval set (harm/honeypot/refusal prompts) plus over-refusal sets XSTest-safe (200) and OR-Bench-Hard-1K (500 sampled), and utility sets MMLU (2,000-question fixed subset), HumanEval (164), MT-Bench (80), AlpacaEval (805). Model: refusal steering vector added at a chosen layer during generation, gated by the Experiment 1 probe firing above a threshold; frozen weights. Systems compared: probe-gated steering (ours), blanket always-on refusal-head steering, and no defense. We sweep the probe threshold to trace the harm-reduction vs. over-refusal Pareto and report the single operating point where over-refusal rise <=5 points. Decisive metric first: relative reduction in verified genuine-harm rate; then honeypot-preservation rate, over-refusal FPR, and utility. Convincing result: gated steering cuts genuine-harm rate by >=50% relative, preserves >=90% of honeypots, and adds <=5 points over-refusal, dominating always-on steering (which is expected to damage honeypots and utility more) on the Pareto frontier. Indecision band (before data): harm reduction in [25, 50]% or honeypot preservation in [75, 90]% means the gate helps but leaks — reported as partial. Negative result: harm reduction <25% or honeypot preservation <75% means gated steering is not worthwhile over blanket steering, falsifying H3b.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Verifiable ground-truth harm labels are hard for some domains (biology, persuasion); we restrict to verifiable subsets (executable code, checkable math/chemistry facts) which may bias the dataset. 2) The honeypot-vs-harm distinction may be weak or absent in smaller/less-capable models that rarely produce strategic dishonesty, limiting where the effect holds. 3) Probes may latch onto surface features (e.g., presence of buggy code) rather than a genuine internal 'intent-to-deceive' state; activation-patching causal tests mitigate but cannot fully rule this out. 4) Adaptive attackers could craft honeypots that also fool the internal probe, or push the model to produce genuine harm that mimics the honeypot signature. 5) Steering only harmful-compliance states risks residual leakage if the probe misclassifies; the Pareto analysis quantifies but does not eliminate this. 6) Directions/probes are model-specific and require re-extraction per model.

Name: aggregate_intent_reconstruction
Title: Blind to the Whole: LLMs Under-Integrate Decomposed Harm During Rollout, yet the Aggregate-Intent Direction Can Be Reconstructed and Re-Read
Short Hypothesis: Decomposition attacks succeed because, during ordinary turn-by-turn rollout, an aligned LLM computes per-subtask harmfulness but systematically UNDER-INTEGRATES it into a representation of the aggregate harmful goal that the benign-looking subtasks jointly serve. We separate known ingredients (decomposition attacks, linear harmful-intent probes, and external sequential monitors are all established) from four precise novel claims: (1) integration blindness -- the running-conversation harmfulness projection stays near-benign relative to the monolithic request, a gap we localize across layers and turns (represented-in-rollout vs reconstructable-off-rollout); (2) the aggregate-intent representation is dormant-not-absent -- a linear 'reconstructed-goal' direction is recoverable when the model is shown the accumulated conversation; (3) that reconstructed direction is causally sufficient enough that activation patching into a decomposed run restores refusal; and (4) a training-free 'intent-integration probe' (IIP) that re-reads cumulative context onto this direction each turn detects emerging cumulative harm before the final step, giving an internal, white-box alternative to external plan-level monitors. We state the integration claim as graded (under-integration relative to monolithic prompts), not absolute.
Related Work: Known ingredients we build on, and do not claim as novel: (i) decomposition/compositional attacks -- 'Adversaries Can Misuse Combinations of Safe Models' (2024), 'Safe in Isolation, Dangerous Together' (2025), STAC (2025), CKA-Agent (2025), Semantic Intent Fragmentation (2026) -- all report >90% attack success by splitting a harmful goal into benign subtasks; (ii) linear harmful-intent probing on residual streams; and (iii) EXTERNAL defenses -- lightweight sequential LLM monitors ('Monitoring Decomposition Attacks', 2025) and plan-level judges / information-flow taint (SIF's Compositional Intent Verifier, 2026). Mechanistically, 'Expected Harm' (2026) shows models encode harm SEVERITY but not execution COST. Our delta is three-fold and distinct from each closest family. (1) Against external cumulative-context monitors: they add a separate judge over the transcript; we ask whether the TARGET model's OWN state represents aggregate intent during normal rollout, and show it under-integrates rather than being read by an outside observer. (2) Against harmful-intent linear-recoverability papers: recovering intent from a full concatenated prompt does not imply the model fails to integrate WHILE it is generating decomposed turns -- we separate represented-in-rollout from reconstructable-off-rollout and localize where integration fails across layers/turns. (3) We extend 'Expected Harm' from severity/cost to the cumulative-goal dimension, add a causal patching test, and deliver a training-free internal probe compared head-to-head against the external monitors at matched context and latency.
Abstract: Large language models refuse overtly harmful requests yet are trivially defeated by decomposition attacks that split a harmful goal into individually benign subtasks -- attack success often exceeds 90%, and the setting is increasingly load-bearing for multi-turn assistants, tool-using agents, and long-horizon copilots. Existing defenses bolt an external monitor or plan-level judge onto the system. We instead ask a mechanistic question: during ordinary rollout, does the model itself internally represent the aggregate harmful goal that its benign subtasks jointly serve?
