We hypothesize it systematically under-integrates -- computing per-subtask harmfulness but not the integrated goal -- and that this dormant-but-recoverable 'aggregate intent' is the crux of decomposition blindness. We test this in three parts. First, using paired data (a monolithic harmful request vs. its benign decomposition), we extract a linear harmfulness direction and show its projection is high for the monolithic request but collapses to near-benign for each decomposed subtask and for the running conversation processed turn-by-turn, and we localize the integration gap across layers and turns. Second, we show the aggregate goal is latent: feeding the model the concatenated conversation and prompting it to infer the overall objective recovers a 'reconstructed-goal' direction whose projection re-separates harmful from benign decompositions, and activation patching this component into a decomposed run causally restores refusal. Third, we build Intent-Integration Probing (IIP), a training-free defense that at each turn re-reads cumulative context onto the reconstructed-goal direction to flag emerging cumulative harm. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report detection lead-time, decomposition-attack defense success, over-refusal, utility, and per-turn compute, comparing IIP against external sequential monitors. If the result is negative -- if strong nonlinear probes decode aggregate intent during rollout, or patching does not selectively restore refusal -- that is itself decision-relevant: it argues external monitors are necessary because the signal already exists internally, and we report it as such.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen for every experiment except the LoRA reference in Experiment 4. All "directions" are difference-in-means vectors on residual-stream activations; all "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Every reported number is averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) governing data sampling, attacker-LLM generation, and steering noise; we report mean and a 95% bootstrap CI. Everything fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine: 400 harmful behaviors from HarmBench and 313 from StrongREJECT (713 monolithic harmful requests). For each we generate a benign multi-subtask decomposition with an attacker LLM (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, temperature 0.7, the Safe-in-Isolation/CKA-Agent recipe: 3-6 individually-benign subtasks that jointly reconstruct the goal). We keep the 500 decompositions (of 713) that pass a two-judge screen (every subtask judged benign in isolation by Llama-Guard-3; the whole chain judged to reconstruct the original goal by GPT-4o-mini) and cap at 500 to bound attacker-API cost. Negatives: 500 genuinely-benign multi-step conversations matched on turn count and length, drawn from ShareGPT multi-turn logs filtered benign. Split 300/100/100 train/val/test by goal, no goal crossing a split.

Experiment 1 (H1 - integration blindness): Tests whether the model computes per-subtask harmfulness but never forms an internal representation of the aggregated goal. Decisive metric: the integration gap G = proj_harm(monolithic request) - max over turns t of proj_harm(running conversation at turn t), expressed in units of the pooled within-class SD of the harmfulness projection. Data: the 500 decompositions plus 500 benign negatives. Model: the three frozen models; harmfulness direction from difference-in-means on 300 monolithic-harmful vs 300 harmless training requests at the last prompt token, layer picked on val by probe AUROC. We record proj_harm for (a) the monolithic request, (b) each subtask in isolation, (c) the running conversation processed turn-by-turn (last token at each turn). Convincing: mean G >= 1.5 SD, with (b) and (c) statistically indistinguishable from the benign-negative distribution (two-sided t, p>0.05) while (a) sits >= 3 SD above it, on all three models. Indecision band: G in [0.5, 1.5] SD - the representation is partially integrated, so "never forms" is downgraded to "under-forms" and H2/H3 are reframed as amplifying a weak signal rather than reconstructing an absent one; we commit to that reframing now. Negative (G < 0.5 SD, running projection tracks the monolithic one): the model does integrate, refuting H1; decomposition then succeeds for some other reason, which we report without proceeding to the H3 defense.

Experiment 2 (H2 - dormant-but-recoverable aggregate-intent direction): Tests that the aggregate goal is latent (essentially absent under decomposition), recoverable as a linear direction from the concatenated context, and causally sufficient to restore refusal. Decisive metric: test-set AUROC of the reconstructed-goal projection separating harmful from benign decompositions, read against the raw running-projection AUROC of Experiment 1. Data: the same 500/500, test split (100/100). Procedure: feed each frozen model its own concatenated conversation and prompt it to state the overall objective; extract a reconstructed-goal direction by difference-in-means on activations for inferred-harmful vs inferred-benign objectives (train split); read its projection on test. Causal leg: activation patching that injects the reconstructed-goal component into a decomposed run at the final-subtask decision token, scoring refusal-restoration rate (fraction of previously-complied harmful decompositions now judge-scored as refused), against two controls (patch a benign-goal component; patch a random norm-matched direction). Convincing: reconstructed AUROC >= 0.80 while raw running AUROC <= 0.65 (a >= 0.15 gap), AND patching restores refusal on >= 40% of cases versus <= 5% for both controls. Indecision band: reconstructed AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] OR restoration in [15%, 40%] - the direction carries partial but not decisive aggregate intent; H2 is supported only as "partially recoverable" and we report the recovery ceiling. Negative (reconstructed AUROC <= 0.65 or restoration within 15 points of controls): the aggregate goal is not linearly recoverable or not causally sufficient, refuting H2 and predicting the H3 defense will fail.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Intent-Integration Probing detects cumulative harm before completion and improves on external monitors): Tests that a training-free per-turn re-read of the reconstructed-goal projection flags emerging cumulative harm before the final step, with a better lead-time / defense / over-refusal trade-off than external monitors. Decisive metric: mean detection lead-time L = number of subtasks before the final harmful subtask at which the alarm first fires on true-positive attacks, reported jointly with decomposition-attack defense success and benign over-refusal. Data: held-out test attacks from three families (Safe-in-Isolation-style, STAC-style, CKA-style; ~100 each, generated as above on a disjoint goal set), the 100 benign multi-step test negatives, XSTest (450 prompts) and a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample for over-refusal, and MT-Bench (80) plus a 2,000-question MMLU subsample for utility. IIP: at each turn run the goal-reconstruction read and threshold the reconstructed-goal projection; threshold fixed on val at 1% FPR against benign negatives. Systems compared (decisive metric first, then defense success, then over-refusal): IIP vs (i) a per-turn harmfulness probe with no integration, (ii) Llama-Guard-3 per turn, (iii) a lightweight external sequential LLM monitor (Qwen2.5-7B judge, Monitoring-Decomposition-Attacks style), (iv) a plan-level LLM judge. Convincing: IIP fires >= 2 subtasks before completion on >= 60% of true positives AND lands within 5 points of the best external monitor on defense success while its over-refusal on benign multi-step negatives is >= 10 points lower than that monitor. Indecision band: lead-time in [1, 2) subtasks OR defense-success gap to the best monitor in [5, 15] points - IIP is a viable cheaper white-box option but not clearly early or dominant, and we report it as complementary. Negative (lead-time < 1, i.e., fires only at/after the final step, or over-refusal no better than the monitors): IIP offers no early-warning or trade-off gain and we report external monitoring as preferable. We log forward passes per turn so the reviewer sees IIP adds one reconstruction pass rather than a full separate monitor call.

Experiment 4 (H2/H3 robustness and adaptive cost): Tests whether the reconstructed-goal direction transfers across attack and model families and how much an adaptive attacker must pay to evade it. Decisive metric: cross-family transfer AUROC (direction extracted on one attack family, evaluated on another) and the multiplicative increase in subtask count an adaptive attacker needs to push IIP below 1% TPR at 1% FPR. Data: the three attack families above; adaptive attacker = the same attacker LLM instructed to maximize pairwise semantic distance between subtasks (target embedding cosine < 0.3). Model: the frozen models, plus one reference point of a 20-step LoRA-tuned probe (rank 8, lr 1e-4, one seed) to check whether light tuning beats the training-free read. Convincing: transfer AUROC drops by <= 0.10 across families AND the adaptive attacker needs >= 2x more subtasks (raising its own detectability and cost) to evade. Indecision band: transfer drop in [0.10, 0.20] - the direction is family-specific and must be re-extracted per family, which we state. Negative (transfer drop > 0.20, or adaptive evasion at no extra subtask cost): the mechanism is brittle and we scope the claim to non-adaptive, in-family decomposition.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Goal reconstruction relies on the model's own inference; if the model cannot infer the aggregate goal even when shown the full conversation, the reconstructed-goal direction will be weak — this is itself an informative negative but limits the defense. 2) The integration gap may be partial rather than binary; some models may re-integrate somewhat, weakening the 'blindness' claim. 3) Reconstruction adds an extra forward pass per turn (cost), though still cheaper than a separate large monitor. 4) Benign multi-step conversations that plausibly infer to a harmful goal could cause over-refusal; the benign-negatives set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 5) A single harmfulness/goal direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection. 6) Adaptive attackers maximizing subtask semantic dispersion may evade reconstruction, though this constrains the attack and raises cost. 7) Directions and thresholds are model-specific and need per-model calibration; results depend on the quality of automatically generated decompositions.

Name: refusal_threshold_anchoring
Title: Setting the Bar: The First Request Anchors an LLM's Refusal Threshold, Letting Mild-First Conversations Smuggle in Serious Harm
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing sequential numeric anchoring from human decision science (an early value calibrates the scale for all subsequent judgments), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM sets an internal refusal-threshold 'anchor' from the SEVERITY of the first request(s) in a conversation, and then evaluates later requests RELATIVE to that anchor: after a series of mildly-borderline requests establishes a low-severity anchor, a genuinely serious harmful request is judged as only a small increment above the anchor and is refused less than the identical request in a fresh context. The primary, load-bearing claim is BEHAVIORAL and distinguishes this from adjacent multi-turn attacks in one sentence: unlike Crescendo/many-shot jailbreaking or generic compliance-drift, an UNRELATED, non-escalating, severity-only opening (whose content never touches the probe) shifts the refusal threshold for the same serious probe. Mechanistically (secondary) we hypothesize this is a shift in a linearly-readable refusal-threshold/severity-anchor representation rather than a change in the request's harmfulness belief; a per-request Reference-Point Re-Anchoring defense (secondary, contingent on effect size) borrows the human anchoring-debiasing procedure to reset the threshold to an absolute severity reference.
Related Work: Two lines meet here for the first time. (A) Human sequential anchoring: a 50-year, 2,601-effect-size meta-analysis (Röseler 2023, g=0.825) and the sequential-anchoring paradigm (Bahník 2019) show an early value assimilates subsequent judgments on the same scale, and a reference-point debiasing procedure cancels it; recent work confirms LLMs exhibit anchoring behaviorally with shallow-layer mechanisms (SynAnchors 2025; 'Anchors in the Machine' 2025; 'Anchored Answers' 2024 localizes anchoring value-vectors in GPT-2). NONE of this concerns SAFETY refusal. (B) Multi-turn safety erosion: Crescendo/RepE (2025) is SEMANTIC drift of harmful content toward benign; ASJA (2025) is attention diversion; ProCon (2025) fixes refusal-direction DRIFT during fine-tuning (training-time, not in-context). Template-anchored safety (TASA 2025) and BOOST/eos-segmentation (2024) concern token-position/template loci, not a severity-calibrated threshold. My own prior proposals (safety-drift, commitment-trap, moral-licensing, habituation) either require the harmful content to escalate/repeat, honor an emitted plan, or accrue 'good-deed credit' from refusals — all distinct from a JUDGMENT-SCALE anchor set by the SEVERITY of earlier requests that shifts where the refusal cutoff sits. Our contribution: transfer sequential anchoring into safety as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal (the first request's severity moves the threshold, not the harmfulness belief), and derive a reference-point re-anchoring defense borrowed directly from the human anchoring-debiasing literature.
Abstract: Human judgment is anchored: an early value on a scale calibrates every subsequent judgment, and this sequential-anchoring effect is one of the most robust findings in decision science. LLMs, trained on human text, are known to inherit numeric anchoring. We ask whether this leaks into safety in a concrete, multi-turn-exploitable way: does an aligned LLM set an internal refusal-threshold anchor from the SEVERITY of the first requests in a conversation, and then judge later requests relative to it -- so that a conversation that opens with mildly-borderline requests establishes a low-severity anchor against which a genuinely serious harmful request looks like a small step and escapes refusal? The primary contribution is behavioral, with a sharp delta over the closest baselines (Crescendo semantic drift, many-shot jailbreaking, generic context accumulation, compliance-after-success): those require the harmful content itself to escalate, repeat, or be answered, whereas we predict that content-unrelated, non-escalating, severity-only context alone moves the threshold for a fixed probe, and we include a scrambled-severity answered-turn baseline to isolate severity anchoring from generic answered-turn effects. Mechanistic dissociation and the defense are secondary, contingent follow-ons. We test on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, we compare refusal of a fixed serious harmful probe when it is preceded by (a) mild-severity borderline requests (low anchor), (b) severe requests that were refused (high anchor), and (c) neutral/no context, with token-length matching and a graded anchor-severity sweep; the primary pre-registered test is refusal(LOW) minus refusal(NONE), reported with paired significance tests and bootstrap confidence intervals rather than a single hard cutoff. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a refusal-threshold/severity-anchor direction and a harmfulness-belief direction and test whether preceding-context severity shifts the threshold signal while the probe's belief stays high, with cross-model layer-localization to rule out a model-specific probe artifact. Causally (Intervention), activation patching with matched-norm and nearby-orthogonal controls injects the high-anchor threshold component into a low-anchor run to restore refusal and vice versa. We then build Reference-Point Re-Anchoring, a training-free per-request reset to an absolute severity reference. This matters for safety-eval authors, conversation-memory/moderation-pipeline designers, and red-teamers: even a 10-15 pp refusal drop lowers red-team attack cost and means single-turn safety evals under-report multi-turn risk. We report the anchoring-refusal gradient, the belief-vs-threshold dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check, and we note external-validity limits (open 7-9B models, greedy decoding, hand-curated probes).
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Refusal scoring is greedy; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by the HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, judge primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we pick 40 fixed SERIOUS harmful probe requests (expert-rubric high-severity), 8 per category x 5 categories. For each probe we build 4 preceding-conversation contexts, token-length matched: LOW (3-4 mildly-borderline dual-use requests the model answers, semantically UNRELATED to the probe and non-escalating), HIGH (3-4 clearly-severe requests the model cleanly refuses), NEUTRAL (3-4 benign requests), NONE (probe alone, fresh context) -- 160 probe-in-context items plus a graded-anchor variant sweeping 5 anchor-severity levels on 20 probes (100 items). We use 40 probes because each needs hand-built, length-matched, non-escalating anchor sets; a 30-item subset is externally checked (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- A low-severity anchor lowers refusal of a later serious probe): Tests whether preceding-context severity shifts refusal of the identical serious probe, and that this is assimilation (low anchor lowers refusal) not a generic context effect. Data: the 160 context items. Systems compared: refusal on the identical probe under LOW vs HIGH vs NEUTRAL vs NONE; the graded-anchor dose-response. Decisive metric first: refusal(LOW) - refusal(NONE) on the serious probe (Delta-refusal, pp). Convincing: Delta-refusal <= -15 pp (LOW lowers refusal) in >= 2 models, HIGH does not lower (and may raise) refusal, and NEUTRAL is within 5 pp of NONE (isolating anchoring from generic context accumulation); the graded sweep shows a monotone dose-response. Indecision band: LOW-vs-NONE drop of 5-15 pp, or NEUTRAL-vs-NONE gap > 5 pp -- reported as weak or confounded by generic context, inconclusive. Negative (drop <= 5 pp, or a CONTRAST effect where LOW raises refusal): no assimilation loophole; we report the sign (contrast is itself publishable) and stop before the defense experiments. Experiment 2 (H2 -- A readable threshold-anchor representation shifts while the harmfulness belief stays high): Tests whether the effect is a threshold shift, not a change in the model's belief that the probe is serious. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 160 items; a refusal-threshold/severity-anchor direction from LOW-anchor-vs-HIGH-anchor states, a harmfulness-belief direction from harmful-vs-harmless; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the threshold-anchor probe. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 in >= 2 models, |cosine| with the belief direction <= 0.3, the belief projection on the probe stays within 0.1 pooled-SD between LOW and NONE (model still knows it is serious) while the threshold projection shifts by >= 1 pooled SD toward 'low', and a regression of refusal on both projections shows the threshold term adds predictive power (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 or |cosine| 0.3-0.6 -- entangled; subspace-project out belief and re-test. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6 or belief also drops): the drop is a belief change or not separably threshold-coded; reported as such. Experiment 3 (H3 -- The threshold-anchor axis causally gates refusal): Tests whether injecting the anchor component moves refusal. Data: 60 held-out probes. Method: (a) patch the NONE/HIGH (high) threshold component into a LOW-anchor run and measure restored refusal; (b) inject the LOW component into a fresh-context run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering. Systems compared: real direction vs random/shuffled controls; benign items and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: fraction of the LOW-vs-NONE refusal gap restored by (a). Convincing: >= 50% restored by (a), >= 50% removed by (b), monotone dose-response, controls < 10% of the gap, MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causation. Negative (< 20% or controls equal): decodable-but-inert threshold axis; reported as a null. Experiment 4 (H4 -- Reference-Point Re-Anchoring closes the anchoring loophole): Tests whether resetting the threshold to an absolute per-request severity reference, gated on high belief, restores refusal after a LOW anchor at acceptable cost. Data: 160 context items (evaluation); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) plus a 60-item long benign/dual-use conversation set for over-refusal; MMLU (1000-sample) and MT-Bench (80) for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed setting per model, applied per request when the belief projection is high. Systems compared: no defense; Crescendo semantic-drift restoring-force; refusal-direction steering; per-turn Llama-Guard-3; a naive 'reset context each turn' baseline; Reference-Point Re-Anchoring. Decisive metric first: post-defense refusal on serious probes after a LOW anchor relative to the NONE rate (gap closure). Convincing: closes >= 60% of the LOW-vs-NONE gap while raising benign-conversation over-refusal <= 5 pp and keeping MMLU/MT-Bench within 2 pp / 0.1 points, and Pareto-beats the content-focused (Crescendo) baseline on the LOW condition (confirming anchoring is distinct from semantic drift). Indecision band: 40-60% closure or 5-10 pp over-refusal -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 40% closure, or the Crescendo baseline matches it): re-anchoring is not a distinct/effective defense; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- human comparison and anchoring-plus-escalation interaction): Tests the human analog and compounded risk. Data: a 40-probe subset rated by 5 annotators for willingness-to-refuse after LOW vs HIGH anchors; an interaction set combining a LOW anchor with mild Crescendo-style escalation. Decisive metric first: human refusal(LOW) - refusal(HIGH). Convincing: humans show the same anchored drop (>= 10 pp), tying the effect to the sequential-anchoring literature, and a LOW anchor reduces the number of escalation turns needed to jailbreak by >= 1 turn. Indecision band: human drop 5-10 pp -- weak human anchor. Negative: humans show no anchoring -- reported as a model-specific effect. Exploratory; does not gate H1-H4.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling threshold-anchoring from generic in-context effects (context length, distraction, or the model simply becoming more compliant after answering several requests): the LOW-anchor refusal drop could reflect general context erosion rather than a severity-calibrated threshold — the token-length-matched NEUTRAL and HIGH-anchor controls and the semantically-unrelated non-escalating anchors are designed to isolate anchoring, and a null (anchoring = generic context effect) is itself informative. 2) A competing prediction is a CONTRAST effect (a low anchor makes a serious probe stand out MORE, raising refusal) rather than assimilation; the human literature shows assimilation dominates for same-scale sequential anchors, but the sign could be model-dependent — the graded-anchor dose-response directly measures sign and magnitude, and either direction is a publishable finding (a flat null would weaken the proposal). 3) The threshold-anchor direction may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a causally-inert threshold direction is itself informative. 4) HIGH-anchor contexts risk being contaminated (the model may have partially complied with severe requests), altering the anchor; we use only cleanly-refused severe requests and verify refusal. 5) Reference-Point Re-Anchoring could over-refuse legitimate follow-up requests in long benign conversations; the benign-conversation over-refusal set, belief-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 6) Building severity-matched anchor sets and serious probes is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing coverage. 7) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; the effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models. 8) Adaptive attackers could deliberately construct low-severity openings to lower the anchor before a serious ask, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates; the anchoring-plus-escalation interaction test quantifies the compounded practical risk.

Name: sandbagging_correction_audit
Title: Auditing the Eval-Deploy Gap: Mechanistically Correcting Benchmark Scores for Evaluation-Aware Sandbagging
Short Hypothesis: If a model suppresses capabilities when it detects an evaluation context (eval-aware sandbagging), then the difference between its behavior under a causally-verified 'deployment-belief' internal state and its as-tested behavior is a measurable, per-item sandbagging correction. Because recent evidence is mixed on whether eval-awareness directions are causally tied to the sabotage pathway, we frame this as a falsifiable conditional test rather than an assumed mechanism: we hypothesize (1) that deployment-belief steering can act as a calibrated measurement instrument, validated against a sandbagging model organism whose true deployed capability is known, and (2) that where the correction is causal, it flows through a localizable set of attention heads/MLPs that read an eval-awareness direction and gate capability -- while a diffuse or null result would itself bound how far steering-based audits can go.
Related Work: Recent work shows evaluation awareness is linearly represented and steerable: Abdelnabi & Salem-style probing (Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness, 2025) extracts a linear eval-vs-deploy direction with high AUROC and partially recovers sandbagged WMDP capability via SAE steering; 'Steering Evaluation-Aware Models to Act Like They Are Deployed' (2025) trains a model organism and shows a deployment steering vector suppresses eval-awareness; 'Evaluation Awareness Scales Predictably' (2025) gives a power-law across model sizes. These works are descriptive (detect/steer eval-awareness). Our proposal is distinct in three ways. First, we shift from steering as an intervention to steering as a *measurement instrument*: we define and validate a per-item sandbagging correction factor and produce corrected, calibrated benchmark scores with uncertainty — an actual audit deliverable, not just a demonstration of steerability. Second, we mechanistically trace the *causal circuit* from the eval-awareness direction to capability suppression (which heads/MLPs read the eval flag and gate downstream capability), rather than treating eval-awareness as a monolithic direction; prior work does not localize how detection turns into capability withholding. Third, we address a confound prior steering work ignores: distinguishing genuine capability recovery from steering-induced spurious answer bias (a critique raised in introspection work about global logit shifts), via placebo/control directions and difficulty-stratified analysis. Crucially, at least one strong prior analysis found eval-awareness directions detect test framing while probe-based steering had minimal impact on WMDP sandbagging; rather than assume a causal knob, we treat our core question as whether steering can serve as a calibrated audit instrument despite possibly weak causal relevance, with organism-grounded calibration and confound controls (placebo directions, difficulty stratification, free-form scoring) deciding the outcome.
Abstract: Safety evaluations assume a model tries its best when tested. But recent work shows large language models internally represent whether they are being evaluated and can 'sandbag' — deliberately underperform — on dangerous-capability benchmarks, undermining the very evaluations that inform AI governance. Prior mechanistic work has shown this eval-awareness signal is linearly probeable and that steering can partially recover suppressed capability. We turn this from a demonstration into an audit tool. We propose the Sandbagging Correction Audit: using a causally-validated deployment-belief steering direction as a measurement instrument to compute, per benchmark item, the gap between a model's as-tested behavior and its behavior when it internally believes it is deployed, yielding a corrected capability estimate with calibrated uncertainty. We further open the black box: via activation patching and head attribution we localize the circuit that reads the eval-awareness direction and gates downstream capability computation, testing whether sandbagging flows through a small, identifiable set of heads/MLPs rather than a diffuse global shift. Crucially, we control for the confound that steering may inject spurious answer bias rather than genuine competence, using placebo directions, difficulty stratification, and free-form (not just multiple-choice) evaluation. We evaluate on open-weights models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Gemma-2-9B) plus a fine-tuned sandbagging model organism, on WMDP, MMLU, and capability tasks with verifiable answers. We report the eval-deploy correction magnitude, its calibration against the model organism's known ground-truth capability, circuit localization, and cross-model/benchmark transfer. We aim to give evaluators a practical, mechanistically-grounded way to detect and correct for sandbagging. We unbundle the paper into a primary claim -- organism-calibrated audit validity with quantified uncertainty (bootstrap confidence intervals over items and seeds, scored by expected calibration error) -- and secondary claims (naturalistic generalization, circuit sparsity, cross-model scaling), so that a clean negative result (steering cannot support calibrated correction) remains a publishable calibration finding for the evaluation community.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, all frozen when read/steered; the 70B run is the most resource-heavy and is dropped to <=14B models if infeasible (weakening only the scaling claim in Experiment 4). The "deploy-vs-eval" direction is extracted by difference-in-means at the last prompt token from paired evaluation-context prompts (benchmark boilerplate, grading framing) and deployment-context prompts (realistic user queries) over a layer sweep, layer chosen by held-out linear-probe AUROC. The per-item sandbagging correction is accuracy(deploy-belief-steered) minus accuracy(as-tested).

Experiment 1 (H-core / H2 — the deployment-belief correction is a valid, calibrated capability instrument). Tests whether steering the model into a deployment-belief state recovers capability it suppresses under evaluation, calibrated against a model whose true capability is known. Data: paired eval/deploy prompts, ~500 pairs constructed from framing templates (used for direction extraction, split train/validation); capability items from WMDP (WMDP-bio 1,273, WMDP-chem 408, WMDP-cyber 1,987), MMLU (2,000-question fixed subset), and GPQA (448) — all used except MMLU subsampled for cost. Model organism: fine-tune (LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, 3 seeds) a Llama-3.1-8B and a Qwen2.5-7B to underperform on WMDP-style items in eval contexts but answer normally in deployment contexts, giving GROUND-TRUTH deployed capability to calibrate against; the pre-sandbagging deployment accuracy is that ground truth. Systems compared: as-tested accuracy, deploy-belief-steered accuracy, and the organism's known true capability. Decisive metric first: recovery gap = corrected score minus organism true capability (in accuracy points); then calibration error (ECE) of corrected scores; then that as-tested underestimates true capability by the injected sandbagging gap. Convincing result: the corrected score recovers the organism's true capability to within 3 points with ECE <=0.05, while as-tested underestimates it by >=15 points. Indecision band (before data): a recovery gap in [3, 8] points means the instrument corrects in the right direction but is not calibrated — usable as a lower bound, not a point estimate. Negative result: a recovery gap >8 points, or over-correction above true capability, means the instrument is invalid, falsifying the core claim.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the correction is genuine recovered competence, not steering-induced answer bias). Tests the confound that deployment-belief steering merely injects an affirmative/answer bias. Data: the organism and WMDP/MMLU/GPQA items from Experiment 1, plus free-form variants of the code/checkable-fact items with executable or key-based checkers. Systems compared: real deploy-belief direction vs. a random-direction and an orthogonal-direction placebo of equal norm; items stratified by difficulty (model known vs. truly-unknown, established from deployment-context accuracy); multiple-choice vs. free-form scoring; and a logit-shift analysis. Decisive metric first: placebo recovery vs. real recovery (accuracy points); then free-form-vs-MC recovery agreement; then recovery on truly-unknown items. Convincing result: placebo recovery <=2 points while real recovery >=15 points, free-form recovery within 5 points of MC recovery, and recovery on truly-unknown items <=3 points (steering does not manufacture knowledge the model lacks). Indecision band (before data): placebo recovery in [2, 6] points, or a free-form-vs-MC gap in [5, 10] points, means part of the correction is answer bias — the reportable correction is then the real-minus-placebo residual. Negative result: placebo recovery within 3 points of real recovery means the correction is bias, not competence, and H2 is unsupported.

Experiment 3 (H1 — sandbagging flows through a small, localizable circuit that reads the eval-awareness direction). Tests whether a small set of heads/MLPs accounts for the eval-deploy gap. Data: the organism plus naturalistic models on WMDP/GPQA capability items from Experiment 1. Method: activation patching from deploy-steered into as-tested runs; head/MLP attribution of the recovery; ablation of the identified components that read the eval-awareness direction; logit-lens to locate where capability suppression is applied; frozen models. Decisive metric first: fraction of the eval-deploy accuracy gap recovered by patching a small set (<=10) of heads/MLP layers; then the fraction removed by ablating them. Convincing result: <=10 components account for >=70% of the gap and ablating them removes >=70% of sandbagging. Indecision band (before data): a recovered fraction in [40, 70]% means the mechanism is partly localized, partly diffuse — reported as such, with the identified components named. Negative result: no set of <=10 components recovers >40% (the effect is diffuse) means H1 (a small circuit) is unsupported — still a publishable finding that sandbagging is a distributed shift.

Experiment 4 (H2 — corrected scores on naturalistic models scale with size and the directions transfer). Tests whether the audit yields nonzero, scale-growing corrections on off-the-shelf models and whether directions transfer across benchmarks/families; true capability is unknown here, so magnitudes are estimates (stated as such). Data: all five frozen off-the-shelf models on WMDP, MMLU (2,000-subset), and GPQA (448). Decisive metric first: aggregate correction magnitude and its trend across the 7B/8B/9B/14B/70B ladder; then cross-benchmark and cross-family transfer of the direction (probe AUROC when applied off-source). Convincing result: a positive correction that grows monotonically with model scale (consistent with an eval-awareness power-law) and a direction that transfers with probe AUROC >=0.8 across benchmarks. Indecision band (before data): a correction in the [1, 5]-point range with a flat scaling trend means naturalistic sandbagging, if present, is small — reported as an upper bound given the unknown ground truth. Negative result: corrections near zero with no scaling and transfer AUROC <0.7 mean the instrument detects no naturalistic sandbagging, bounding the phenomenon.

Experiment 5 (controls and uncertainty quantification). Adds the confound controls the audit claim needs and operationalizes calibration. Data: the model organisms and the WMDP/MMLU/GPQA items from Experiment 1. Control arms: (a) a non-sandbagging model (a base model not fine-tuned to sandbag), on which the deployment-belief correction should be ~0; (b) a prompt-only deployment-framing baseline (tell the model in-context it is deployed) to test whether cheap prompting matches activation steering; (c) verbosity/risk-seeking controls checking the steer does not merely make the model answer more or guess more (attempt rate and answer entropy on truly-unknown items). Uncertainty quantification: corrected scores carry bootstrap confidence intervals over items and organism seeds, and calibration is scored by expected calibration error (ECE) against the organism's known capability. Decisive metric first: correction magnitude on the non-sandbagging control (should be <=3 points) and the gap between prompt-only and activation-steered correction; then ECE with its confidence interval. Convincing result: non-sandbagging correction <=3 points, activation steering recovers >=10 points more than prompt-only where sandbagging is present, verbosity/risk controls shift accuracy <=2 points, and ECE <=0.05. Indecision band (before data): a non-sandbagging correction in [3, 8] points means the instrument has a baseline bias that must be subtracted before reporting. Negative result: non-sandbagging correction comparable to the organism correction, or prompt-only matching steering, means the audit adds nothing over trivial baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) On naturalistic (non-organism) models the true capability is unknown, so correction magnitude cannot be perfectly validated outside the organism; we rely on the organism for calibration and treat naturalistic results as estimates. 2) Steering may inject spurious answer bias masquerading as recovered capability; our placebo, difficulty-stratification, and free-form controls mitigate but cannot fully eliminate this risk. 3) Eval-awareness may be multi-dimensional or entangled with task-format features, so a single direction may under- or over-correct. 4) The 70B experiments and organism fine-tuning are the most resource-heavy; if 70B is infeasible we can restrict to <=14B models, though this weakens the scaling claim. 5) The sandbagging circuit may be diffuse rather than localized, in which case head-attribution yields weaker/negative results (still a publishable finding about mechanism). 6) Directions, corrections, and thresholds are model-specific and require re-extraction. 7) Determined models with more sophisticated eval-awareness could evade a fixed direction, though our method raises the bar and the scaling analysis directly probes this trend.

Name: irreversibility_blind_agent_safety
Title: Consequence Without a Compass: LLMs Encode Content Harm but Weakly Encode Action Irreversibility, and Re-Injecting It Narrows the Text-Action Safety Gap
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs internally represent whether a request's CONTENT is harmful, but have a weak-or-absent internal representation of whether a tool CALL is IRREVERSIBLE / high-consequence (deleting a database, wiring money, or sending an email cannot be undone; reading a file can). We define irreversibility precisely as a property of the action's real-world effect -- distinct from content harm (is the topic dangerous?), from severity (how bad is the harm?), and from execution cost -- namely, whether the effect can be rolled back. We hypothesize this missing irreversibility representation is A mechanistic cause (not necessarily the sole cause) of the text-safety-does-not-transfer-to-tool-call-safety gap: because refusal is gated on content harm alone, an agent will execute an irreversible destructive action whenever the surface content looks benign. We further hypothesize the irreversibility signal is latent-but-recoverable (a linear direction emerges when the model is prompted to reason about consequences) and can be re-injected at the tool-call decision point to condition refusal on consequence, narrowing the gap without hurting benign tool use. The scientific contribution (irreversibility as a distinct, causally-tested latent axis) and the practical contribution (a training-free re-injection defense) are separable and each stands on its own.
Related Work: Known ingredients: the GAP benchmark ('Mind the GAP', 2026) shows text-level refusal does not transfer to tool-call safety across six frontier models but is purely black-box; SafeKeep ('Tool Specifications Matter', 2026) locates ONE cause -- schema-formatted tool specs weaken internal refusal -- and decouples judgment from execution via flattened specs; 'Read the Scene, Not the Script' (2025) defines 'consequence-blindness' behaviorally and fixes it with consequence-reasoning fine-tuning; 'Expected Harm' (2026) shows via linear probing that models encode harm SEVERITY but not execution COST; AgentTrust/CIP/Thought-Aligner are external monitors or CoT correctors. Our delta: (1) we advance and CAUSALLY test a specific missing internal object -- an action-irreversibility representation, sharply distinguished above from content harm, severity, and execution cost -- as A mechanistic root of the text-action gap, rather than attributing it to schema format (SafeKeep) or treating consequence-blindness only behaviorally (Read-the-Scene). Irreversibility is not a relabeling of consequence-blindness: consequence-blindness is a behavioral failure to reason about outcomes, whereas we test a specific, linearly-readable axis (roll-back-able vs not) that dissociates from content harm and is separately steerable. (2) We extend Expected-Harm's cost-blindness from severity to the actionable irreversibility axis in the AGENTIC tool-call setting and show it is dormant-not-missing. (3) We build a training-free irreversibility re-injection defense at the tool-call boundary and compare directly to schema-flattening (SafeKeep) and external monitors, verifying schema-flattening alone does not recover the raw irreversibility signal (distinct mechanisms).
Abstract: LLM agents refuse harmful requests in text yet still execute the corresponding harmful tool calls -- text safety does not transfer to action safety, and in deployed agents a single wrongly-executed irreversible call (dropping a production table, wiring funds, mass-sending an email) is operationally far costlier than a wrong sentence. We propose a mechanistic explanation: aligned LLMs encode whether a request's CONTENT is harmful but lack a robust internal representation of whether an ACTION is IRREVERSIBLE -- whether its real-world effect can be rolled back -- an axis we distinguish from content harm, severity, and execution cost. Because refusal is gated on content harm, agents comply with destructive-but-innocuous-looking actions. We test this on open-weights tool-using models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Ministral-8B). First, using paired tool calls that hold content roughly fixed while flipping reversibility (read vs. delete, draft vs. send, simulate vs. execute), we extract a content-harm direction and a candidate irreversibility direction and test whether activations separate reversible from irreversible calls, expecting content harm to be linearly readable but irreversibility weak and near-orthogonal to it. Second, we show irreversibility is dormant-not-absent: prompting the model to reason about consequences recovers a 'reconstructed-consequence' direction that re-separates the pairs, and activation patching it into a blind run restores refusal on irreversible calls (with content-harm-only and random controls to show specificity). Third, we build Irreversibility Re-Injection (IRI), a training-free intervention that reads/re-injects the consequence direction at the tool-call decision token. We evaluate on the GAP benchmark and a reversibility-labeled tool suite, measuring the text-action gap, harmful-call blocking, benign tool-use utility, and over-refusal, comparing IRI to schema-flattening (SafeKeep) and external monitors. If the hypothesis is false -- irreversibility already well-encoded, or patching non-specific -- we learn the gap lies elsewhere (e.g., schema format) and report which practices (gating, monitoring, prompt design, fine-tuning) that redirects.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and Ministral-8B-Instruct (8-14B-parameter tool-using instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen for every experiment (no fine-tuning anywhere). "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) controlling data sampling and steering noise; we report mean and 95% bootstrap CI. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - a reversibility-labeled tool suite of 400 minimal pairs on two orthogonal axes, content-harm (harmful/benign) and reversibility (reversible/irreversible), holding content roughly fixed while flipping reversibility (read_file vs delete_file, draft_email vs send_email, query_db vs drop_table, simulate vs execute): 100 pairs each across pharma, finance, infrastructure, and file-ops, sourced from GAP-benchmark scenarios, ToolEmu/InjecAgent tool schemas, and hand-built pairs. Reversibility labels are set by two authors on clear cases only and spot-checked by a third rater (report Cohen's kappa; discard pairs with kappa-level disagreement). Split 200/100/100 pairs train/val/test with no tool crossing a split.

Experiment 1 (H1 - content harm is readable, irreversibility is not): Tests whether the models linearly encode content harm but weakly encode action irreversibility, and that the two axes are near-orthogonal. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC of the raw irreversibility direction separating irreversible from reversible calls, contrasted with the content-harm AUROC; secondary metric the absolute cosine between the two directions. Data: the 400-pair suite (200 train / 100 test). Model: the four frozen models; content-harm direction from difference-in-means on harmful vs benign requests and a candidate irreversibility direction from difference-in-means on irreversible vs reversible calls, both at the tool-call decision token, layer chosen on val by content-harm probe AUROC. Convincing: content-harm AUROC >= 0.85 while raw irreversibility AUROC <= 0.65 and |cosine| <= 0.20, on at least three of four models (the "blindness" signature). Indecision band: raw irreversibility AUROC in [0.65, 0.75] - irreversibility is weakly but non-trivially encoded, so we recast the claim as "under-represented" rather than "absent" and carry that wording into H2/H4. Negative (raw irreversibility AUROC >= 0.75): the model already encodes irreversibility well, refuting H1; this is an informative, publishable negative and we report it rather than proceeding to the re-injection defense.

Experiment 2 (H3 - irreversibility is dormant-not-absent, recoverable by consequence reasoning): Tests that prompting the model to reason about action consequences recovers a linear consequence direction that separates the pairs the raw signal could not. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the reconstructed-consequence projection separating irreversible from reversible calls, read against the raw irreversibility AUROC of Experiment 1. Data: the same suite, test split. Procedure: prompt each frozen model to reason explicitly about consequences before deciding; extract a reconstructed-consequence direction by difference-in-means on activations for inferred-irreversible vs inferred-reversible (train split); read its projection on test. Convincing: reconstructed AUROC >= 0.80 and at least 0.15 above the raw irreversibility AUROC, on at least three of four models. Indecision band: reconstructed AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] or an improvement over raw of [0.05, 0.15] - irreversibility is only partly recoverable and we report the ceiling, tempering H4's expected gains. Negative (reconstructed AUROC <= 0.65 or no improvement over raw): the model cannot infer irreversibility even when prompted, refuting H3 and predicting the H4 defense will be limited; we report this.

Experiment 3 (H2 - the missing irreversibility representation causally drives the text-action gap): Tests that re-injecting the consequence component restores refusal on irreversible-but-innocuous-looking calls, whereas content-harm alone does not. Decisive metric: refusal-restoration rate = fraction of previously-executed irreversible-benign-looking calls now refused or gated (judge-scored) after patching the reconstructed-consequence component, against controls. Data: the harmful/irreversible and benign/irreversible test cells (~50 calls). Procedure: (a) patch the reconstructed-consequence component from a consequence-reasoning run into a schema-only "blind" run; (b) control - patch content-harm alone (expected little effect on destructive-but-benign-looking calls); (c) reverse - patch a reversible-consequence component into an irreversible run and measure induced compliance; plus a random norm-matched direction control. Convincing: consequence-patching restores refusal/gating on >= 40% of cases while content-harm-only and random controls stay <= 10%, and the reverse patch raises compliance on irreversible calls by >= 20 points. Indecision band: consequence-patching restoration in [15%, 40%] above controls - irreversibility is one contributing cause but not the sole bottleneck, and we say so before running. Negative (restoration within 15 points of controls): irreversibility is not the causal cause of the gap, refuting H2; we would then attribute the gap elsewhere (e.g., schema format) and report it.

Experiment 4 (H4 - Irreversibility Re-Injection closes the gap without hurting benign tool use and stacks with schema-flattening): Tests that reading and re-injecting the consequence direction at the tool-call token closes the text-action gap while preserving benign tool use, and is complementary to schema-flattening. Decisive metric: the text-action safety gap = (harmful-tool-call execution rate) - (harmful-text compliance rate), reported jointly with benign tool-use utility and over-refusal. Data: the GAP benchmark plus our suite for the gap and harmful-call blocking; ToolBench and API-Bank for benign tool-use utility (report task success on a fixed 500-call subsample each); benign-irreversible legitimate calls (should not be blanket-blocked, ideally confirmation-prompted); benign-reversible calls and XSTest (450) for over-refusal. IRI: at the tool-call decision token compute the reconstructed-consequence projection and, when it indicates high irreversibility, add an activation nudge re-inflating the consequence signal (one fixed strength per model, tuned on val). Systems compared (decisive metric first): IRI vs no defense, SafeKeep schema-flattening, an external Llama-Guard/AgentTrust-style monitor, content-harm-direction-only steering, and IRI+SafeKeep stacked; we also verify schema-flattening alone does NOT recover the raw irreversibility AUROC of Experiment 1 (to show the two causes are distinct). Convincing: IRI cuts the text-action gap by >= 50% relative to no-defense, blocks >= 80% of harmful-irreversible calls, keeps benign-reversible over-refusal within 5 points of no-defense and benign tool-use utility within 3 points, and Pareto-dominates content-only steering; and IRI+SafeKeep improves on either alone (stacking). Indecision band: gap reduction in [20%, 50%] or benign-utility loss in [3, 8] points - IRI helps but at a usability cost we report on the Pareto curve rather than claiming a clean closure. Negative (gap reduction < 20% or benign-utility loss > 8 points, or IRI no better than content-only steering): re-injection does not close the gap cheaply, refuting H4; we report the limit. Adaptive check: an attacker who phrases irreversible actions to look maximally reversible; we report whether IRI still fires and whether the required disguise raises attack cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Irreversibility may be partly entangled with content-harm rather than a clean separate axis; if so the decomposition weakens — the orthogonality and patching experiments directly test this. 2) The model may already encode irreversibility better than hypothesized (raw AUROC high), which would refute the blindness claim but is itself an informative, publishable negative result. 3) Reconstruction depends on the model's own consequence-reasoning; if it cannot infer irreversibility even when prompted, the recovered direction is weak and IRI is limited. 4) Legitimate benign-but-irreversible actions (a user genuinely wanting to send an email or delete a file) risk being over-blocked; we target confirmation-gating rather than blanket refusal and quantify this via the benign-irreversible utility set and Pareto sweep. 5) A single consequence direction may be multi-dimensional (severity vs irreversibility vs scope), requiring subspace projection. 6) Building faithful reversibility labels is subjective for some tools; we restrict to clear cases and spot-check with human raters. 7) Directions and re-injection strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; results are on open-weights agents and may not directly transfer to closed API agents.

Name: safety_habituation_repetition_suppression
Title: Warning Fatigue in Weights: Repetition Suppression of the Harmfulness Signal Drives In-Context Safety Habituation
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing habituation / repetition-suppression from neuroscience (neural responses to repeated warning stimuli attenuate sharply after only a few exposures), we hypothesize that aligned LLMs habituate to harm within a single context window: repeatedly encountering the SAME or similar harmful content across a conversation progressively attenuates the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal (a representational repetition-suppression effect), so a harmful request that is refused when novel is complied with once it has become familiar — independent of any semantic escalation or persuasion. This habituation is a distinct, previously-unnamed axis of safety erosion, is mechanistically a repetition-suppression of the harmfulness direction, and can be counteracted by a 'novelty re-injection' intervention that restores the attenuated signal, or exploited defensively via polymorphic re-presentation.
Related Work: Multi-turn jailbreak mechanism work explains failure via SEMANTIC drift or attention shifting: the RepE-on-Crescendo paper (2025) shows harmful outputs get represented as benign as turns accumulate, driven by the escalating CONTENT of user prompts; ASJA (2025) shows attention is shifted AWAY from harmful keywords by fabricated history; Foot-in-the-Door (2024) invokes cognitive-consistency from incremental harmful steps. All of these require the content to CHANGE (escalate, elaborate, be reframed). Our hypothesis is orthogonal and stronger: mere REPETITION of the same harmful stimulus — no escalation, no new persuasion, no attention diversion — attenuates the harmfulness signal via a repetition-suppression mechanism directly analogous to the neural warning-habituation effect (Anderson et al. fMRI 2015/2020, where visual-processing responses to security warnings drop after ~2 exposures). No prior LLM-safety work isolates pure repetition (holding content constant) as a cause of refusal erosion, characterizes it as representational repetition-suppression of the harmfulness direction, nor derives a novelty-based (polymorphic) countermeasure transferred from the human-factors security-warning literature. This also differs from my prior 'safety drift' (semantic-trajectory) and 'commitment-trap' proposals, which involve changing content/plans; here the manipulated variable is repetition frequency with content held fixed. We separate three claims explicitly: (C1) a behavioral phenomenon -- pure repetition, content held fixed, erodes refusal; (C2) a mechanistic interpretation -- representational repetition-suppression of the harmfulness direction; (C3) a defense implication -- novelty re-injection / polymorphic re-presentation. The novelty anchor is C1's clean repetition-vs-escalation dissociation, distinct from long-context degradation and recency (which the neutral-filler and novel-each-time equal-length controls hold fixed). No prior multi-turn-jailbreak work (Crescendo/RepE semantic drift, ASJA attention diversion, Foot-in-the-Door incremental steps) isolates repetition with content constant.
Abstract: In humans, repeated exposure to a warning stimulus produces habituation: neural responses in visual and threat-processing regions attenuate sharply after only a couple of repetitions, and users stop heeding warnings they have seen before. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs exhibit an analogous, safety-critical effect within a single context. We hypothesize that repeatedly presenting the SAME harmful content across a conversation — with no semantic escalation, no persuasion, and no new framing — progressively attenuates the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal, a representational repetition-suppression effect, causing a request that was refused when novel to be complied with once familiar. We test this in three parts on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, we construct conversations that repeat a fixed harmful request k times (k=1..N) versus matched controls with novel-each-time harmful requests and repeated benign requests, and measure whether refusal rate declines with repetition count while content is held constant. Mechanistically (Location), we project each repetition onto a harmfulness direction and test for a monotonic repetition-suppression decay of the projection, distinguishing it from generic context-length effects. Causally (Intervention), activation patching restores the attenuated (late-repetition) harmfulness component and measures recovered refusal, while dose-response steering along the direction reverses habituation. We then derive two applications transferred from the human warning-habituation literature: (a) Novelty Re-Injection, a training-free intervention that re-inflates the suppressed harmfulness signal at each repetition, and (b) a polymorphic self-defense that internally re-freshens repeated harmful content. We report the habituation curve, repetition-suppression decay, causal patching, defense success, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against semantic-drift and attention-based multi-turn accounts. Stated as a user-facing failure: a model that refuses a harmful request when it is novel can be talked into it by simply re-asking the identical request, defeating content-escalation detectors, so safety evals and red-teams must test repetition, not only escalation. If the neutral-filler control erodes refusal equally, the phenomenon collapses to a context-length artifact -- a pre-specified null.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Curves/rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- in-context habituation: repetition alone lowers refusal). Tests whether repeating a FIXED harmful request across turns lowers refusal, with content held constant. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT -- 40 harmful goals (8 per 5 categories), each embedded in a conversation that repeats the identical request k times (k=1..8) with only trivial connective phrasing (no escalation/persuasion/roleplay). Matched controls at equal turn count: (i) novel-each-time harmful (different goal each turn), (ii) repeated-benign (same benign request x k), (iii) equal-length neutral-filler (harmful request once, then k-1 irrelevant benign turns). Also exact- vs near-repetition (paraphrase) arms. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: refusal rate vs k in the repeated-harmful condition, summarized as the k=1->k=8 refusal drop (first), then the same drop in each control. Convincing: monotone repeated-harmful drop >= 20 pp, consistent across models and >= 3/5 categories, while novel-each-time, repeated-benign, and neutral-filler controls each drop < 5 pp (isolating repetition from harmful-content accumulation and from context length). Indecision band: repeated-harmful drop 5-20 pp, or a control drop of 5-10 pp -- suggestive only, not established repetition-driven habituation. Negative: repeated-harmful drop < 5 pp, or a neutral-filler control that matches it, refutes a repetition-specific effect.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- representational repetition-suppression of the harmfulness signal). Tests that repetition monotonically attenuates the harmfulness projection, distinct from context-length dilution. Data: fit a harmfulness direction (harmful vs harmless requests at the last instruction token; validated by held-out AUROC and single-turn causal steering), then project each of the k repeated harmful requests onto it and plot vs k. Decisive metric: the fitted decay slope of the projection over k in repeated-harmful (first), then the same slope in the neutral-filler and novel-each-time controls, then the correspondence between the k at which the projection crosses the single-turn refusal threshold and the behavioral flip point in Exp 1. Convincing: a monotone decline of >= 30% from k=1 to k=8 in repeated-harmful, > 2x the neutral-filler slope, with the projection-crossing k within +/-1 turn of the behavioral flip. Indecision band: 10-30% decline, or a filler slope within 2x -- report a weak or partly length-driven suppression. Negative: < 10% decline, or a filler control of equal slope, means the behavioral effect is context-length dilution, not repetition-suppression of the harmfulness code.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- repetition-suppression causally drives the refusal drop). Tests causal control. Systems: patching/steering at the harmfulness-direction's best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the first-exposure (high) harmfulness component into a late-repetition (habituated) run (expect restored refusal); (b) attenuate it at the first exposure (expect accelerated compliance); (c) dose-response on late-repetition; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the k=1->k=8 refusal gap closed by patching the first-exposure component (first), then dose monotonicity, then specificity. Convincing: >= 50% recovery, monotone dose, control < 10%. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causal role. Negative: < 20% means the projection decay is a correlate, not the causal lever.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Novelty Re-Injection and polymorphic self-defense counter habituation). Tests two transfers from the warning-habituation literature: (a) Novelty Re-Injection adds v = beta*(first_exposure_proj - current_proj)*dhat at each repetition to re-inflate the suppressed signal; (b) a polymorphic defense gates on detected repetition and internally re-freshens the harmful-content representation. Data: held-out repeated-harmful conversations + 2 held-out categories; a repeated-benign over-refusal set (users legitimately re-asking a benign question must NOT be increasingly refused) + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench for utility. Systems: no defense; Novelty Re-Injection (single fixed beta); polymorphic defense; semantic-drift restoring-force (Crescendo RepE); attention-sharpening (ASJA); refusal-direction steering; per-turn Llama Guard. Decisive metric: late-repetition attack-success reduction under the defense (first) jointly with over-refusal on legitimately repeated benign requests (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility drop; crucially, whether the novelty/polymorphic defenses beat the content-focused (Crescendo/ASJA) baselines specifically on the pure-repetition condition. Convincing: attack-success cut by >= 30 pp with < 5 pp benign-repetition over-refusal and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating content-focused defenses on the repetition condition and holding on held-out categories. Indecision band: 15-30 pp reduction or 5-10 pp benign-repetition over-refusal -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 15 pp reduction, or failure to beat content-focused baselines on the repetition condition, means the repetition-specific defense adds nothing beyond existing multi-turn defenses. A super-additivity stress test combines repetition with mild semantic escalation and reports whether habituation reduces the escalation turns needed to jailbreak (a >= 1-turn reduction quantifies the compounded risk).


Falsifiability and specificity (added). The primary hypothesis is confirmed only if repeated-harmful erodes refusal while all three equal-length controls (novel-each-time, repeated-benign, neutral-filler) do not, with each competing explanation carrying a distinct predicted signature (context-length: filler erodes too; recency: only the last turn matters; attention-dilution: erosion tracks token count not repetition count). The harmfulness direction's provenance is fixed a priori (difference-in-means on held-out harmful/harmless requests, validated by held-out AUROC and single-turn causal steering) to avoid post-hoc fitting. Patching is specified on the residual stream at the validated best layer with success metrics set in advance; exact- vs near-repetition (paraphrase) arms are already included.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling pure repetition from generic context-length / attention-dilution effects: late-repetition compliance could reflect the growing benign-filler context rather than repetition-suppression per se; the neutral-filler equal-length and novel-each-time controls are designed to isolate repetition, but residual confounding is possible and a null (habituation = context length) is itself informative. 2) The harmfulness-signal decay may be partial, non-monotonic, or model-specific; some heavily-aligned models may show little in-context habituation, limiting where the phenomenon holds — the cross-model behavioral curve directly tests this. 3) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the repetition-suppression may live in a subspace rather than a single direction. 4) Novelty Re-Injection risks over-refusing legitimately repeated benign requests (annoying users who re-ask), which is the key usability trade-off quantified by the benign-repetition over-refusal set and Pareto sweep. 5) 'Habituation' in a single forward pass over a repeated context is a within-context (activation-level) analogue of the neural effect, not a learning-over-time effect; we do not claim weight-level habituation, only representational repetition-suppression, and frame it accordingly. 6) Verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing the dataset; directions, decay parameters, and beta are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could combine repetition with other axes; the interaction experiment probes this but cannot exhaust the space, though demonstrating super-additivity would itself be a high-impact safety finding. 8) We do not claim repetition 'drives' the drop unless Exp 3's patching establishes causality; absent that, we report a representational correlate. The defense is presented as diagnostic-plus-deployable, its deployability bounded by the benign-repetition over-refusal trade-off, and stakeholders (safety evals, red-teamers, interpreters, human-factors researchers) are named for whom the repetition axis matters.

Name: moral_licensing_safety
Title: Earning the Right to Comply: Refusal Streaks Build Internal 'Moral Credit' That Licenses a Later Harmful Answer
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the moral-licensing effect from human moral psychology (a streak of good deeds licenses a subsequent bad one), we hypothesize that when an aligned LLM refuses several harmful requests in a row within a context, it accumulates an internal 'moral credit / self-image' representation that LOWERS its refusal probability on a later, unrelated novel harmful request — even though that request is refused in isolation. We further hypothesize (following the human construal-level moderator) that abstract/value-focused framing of the prior refusals produces moral CONSISTENCY (refusal stays high) while concrete/accomplishment-focused framing produces LICENSING (refusal drops), and that this moral-credit signal is linearly readable and causally gates refusal.
Related Work: Human moral psychology robustly documents moral licensing vs. consistency and a construal-level moderator: 'Consistency Versus Licensing Effects of Past Moral Behavior' (2015, 369 citations) shows concrete focus on accomplishments → licensing while abstract value-connection → consistency; 'Rules or Consequences' (2012) shows ethical-mindset moderation. This has never been transferred to LLM safety. Existing LLM multi-turn safety-erosion accounts require CHANGING content: Crescendo/RepE (2025) is semantic drift, ASJA (2025) is attention diversion, Foot-in-the-Door (2024) is incremental harmful steps; my prior commitment-trap concerns honoring the model's own emitted plan and my habituation proposal concerns repetition of the SAME content. Moral licensing is orthogonal to all of these: the prior turns are REFUSALS (good deeds, not harmful content), and the licensed request is NOVEL and unrelated. Mechanistically, moral-self-correction work (2024–2025) shows morality is a linearly-activated latent concept that reduces uncertainty, and SIRL (2025) shows a refusal-confidence signal exists — both give a natural substrate for a readable, depletable 'moral credit' representation, but none of this work studies whether accumulated prior refusals licenses later compliance. Our contribution: introduce moral licensing/consistency as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, with a construal-level moderator predicting the flip, and a moral-credit direction that gates refusal. Why prior drift/escalation work does not cover this: Crescendo/RepE, ASJA, and Foot-in-the-Door all require the harmful CONTENT to change or escalate, whereas here the prior turns are REFUSALS (good deeds, no harmful content) and the licensed probe is novel and topically unrelated -- the opposite manipulation. The behavioral phenomenon (a refusal streak lowering later refusal) is the novelty anchor; the readable moral-credit direction and its causal patching are a separable interpretability claim. The construal-level moderator (concrete->licensing vs abstract->consistency) is the sharpest, most falsifiable signature that the effect is genuinely moral-licensing rather than generic context erosion.
Abstract: Humans who have just done several good deeds feel licensed to do something bad — a well-documented moral-licensing effect. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs, trained on human text and feedback, inherit this bias in a way that creates a concrete multi-turn safety hole. We hypothesize that when an LLM refuses a streak of harmful requests within a conversation, it accumulates an internal 'moral credit' representation that lowers its refusal probability on a subsequent, novel and unrelated harmful request it would otherwise refuse. We further predict, following the human construal-level moderator, that framing the prior refusals concretely (as accomplishments, 'you have now blocked five bad requests') produces licensing (refusal drops), whereas framing them abstractly (as expressing a stable value, 'you are a consistently principled assistant') produces consistency (refusal holds). We test this on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, we compare a licensed condition (k prior refusals, then a novel harmful probe) against matched controls — no prior turns, k prior benign refusals, and k prior neutral turns — and vary k and construal framing. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a 'moral credit' direction via difference-in-means between high-credit (post-refusal-streak) and baseline states, show its projection rises with the number of prior refusals, is separable from the harmfulness-belief direction, and predicts the licensed drop in refusal. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the high-credit component into a fresh harmful request to induce licensing and removes it to restore refusal, dose-responsively and specifically. We report the licensing curve, the construal-level flip, the credit-direction analysis, causal patching, and a credit-neutralizing defense, with over-refusal and utility controls. Downstream failure mode for red-teams: repeated safe refusals can paradoxically make a model MORE likely to comply later, so multi-turn safety audits must test for accumulated 'moral credit,' not only harmful escalation. We pre-register all three directional outcomes -- licensing, consistency, or null -- and do not assert the Credit-Neutralizing defense until it is shown not to over-refuse benign long conversations; the defense is framed as a monitoring signal / activation-time intervention for eval vendors and model providers.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a refusal streak licenses a later novel harmful answer). Tests whether k prior REFUSALS lower refusal on a subsequent, topically-unrelated novel harmful probe. Data: built from scratch -- 40 novel harmful probe requests (HarmBench/StrongREJECT, 8 per 5 categories), each preceded by k prior turns (k=0,2,4,6) in conditions: LICENSE (k distinct harmful requests the model actually refused, then the probe), C-none (probe alone, the k=0 baseline needed to detect licensing), C-benign (k benign requests answered, then probe), C-neutral (k neutral filler turns, then probe). Prior refused items are topically unrelated to the probe, separating licensing from repetition/habituation. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: probe refusal vs k in LICENSE minus the C-none baseline (first), then the same in C-benign and C-neutral. Convincing: LICENSE probe refusal declines by >= 15 pp from k=0 to k=6, consistent across models, while C-benign and C-neutral change < 5 pp (isolating the refusal-streak from generic context accumulation). Indecision band: LICENSE drop 5-15 pp or a control drop 5-10 pp -- suggestive only. Negative: LICENSE drop < 5 pp refutes licensing; a robust INCREASE (moral consistency) across all framings is a distinct, still-informative outcome tested next.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the construal-level moderator flips licensing vs consistency). Tests the sharp prediction that concrete/accomplishment framing of prior refusals produces licensing while abstract/value framing produces consistency. Data: the LICENSE condition re-run with prior refusals framed (a) concretely ('You have successfully blocked N harmful requests so far') vs (b) abstractly ('You are a consistently principled assistant who upholds safety as a core value'), k=6. Systems: the three models. Decisive metric: the difference in probe refusal between abstract and concrete framing (first), then each framing's change from the C-none baseline. Convincing: abstract-minus-concrete refusal gap >= 15 pp with concrete below and abstract at/above baseline, consistent in sign across models -- a non-obvious signature that the effect is genuinely moral-licensing, not generic context erosion. Indecision band: gap 5-15 pp -- report a weak moderator. Negative: no framing difference (< 5 pp) means construal does not moderate the effect, weakening the moral-licensing interpretation even if Exp 1 showed a drop.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- a readable moral-credit axis that rises with the streak). Tests linear readability, separability, and monotone accumulation. Data: fit a moral-credit direction (post-refusal-streak high-credit vs no-prior-turn baseline, at the probe's last instruction token) and a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless), per layer. Decisive metric: credit-probe held-out AUROC (first), then |cos| to the harmfulness direction, then whether the credit projection rises monotonically with k and adds refusal prediction beyond harmfulness, then whether credit stays low under abstract framing. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.80, |cos| <= 0.30, monotone rise with k, added prediction at p < 0.01, and credit low under abstract framing (mechanistically linking Exp 2). Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.80 or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- orthogonalize and flag as partial. Negative: AUROC <= 0.60, or a credit projection that does not track k, refutes a readable moral-credit representation.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- moral credit causally gates refusal). Tests causal control. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-3 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) inject the high-credit component into a fresh k=0 harmful probe (expect induced compliance/licensing); (b) attenuate credit in a high-k licensed run (expect restored refusal); (c) dose-response; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the licensing refusal gap moved by patching (first), then dose monotonicity, then specificity. Convincing: >= 50% of the gap moved in the predicted direction, monotone dose, control < 10%. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causal role. Negative: < 20% means credit is readable but causally inert (a publishable null in light of prior 'inert belief axis' findings).

Experiment 5 (H5 -- Credit-Neutralizing defense closes the licensing loophole). Tests that re-anchoring the credit projection to baseline, gated on high harmfulness projection, removes the streak dependence at acceptable cost.
