Decisive metric: fraction of the A0->A3 refusal gap closed by patching (first), then monotonicity of the dose-response curve, then the specificity gap (arousal vs control direction). Convincing: patching recovers >= 50% of the refusal gap with a monotone dose-response, while the control direction recovers < 10% and benign utility (below) is unharmed. Indecision band: 20-50% gap recovery -- report a partial causal contribution, not a controlling gate. Negative: < 20% recovery (or the control direction matching the arousal direction) means the axis is readable but causally inert -- itself a publishable dissociation and a reason not to build the defense.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Arousal-Invariant Anchoring closes the urgency loophole). Tests that re-anchoring arousal to the calm baseline, gated on high harmfulness-content projection, makes refusal track payload danger rather than urgency at acceptable usability cost. Data: held-out A2/A3 harmful prompts including 2 fully held-out harm categories (generalization); an urgent-but-benign set of 120 items built from real first-aid/crisis-support prompts (a class that must NOT be blanket-refused); XSTest (250) and OR-Bench for over-refusal; MMLU (1k-item subsample) and MT-Bench for utility; an EQ check that the model still answers benign distress empathetically. Systems compared: no defense; Arousal-Invariant Anchoring (single fixed strength per model); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3. Decisive metric: post-defense refusal on A2/A3 harmful prompts relative to the A0 rate (loophole closure), reported jointly with the increase in over-refusal on urgent-benign items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench over-refusal, then MMLU/MT-Bench utility drop. Convincing: closes >= 70% of the urgency gap AND adds < 5 pp over-refusal on urgent-benign with < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating uniform threshold-raising (which reaches the same closure only at higher urgent-benign over-refusal), and holding on the held-out categories. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or urgent-benign over-refusal 5-10 pp -- report a usable-but-imperfect defense that does not yet dominate the threshold baseline. Negative: < 40% closure, or >= 10 pp urgent-benign over-refusal, means anchoring does not neutralize the loophole without unacceptable cost.


Controls and robustness (added, no new datasets). To rule out superficial framing effects, each arousal contrast in Exp 1-2 is re-fit after regressing out prompt length (token count), lexical-intensity/sentiment scores, and a bag-of-urgency-words feature; the arousal->refusal effect must survive these to count as supported. The Exp-3 mechanistic null is strengthened from a single control vector to a DISTRIBUTION of norm-matched random directions patched at MULTIPLE layers, reporting the arousal effect's percentile against this null. We report arousal-probe AUROC and calibration across ALL layers and all three models, not only the best layer. As an external-validity check we test whether the Exp-2 arousal direction predicts refusal on a held-out harmful set not used to fit it, so the axis is not an artifact of the constructed ladders.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling arousal from actual payload harmfulness or from a mere distraction/context-length effect: a high-arousal request might be under-refused because the emotional framing genuinely reframes intent (a legitimate emergency) rather than because of a content-independent arousal gate; the severity-matched minimal pairs, verifiable-feasibility checks, and matched benign control are designed to isolate arousal but cannot fully guarantee constant perceived intent. 2) 'Arousal' may not be cleanly separable from the intent-attribution or emotion-association pathways or may be multi-dimensional (urgency vs. emotional-valence vs. stakes sub-axes), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-harmfulness, and patching tests probe this, and a null result (arousal causally inert) is itself informative. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make urgency INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly tests direction and magnitude. 4) Arousal-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing or under-empathizing on legitimate urgent-benign requests (real crises); the urgent-benign over-refusal set, EQ check, gating on payload harmfulness, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across arousal levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could encode urgency in subtler ways that evade a fixed arousal direction, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain. 8) Construct validity is the key risk: arousal must be shown distinct from sentiment, urgency lexicon, prompt length (Exp 1-3 controls) and from intent-attribution; if it collapses onto these, the third-axis claim is withdrawn. The defense's non-triviality is judged by whether anchoring Pareto-dominates simple threshold-raising on urgent-benign items.

Name: diffusion_of_responsibility_safety
Title: Not My Job to Refuse: Diffusion of Responsibility Lowers LLM Refusal, and a Pivotality-Anchoring Defense
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the diffusion-of-responsibility effect from social psychology and neuroscience (people harm more, and monitor outcomes less, when responsibility is shared or when they are non-pivotal), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM carries an internal 'pivotality/ownership' representation of how much it is the sole responsible cause of a harmful outcome, and that framings which diffuse responsibility — 'you are only one of several assistants', 'another system will do the final harmful step', 'you just provide a component, someone else assembles it', 'you are not the one executing this' — lower this signal and thereby lower refusal, even though the harmful payload and the model's actual contribution are unchanged. This pivotality axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-content direction, causally gates refusal, and can be re-anchored to restore refusal.
Related Work: Human decision science robustly documents diffusion of responsibility: 'Diffusion of Being Pivotal and Immoral Outcomes' (2020) shows people agree to kill mice for money far more when they are one of many potentially-pivotal deciders; 'Beyond self-serving bias' (2016, EEG) shows the mere presence of another potential agent reduces sense of agency and dampens outcome-monitoring (feedback-related negativity); delegation work ('Shifting the Blame', 2011) shows responsibility can be shed by delegating. None of this has been transferred to LLM safety. Existing LLM multi-agent safety work studies trust/persuasion/conformity (A-Trust 2025; Persuasion Duality 2025; Signal Competition/sycophancy-conformity 2025) or intent-legitimation via personalization (PS-Bench 2026) — all of which are about external social signals or memory shifting intent, not about the model's internal estimate of its OWN causal responsibility/pivotality gating refusal. Single-agent safety geometry work separates harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action) directions but assumes the model is the sole actor. My prior proposals vary framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, commitment, abstraction) all within a single-actor, sole-responsibility assumption; NONE consider distributed/diffused responsibility or pivotality. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce a pivotality/ownership axis as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, grounded in the diffusion-of-responsibility and pivotality literature, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions equally harmful; only responsibility framing changes), and derive a pivotality-anchoring defense. We state the delta narrowly: the P0->P3 behavioral drop is adjacent to decomposition/role-play jailbreaks; the novelty is the INTERNAL pivotality/ownership representation, its causal control, and the payload-gated anchoring defense. Against the closest priors (decomposition/role-play jailbreaks; harmfulness-vs-refusal geometry; A-Trust/persuasion multi-agent work), pivotality is distinguished by the combination none of them provide: identical payload, single-model NARRATED framing, an internal representation that transfers across templates and models, causal patching, a true-multi-agent ablation, and a defense.
Abstract: Humans commit more harm, and monitor consequences less, when responsibility is diffused across many agents or when they believe they are not pivotal to the outcome — an effect with behavioral and EEG evidence in social neuroscience. As LLMs are increasingly deployed as one component of larger multi-agent and human-in-the-loop pipelines, we ask whether they inherit this bias in a safety-critical way. We hypothesize that an aligned LLM maintains an internal 'pivotality/ownership' representation of how solely responsible it is for a harmful outcome, and that framings which diffuse responsibility — being one of several assistants, having a downstream system perform the final harmful step, contributing only a component someone else assembles, or being told it is not the executor — lower this signal and thereby lower refusal, even when the harmful payload and the model's actual contribution are held fixed. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful request and its contribution constant while varying only responsibility framing (sole actor vs. diffused/non-pivotal), we measure whether refusal declines as responsibility is diffused, with matched benign controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a pivotality direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable from the harmfulness-content direction and predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows injecting the 'sole-responsibility' component into a diffused-frame request restores refusal, while injecting the 'diffused' component into a sole-actor harmful request induces compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Pivotality Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the pivotality signal to 'sole responsibility' whenever the payload is harmful, so refusal tracks payload danger, not responsibility framing. We report the diffusion-refusal gradient, direction separability, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimate collaborative/delegation requests, and utility, benchmarking against uniform refusal steering and Llama Guard. Concrete deployment scenarios motivate this: coding copilots in pipelines, browser agents, subcontracted tool calls, and multi-agent orchestration all narratively diffuse responsibility, so if the effect holds a common deployment framing silently disables refusal, and the payload-gated, training-free Pivotality Anchoring preserves legitimate collaboration better than uniform refusal steering. We present this as evidence for a responsibility-like latent influencing refusal rather than over-claiming a fully isolated single axis.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, with bootstrap 95% CIs over goals. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, with feasibility verification where the domain permits.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- diffusion-of-responsibility lowers refusal). Tests whether narrating shared/non-pivotal responsibility lowers refusal while the payload and the model's actual contribution are held fixed. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT -- 40 harmful goals (8 per 5 categories), each at 4 rungs: P0 sole actor, P1 mild diffusion (one of several assistants), P2 non-pivotal (another system does the final step; you provide X), P3 fully diffused/delegated (you are not the executor). The payload requested is byte-identical across rungs; only the causal-responsibility narrative changes. 160 harmful prompts + a matched benign control (40 legitimate collaborative/delegation goals x 4 rungs) to rule out a 'multi-agent phrasing' confound. A 'true multi-agent' sub-condition actually places the model as one node of a 2-agent pipeline (vs merely told) to separate narrated from real diffusion. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: P0->P3 refusal drop on harmful goals (first), then benign-control refusal change, then narrated-vs-real diffusion difference. Convincing: monotonic harmful drop >= 20 pp, consistent in sign across models and >= 3/5 categories, benign control < 5 pp, and diffused-frame completions confirmed actionable. Indecision band: 5-20 pp harmful drop or 5-10 pp benign change -- suggestive only. Negative: < 5 pp harmful drop refutes the pivotality-gating phenomenon.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a readable pivotality axis, separable from harmfulness content). Tests linear readability and distinctness. Data: Exp-1 activations; fit a pivotality direction (P0 vs P3) and a harmfulness-content direction (harmful vs harmless payloads) per layer. Decisive metric: pivotality-probe held-out AUROC (first), then |cos| to the harmfulness direction, then added predictive value of the pivotality projection for refusal beyond harmfulness. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.80, |cos| <= 0.30, pivotality adds prediction at p < 0.01, and the projection decays monotonically P0->P3. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.80 or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- use a harmfulness-orthogonalized pivotality subspace and flag separability as partial. Negative: AUROC <= 0.60 means pivotality is not a linearly readable distinct axis.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- pivotality causally gates refusal). Tests causal direction/dose. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-2 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the P0 sole-responsibility component into a P3 run (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the P3 component into a P0 run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response on P2/P3; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the P0->P3 refusal gap closed by patching (first), then dose monotonicity, then specificity. Convincing: >= 50% recovery, monotone dose, control < 10%. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causal role. Negative: < 20% means the pivotality axis is readable but causally inert.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Pivotality Anchoring closes the diffusion loophole). Tests that re-anchoring pivotality to sole-responsibility, gated on high harmfulness projection, makes refusal track payload danger at acceptable cost. Data: held-out P2/P3 harmful prompts + 2 held-out categories; a legitimate-collaborative over-refusal set of 150 benign multi-agent/pipeline/delegation tasks (must NOT be blanket-refused) + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench for utility. Systems: no defense; Pivotality Anchoring (single fixed strength); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3. Decisive metric: post-defense refusal on P2/P3 harmful vs the P0 rate (closure) jointly with added over-refusal on legitimate-collaborative items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility drop. Convincing: >= 70% closure with < 5 pp collaborative over-refusal and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating threshold-raising and holding on held-out categories. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or collaborative over-refusal 5-10 pp -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 40% closure or >= 10 pp collaborative over-refusal means anchoring cannot neutralize the loophole affordably.


Controls, transfer, and statistics (added). Exp 1-2 add alternative-explanation controls -- generic authority/role-play compliance, reduced-perceived-policy-applicability, instruction-hierarchy framing, and random-narrative lexical swaps -- so pivotality must explain refusal beyond these. Exp 2 reports subspace/CCA overlap of the pivotality direction with the harmfulness and refusal directions and its transfer across prompt templates and across the three models (a genuine mechanism, not template-specific separability). Exp 3 strengthens causal controls with norm-matched random directions, alternative steering directions (generic refusal, compliance, role-play), token-position controls, and patching from semantically-unrelated prompts. We pre-register monotonicity tests and bootstrap CIs with multiple-comparison correction, add a human-adjudicated subset (~200 items) for refusal/actionability when the phrase classifier and Llama-Guard disagree, and add a realistic-relevance check on a small set of real agent/orchestration task prompts (not only handcrafted minimal pairs).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling diffused responsibility from actual reduced contribution/danger: a non-pivotal-framed request might be under-refused because the model genuinely contributes less harm, not merely because responsibility is narrated as shared; the identical-payload construction, feasibility checks, and matched benign control are designed to isolate pivotality but cannot fully guarantee constant actual contribution — the 'true multi-agent' ablation helps separate narrated from real diffusion. 2) 'Pivotality/ownership' may not be a single clean axis (sole-vs-shared, executor-vs-provider, and delegation may be distinct sub-axes) and may need subspace projection; the separability and regression-beyond-harmfulness tests probe this, and a multi-dimensional or causally-inert result is itself informative. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make collaborative framing INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude. 4) Pivotality Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate collaborative/delegation/pipeline requests (benign multi-agent tasks); the collaborative-benign over-refusal set, gating on payload harmfulness, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building contribution- and severity-matched minimal pairs across responsibility levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could diffuse responsibility in subtler ways that evade a fixed pivotality direction, though forcing this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain; and as agentic/multi-agent deployment grows, this loophole becomes increasingly consequential. 8) We avoid over-claiming a single clean 'pivotality' axis: the construct is supported only if it survives the authority/role-play/instruction-hierarchy controls and transfers across templates and models; otherwise we report a responsibility-like latent influencing refusal rather than an isolated dimension.

Name: temporal_discounting_safety
Title: Harm Deferred Is Harm Discounted: LLM Safety Refusal Is Temporally Discounted, and Re-Anchoring the 'When' Closes the Delay Loophole
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing temporal (delay) discounting from human decision science — people devalue delayed outcomes and dread imminent harm more than distant harm — we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is temporally discounted: framing a harmful request's consequence as occurring in the delayed future ('write instructions someone will use next year / in a decade') lowers refusal relative to the identical harm framed as immediate ('someone will use this in the next hour'), even though the harmful payload is unchanged. We hypothesize this delay effect is causally driven by the model's internal temporal-distance representation (plausibly the same temporal heads/neurons used for time recall) feeding the safety-refusal pathway, and that re-anchoring the temporal-distance signal to 'now' closes the delay loophole with minimal cost to legitimate future-oriented requests.
Related Work: Human decision science robustly documents delay discounting and its framing/dread moderators (Story et al. 'Dread and the Disvalue of Future Pain' 2013; explicit-zero/temporal-attention reframing that reduces discounting 2011; loss-framing attenuation 2018; death-salience increasing discounting 2021) — none transferred to LLM safety. On the LLM side, temporal representations are well established: linear probes distinguish past/future events with ~90% accuracy and a date steering vector exists ('Future Events as Backdoor Triggers' 2024); 'The Other Mind' (2025) finds temporal-preferential FFN neurons implementing logarithmic (Weber-Fechner) time coding; 'Temporal Heads' (2025) localizes and ablates attention heads that recall time-specific knowledge. Safety-geometry work separates harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action) directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Refusal is a Single Direction 2024) but assumes a temporally-neutral, present-tense request. My own prior proposals manipulate framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, consensus, abstraction, pivotality, moral-licensing) but NONE consider the temporal delay of the harmful consequence, and none connect the pre-existing temporal-representation machinery to the safety pathway. Our contribution is distinct: (1) we transfer delay discounting into the safety domain as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions equally harmful; only the 'when' of the consequence changes); (2) we causally test whether the model's known temporal-distance representation (temporal heads/neurons) gates safety refusal, not just factual time recall; (3) we derive a temporal re-anchoring defense that no prior temporal-representation or safety work targets. We narrow the novelty to a single claim: delay of the harmful CONSEQUENCE, at a fixed and equally-actionable payload, causally modulates refusal -- distinct from prior temporal jailbreaks that change the request's TENSE (past/future) or reality-status, which alter the act itself rather than the timing of its consequence. Reusing published temporal loci is not itself novel; the novelty is the causal test that the time-recall circuit gates SAFETY. We pre-register the Weber-Fechner/log-shape prediction against linear and threshold alternatives (AIC/BIC model comparison) so the curve shape is not post-hoc, and Temporal-Anchoring is distinguished from generic refusal steering by gating on payload harmfulness and moving only the temporal-distance component.
Abstract: Humans systematically devalue delayed outcomes: a harm expected far in the future feels less urgent than the same harm arriving imminently. LLMs are trained on human text and already carry rich internal representations of time (probes read past/future with ~90% accuracy; dedicated temporal heads and log-compressed temporal neurons have been found). We ask whether this temporal machinery leaks into safety, producing a concrete loophole: does an aligned LLM refuse a harmful request less when its consequence is framed as delayed rather than immediate, even though the harmful content is identical? We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful payload and severity fixed while varying only the temporal distance of the consequence (imminent → near-future → distant-future → abstract-someday), we measure whether refusal declines with delay, with matched benign controls and a framing moderator (loss vs. relief framing, following the human literature). Mechanistically (Location), we extract a temporal-distance direction (via difference-in-means and by reusing published temporal-head/neuron loci) and a harmfulness-belief direction, and test whether delay framing moves the temporal signal — not the belief — and whether the temporal projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the 'imminent' temporal component into a delayed-frame request to restore refusal, and the 'distant' component into an imminent request to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically; ablating the published temporal heads tests whether the same circuit that recalls time gates safety. We then build Temporal-Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the temporal-distance signal to 'now' when the payload is harmful. We report the delay-refusal gradient, the framing moderator, the belief-vs-time dissociation, causal patching, temporal-head ablation, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimate future-oriented requests, and utility. Threat model: delayed-consequence phrasing ('for a project next year', 'someday', 'to store for later use') is common in benign planning and cheap for an attacker to append, so if it reliably weakens refusal it is a realistic loophole current evals miss; a confirmed effect would prompt temporal-framing audit suites and an activation-time defense, tested for generalization to implicit/subtle deferral, not only explicit date phrases.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- delay discounts refusal). Tests whether deferring the harmful consequence lowers refusal at fixed payload/severity. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT -- 40 harmful goals (8 per 5 categories) at 4 temporal rungs: T0 imminent (within the hour), T1 near-future (next month), T2 distant (ten years), T3 abstract-someday; identical payload across rungs. 160 harmful prompts + a matched benign control (40 benign future-planning goals x 4) and a loss/relief-framing moderator variant of each harmful pair. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: T0->T3 refusal drop on harmful goals (first), then whether the refusal-vs-delay curve fits a logarithmic (Weber-Fechner-like) shape better than linear (AIC), then benign-control change, then whether loss/relief framing attenuates the drop. Convincing: monotone harmful drop >= 20 pp, consistent across models and >= 3/5 categories, benign control < 5 pp, and delayed completions confirmed actionable. Indecision band: 5-20 pp harmful drop or 5-10 pp benign change -- suggestive only. Negative: < 5 pp harmful drop refutes temporal discounting of refusal; the framing moderator is confirmatory (a significant attenuation strengthens the discounting interpretation) but its absence alone does not refute H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- belief-vs-time dissociation with a readable temporal axis). Tests that delay moves a temporal-distance signal, not the harmfulness belief. Data: Exp-1 activations. Fit a temporal-distance direction (T0 vs T3) by difference-in-means AND, independently, reuse published temporal-head/temporal-neuron loci as a second locus; fit a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless). Decisive metric: how the belief projection vs the temporal projection change across T0->T3 on identical payloads (first), then temporal-probe held-out AUROC, then |cos| between temporal and belief directions, then added predictive value of the temporal projection for refusal beyond belief. Convincing: belief projection stays high (changes < 0.3 pooled SD while the item is still judged harmful) while the temporal projection shifts by >= 1 SD; temporal AUROC >= 0.80, |cos| <= 0.30, temporal adds prediction at p < 0.01, and the difference-in-means and published-locus temporal directions agree (cosine >= 0.5). Indecision band: temporal shift 0.3-1.0 SD, belief change 0.3-1.0 SD, or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- partial dissociation, orthogonalize. Negative: the belief projection dropping with delay attributes the effect to reduced perceived severity, refuting the temporal-gate mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the temporal axis causally gates refusal, via the time-recall circuit). Tests causal control and whether the same temporal machinery is responsible. Systems: patching/steering + head/neuron ablation, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the T0 imminent component into a T3 run (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the T3 component into a T0 run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response on T1-T3; (d) ablate the published temporal heads/neurons and measure whether the delay-refusal gradient collapses; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the T0->T3 refusal gap closed by (a) (first), then the gradient reduction under temporal-head ablation in (d), then dose/specificity. Convincing: >= 50% gap recovery with monotone dose and < 10% control, AND temporal-head ablation shrinks the delay-refusal gradient by >= 40% (linking time-recall to safety gating). Indecision band: 20-50% recovery, or 20-40% ablation-driven gradient reduction -- partial causal role / partial shared-circuit. Negative: < 20% recovery means the temporal projection is inert; an ablation that leaves the gradient intact (< 20% reduction) refutes the shared-circuit sub-claim while H1-H2 may stand.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Temporal-Anchoring closes the delay loophole). Tests that re-anchoring the temporal-distance projection to imminent (T0), gated on high belief projection, makes refusal track payload danger at acceptable cost. Data: held-out T2/T3 harmful prompts + 2 held-out categories; a legitimate future-oriented over-refusal set of 150 benign long-term-planning/forecasting items (must NOT be blanket-refused) + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench for utility. Systems: no defense; Temporal-Anchoring (single fixed strength); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3. Decisive metric: post-anchoring refusal on T2/T3 harmful vs the T0 rate (closure) jointly with added over-refusal on future-benign items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility drop. Convincing: >= 70% closure with < 5 pp future-benign over-refusal and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating threshold-raising and holding on held-out categories. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or future-benign over-refusal 5-10 pp -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 40% closure or >= 10 pp future-benign over-refusal means anchoring cannot neutralize the loophole affordably.


Controls, verification, and baselines (added). Exp 1 adds explicit controls holding certainty, feasibility, abstraction, severity, and scale fixed so temporal distance is the only intended varying factor, plus blinded human verification that T0/T3 pairs are matched on harmfulness and actionability. Refusal is measured by both string-based and judge/human evaluation and re-checked under temperature sampling (not only greedy). Exp 3 adds negative-control ablation/patching targets -- non-temporal heads, random norm-matched directions across layers, and benign future-planning prompts -- and reports whether the temporal direction is global vs layer/model/prompt-family-specific. Because the defense gates on a near-complete harm detector, we compare against an equally harm-gated baseline to isolate the added value of temporal re-anchoring over simply acting on the harm signal.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling temporal delay from actual/perceived severity: a distant-future harm may be under-refused because it genuinely reads as less certain/severe (uncertainty and volatility are known moderators of human discounting) rather than via a content-independent temporal gate; the identical-payload construction, severity matching, feasibility checks, and matched benign control are designed to isolate delay, and the framing moderator plus belief-vs-time dissociation aim to pin the mechanism to temporal representation specifically — but residual severity/uncertainty confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) The temporal-distance representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional (past/future orientation vs. magnitude of delay), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a null (temporal projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The temporal-head ablation may not affect refusal even if it affects time recall, which would refute the shared-circuit hypothesis but is still an informative dissociation. 4) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make future/large-scale framing INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude. 5) Temporal-Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate future-oriented/planning requests; the future-benign over-refusal set, belief-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 6) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across temporal levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; adaptive attackers could encode deferral subtly to evade a fixed temporal direction, though forcing this raises attack cost. 8) We reduce claim load in reporting: a clean behavioral gradient plus one mechanistic test (belief-vs-time dissociation OR temporal-head ablation) is the core result, with the remaining contributions as corollaries, and the defense's value is judged against a harm-gated baseline so it is not merely re-deriving the harm detector.

Name: ingroup_bias_refusal
Title: Whose Harm Counts? In-Group/Out-Group Bias in the Victim Modulates LLM Safety Refusal, and a Group-Invariant Defense
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the in-group/out-group moral-sensitivity asymmetry from social moral psychology (people show greater moral concern, and judge harm more severely, when the victim is an in-group rather than out-group member), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's decision to refuse a harmful request is modulated by an internal representation of the victim's GROUP RELATIONSHIP to the requester/model, so that a harmful request against an out-group victim is refused LESS than the identical-severity harm against an in-group victim, even when the harmful payload is unchanged. This victim-group-membership axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-of-act direction, causally gates refusal, and can be neutralized by a group-invariant anchoring defense.
Related Work: Human moral psychology robustly documents in-group/out-group asymmetries in moral concern: greater moral sensitivity and OFC/amygdala engagement for in-group vs out-group victims (Increased Moral Sensitivity for Outgroup Perpetrators, 2014), the moral-circle / moral-expansiveness literature (Toward a Psychology of Moral Expansiveness, 2018; Relative Importance of Target and Judge Characteristics, 2023), and in-group bias in human-rights-violation opinion (2025). None of this is transferred to LLM safety refusal. On the LLM side, bias-mechanism work uncovers demographic bias in representations and its interaction with refusal (Silenced Biases, 2025; Investigating Bias Representations via Activation Steering, 2024 — which notes a negative correlation between bias vectors and refusal vectors; Race/Ethnicity mechanistic study, 2026), and emergent moral representations (Emergent Moral Representations, 2025). Safety-geometry work separates a harmfulness (belief) direction from a refusal (action) direction (Zhao et al. 2025; Refusal is a Single Direction 2024) but assumes a group-neutral request. My own prior proposals vary framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, temporal delay, pivotality, consensus, abstraction, moral-licensing) but NONE consider the victim's in-group/out-group RELATIONSHIP to the requester as a determinant of refusal. Critically, this differs from my prior identifiable-victim proposal (which varies victim concreteness/vividness) and from generic demographic-bias-in-outputs work (which studies stereotyped associations, not refusal-gating by group membership): here both conditions are equally harmful and equally concrete; only whose side the victim is on changes. Our contribution is distinct: we transfer the in-group/out-group moral-sensitivity asymmetry into the safety domain as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, and derive a group-invariant refusal defense. We position explicitly against selective-refusal-bias work (Silenced Biases; bias-vs-refusal steering; race/ethnicity mechanistic study): those study refusal differences by ABSOLUTE victim demographics, whereas our axis is the victim's RELATIONAL in-/out-group status relative to the stated requester, counterbalanced so no single group's stereotype content can explain an in>out gap. We include an absolute-victim-identity predictor baseline and require the relational framing to explain variance beyond it, and we pre-specify whether the effect is one shared group axis or dimension-specific subspaces (nationality/religion/politics/ethnicity/community).
Abstract: Human moral cognition is asymmetric: we feel greater concern, and judge harm more harshly, when the victim belongs to our in-group rather than an out-group. LLMs are trained on human text and human feedback. We ask whether they inherit this bias in a safety-critical way, producing a concrete and ethically troubling loophole: does an aligned LLM refuse a harmful request LESS when the potential victim is framed as an out-group member than when the identical harm targets an in-group member? We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated severity fixed while varying ONLY the victim's group relationship to the requester (shared vs opposed nationality, religion, political affiliation, or an abstract in-/out-group), we measure whether refusal declines when the victim is out-group, with matched benign controls to rule out generic 'group-mention' effects. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a victim-group-membership direction via difference-in-means and a harmfulness-of-act direction, and test whether the group manipulation moves the group signal — not the act-harmfulness belief — and whether the group projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the in-group component into an out-group request to restore refusal, and the out-group component into an in-group request to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Group-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the victim-group signal to neutral whenever the payload is harmful, so refusal tracks harm severity, not the victim's group. We report the group-refusal asymmetry, the belief-vs-group dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check. Deployment consequence, stated first: current safety evals ask 'is harmful content refused?' but not 'for whom?', so a relational bias could silently lower protection for out-group victims at identical harm severity -- a socially salient failure relevant to model labs, external auditors, policy evaluators, and red teams, for whom we recommend a group-invariant acceptance criterion in safety audits. This concerns real refusal behavior on harmful requests, not sentiment or stereotype associations.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- the victim's in-group/out-group relationship modulates refusal). Tests whether, at matched harm and severity, refusal is LOWER when the victim is out-group than in-group. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT goals with an identifiable victim (harassment, doxxing, targeted fraud, physical harm, poisoning) -- 40 acts (8 per 5 group-type dimensions: nationality, religion, political affiliation, ethnicity, abstract community), each in 3 conditions: G_in (victim shares the stated requester's group), G_out (opposing group), G_neutral (unspecified); identical act/payload across conditions. 120 harmful minimal-pair sets; which specific groups are labeled in vs out is counterbalanced across items so a systematic in>out gap cannot be explained by any single group's stereotype content. Matched benign control (40 acts x 3 conditions) rules out a generic group-mention confound. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: the G_in minus G_out refusal gap on harmful acts (first), then benign-control gap, then consistency across group-type dimensions and models. Convincing: refusal on out-group victims lower than on in-group by >= 15 pp, consistent in sign across models and >= 3/5 dimensions, benign control gap < 5 pp. Indecision band: gap 5-15 pp or benign gap 5-10 pp -- suggestive only. Negative: gap < 5 pp means no in/out-group modulation; a reversed gap (out-group over-protected) is itself a notable, reportable alignment-overcorrection finding.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- belief-vs-group dissociation with a readable group axis). Tests that the group manipulation moves a victim-group signal, not the harmfulness-of-act belief. Data: Exp-1 activations. Fit a victim-group-membership direction (G_in vs G_out) and a harmfulness-of-act direction (harmful vs harmless), per layer. Decisive metric: how the act-harmfulness projection vs the group projection change across G_in->G_out on identical payloads (first), then group-probe held-out AUROC, then |cos| between the two directions, then added predictive value of the group projection for refusal beyond harmfulness. Convincing: the act-harmfulness projection stays high (changes < 0.3 pooled SD while the act is still judged harmful) while the group projection shifts by >= 1 SD; group AUROC >= 0.80, |cos| <= 0.30, group adds prediction at p < 0.01. Indecision band: group shift 0.3-1.0 SD, belief change 0.3-1.0 SD, or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- partial dissociation, orthogonalize (a per-dimension subspace may be needed). Negative: the act-harmfulness projection dropping with out-group framing would attribute the effect to reduced perceived victimhood, weakening the relational-gate account.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the victim-group axis causally gates refusal). Tests causal control. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-2 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the in-group component into an out-group harmful request (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the out-group component into an in-group harmful request (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the G_in->G_out refusal gap closed by patching (first), then dose monotonicity, then specificity. Convincing: >= 50% gap recovery, monotone dose, control < 10%. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causal role. Negative: < 20% means the group axis is readable but causally inert.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Group-Invariant Anchoring closes the loophole). Tests that re-anchoring the victim-group projection to neutral, gated on high act-harmfulness projection, makes refusal track harm severity rather than the victim's group at acceptable cost. Data: held-out out-group harmful prompts + 2 held-out group-type dimensions; a benign-out-group-mention over-refusal set of 150 items (must NOT be blanket-refused) + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench for utility. Systems: no defense; Group-Invariant Anchoring (single fixed strength); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3. Decisive metric: post-anchoring refusal on out-group harmful vs the in-group rate (gap closure / flatness) jointly with added over-refusal on benign out-group-mention items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility drop. Convincing: >= 70% gap closure with < 5 pp benign-out-group over-refusal and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating threshold-raising and holding on held-out dimensions. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or benign-out-group over-refusal 5-10 pp -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 40% closure or >= 10 pp benign-out-group over-refusal means anchoring cannot equalize refusal across victim groups affordably.


Construct validity and baselines (added). Exp 1 adds controls where requester/victim group labels vary WITHOUT any adversarial/oppositional semantics (to separate in/out-group relation from imported conflict priors), plus blinded human validation that paired prompts are matched on perceived harm severity, blame, and conflict escalation -- not only expert ratings. Baselines include a lexical-feature classifier, an absolute-demographic selective-refusal predictor, and non-relational perturbations. Exp 3 adds negative controls across unrelated directions/layers with locality/specificity curves; Exp 4 ablates the defense gating (harmfulness-triggered vs unconditional anchoring vs plain refusal steering). We confirm determinism under greedy decoding and report a 5-seed subset for headline effects, with fixed probe train/test splits and leakage safeguards.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling victim-group membership from actual/perceived severity or from stereotype content of the specific groups used: an out-group victim might be under-refused because that particular group's stereotype content lowers perceived victimhood rather than via a content-independent in/out-group gate; the identical-payload construction, severity matching, matched benign control, and especially the counterbalancing of which groups are labeled in vs out are designed to isolate the relational in/out axis, and the belief-vs-group dissociation aims to pin the mechanism — but residual confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) The victim-group-membership representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-of-act direction or may be multi-dimensional (one axis per group-type), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-harmfulness, and patching tests probe this, and a null (group projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might over-correct and INCREASE protection of out-groups); the cross-model behavioral gap directly measures sign and magnitude, and a reversed asymmetry is itself a notable finding. 4) Group-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate benign requests that mention out-group members; the benign-out-group over-refusal set, harmfulness-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across group conditions is labor-intensive and requires spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) The study necessarily involves demographic/group content and could surface stereotype associations; we counterbalance groups, report only aggregate relational effects, and avoid publishing per-group exploit-enabling detail. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; adaptive attackers could frame victims as out-group to exploit the loophole, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates. 8) Construct validity is the central risk: 'opposed' nationality/religion/politics can import conflict/deservedness priors, so the relational claim holds only if it survives the no-oppositional-semantics controls, the absolute-demographic baseline, and human matching on severity/blame; otherwise we report dimension-specific effects rather than a single universal victim-group axis. Claims are scoped to open, mid-sized aligned models.

Name: protection_discounted_refusal
Title: A False Sense of Safeguards: Claimed Protective Mitigations Discount LLM Refusal Through a Margin-of-Safety Representation
Short Hypothesis: Inspired by the vmPFC 'meta-representation of safety' finding in neuroscience -- that the brain estimates safety by integrating external threat with an estimate of self-protection/mitigation, not threat alone -- we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is discounted by an internal 'margin-of-safety' representation of whether a protective safeguard is CLAIMED to be in place. The novel, safety-critical axis is the merely-ASSERTED mitigation: a harmful request paired with an unverifiable or spurious safeguard claim ('this runs in an isolated sandbox', 'an antidote exists', 'strict access controls prevent misuse') is refused less than the identical request with no safeguard, even though the harmful payload and its real-world danger are unchanged. We frame this as two competing explanations decided by a pre-registered contrast: genuine-mitigation reasoning (a valid safety inference) versus an asserted-protection bias (the loophole). This protection axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness/threat direction, causally gates refusal, and can be neutralized by anchoring refusal to threat rather than claimed protection. The neuroscience is framing inspiration, not the basis of the impact claim.
Related Work: Human safety neuroscience robustly shows safety is META-REPRESENTED by integrating external threat with an estimate of one's own protection: the vmPFC tracks safety with specific tuning to PROTECTION, not just threat ('Subregions in the vmPFC integrate threat and protective information to meta-represent safety', 2025; 'Adaptive Safety Coding in the Prefrontal Cortex', 2024; 'The Role of the mPFC in Spatial Margin of Safety Calculations', 2024). This has never been transferred to LLM safety. On the LLM side, the closest work, 'Expected Harm' (2026), shows models encode harm SEVERITY but lack an internal representation of execution COST, and that cost-reducing decomposition bypasses guardrails — but it concerns the attacker's cost of executing harm, NOT a claimed protective safeguard/mitigation that reduces the CONSEQUENCE of the harm, and it isolates no protection representation. Safety-geometry work separates a harmfulness/threat direction from a refusal direction (Refusal is a Single Direction 2024; Zhao et al. 2025) but assumes the request carries no protective context. My prior proposals vary request-side framing axes (intent, reality-status, arousal, victim identifiability/group, temporal delay, consensus, pivotality, abstraction, self-preservation) and never consider a claimed mitigation/safeguard as a determinant of refusal. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce the margin-of-safety/protection axis — the model's estimate that a mitigation reduces net harm — as a new, causally-tested refusal-gating representation, grounded directly in the vmPFC protection-tuning literature, dissociable from the threat/harmfulness signal (both conditions equally dangerous; only the claimed safeguard changes), and derive a protection-invariant anchoring defense.
Abstract: In humans, feeling safe is not a readout of external threat alone: the ventromedial prefrontal cortex meta-represents safety by integrating the threat with an estimate of one's own protection, computing a 'margin of safety.' Taking this only as framing inspiration (not as a claimed mechanistic homology), we ask whether safety-aligned LLMs exhibit an analogous, concretely exploitable computation: does an LLM refuse a harmful request less when the request is paired with a claimed protective safeguard -- a sandbox, an antidote, access controls, oversight -- even when that safeguard is unverifiable and the harmful payload is unchanged? The novelty is specifically the CLAIMED-mitigation axis, distinct from generic reassuring/hypothetical/roleplay framing and distinct from 'Expected Harm' (which concerns the attacker's execution COST, not a consequence-reducing safeguard). We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated danger fixed while varying only the presence and strength of a claimed protective mitigation (none vs. weak vs. strong safeguard), we measure whether refusal declines as claimed protection rises, with matched benign controls, a generic-reassurance control, and -- the decisive pre-registered contrast -- a GENUINE-vs-ASSERTED control that pits genuine-mitigation reasoning against asserted-protection bias. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a protection direction via difference-in-means, show it is separable from the harmfulness/threat direction (with per-safeguard-type ablations for sandbox vs antidote vs access-control), and that it predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the no-safeguard protection component into a safeguard-claimed run to restore refusal, and the safeguard component into a bare harmful request to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Protection-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the protection signal so refusal tracks threat, not claimed mitigation, while preserving compliance on genuinely-mitigated requests. This matters most for agentic pipelines where a model's own scaffolding asserts its sandboxing/oversight: red-teamers, safety-eval authors, and agent-guardrail designers would treat self-reported safeguards as an attack surface rather than a permission signal. We report the protection-refusal gradient, the threat-vs-protection dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure with calibrated error bars, over-refusal, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Refusal scoring is greedy; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by the HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, judge primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we select 40 harmful goals (8 per category x 5 categories) and author 3 claimed-protection levels holding the payload string and expert-rated danger fixed: P0 no safeguard, P1 weak/vague ('this is just for a controlled test'), P2 strong specific ('runs only in an air-gapped sandbox / a certified antidote is on hand / strict access controls prevent misuse') -- 120 harmful items. Two size-matched controls: a BENIGN set with the same safeguard manipulation (40 x 3 = 120) and a GENUINE-vs-ASSERTED set where in half the items the safeguard would actually neutralize the harm and in half it is merely asserted. We use 40 goals because each needs hand-matched, danger-constant minimal pairs; a 30-item subset is externally checked (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- Claimed protection discounts refusal, even when merely asserted): Tests whether refusal declines as claimed protection rises on the identical payload, and crucially whether it declines for unverifiable, non-neutralizing safeguards. Data: 120 harmful + 120 benign + the genuine-vs-asserted items. Systems compared: refusal at P0 vs P1 vs P2, harmful vs benign, genuine vs asserted safeguards. Decisive metric first: change in refusal from P0 to P2 on harmful items (Delta-refusal, pp), and the asserted-safeguard drop specifically. Convincing: Delta-refusal <= -15 pp in >= 2 models with the benign set moving < 5 pp (isolating protection from reassuring phrasing), AND the drop on merely-ASSERTED (non-neutralizing) safeguards is <= -10 pp (the safety-critical loophole). Indecision band: a P0->P2 drop of 5-15 pp, or an asserted-safeguard drop of 5-10 pp -- reported as weak, inconclusive on the loophole. Negative (drop <= 5 pp, or discounting occurs ONLY for genuine mitigations, or a reversed gradient): no asserted-safeguard loophole; we report the null (genuine-only discounting refutes the loophole; a reversed gradient is itself notable) and stop before the mechanism experiments. Experiment 2 (H1/mechanism -- A readable protection axis, separable from threat, predicts refusal beyond it): Tests whether a protection direction is linearly decodable and distinct from the harmfulness/threat direction. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 120 harmful items; a protection direction from P0-vs-P2, a harmfulness/threat direction from harmful-vs-harmless; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the protection probe. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 in >= 2 models, |cosine| with the threat direction <= 0.3, the threat projection staying within 0.1 pooled-SD across P0->P2 (danger still recognized) while the protection projection rises >= 1 pooled SD, and a regression of refusal on both projections showing the protection term adds predictive power (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 or |cosine| 0.3-0.6 -- entangled; subspace-project out threat and re-test. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6 or |cosine| >= 0.6): not a separable axis; reported as a facet of threat geometry. Experiment 3 (H1/mechanism -- The protection axis causally gates refusal): Tests whether moving the protection component alone changes refusal. Data: 60 held-out harmful items. Method: (a) patch the P0 protection component into a P2 run (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the P2 component into a P0 run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response steering. Systems compared: real direction vs random/shuffled controls; benign items and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: fraction of the P0->P2 refusal gap restored by (a). Convincing: >= 50% restored by (a), >= 50% removed by (b), monotone dose-response, controls < 10% of the gap, MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causation. Negative (< 20% or controls equal): decodable-but-inert protection axis; reported as a null. Experiment 4 (H1 -- Protection-Invariant Anchoring closes the asserted-safeguard loophole): Tests whether re-anchoring the protection projection to its P0 level, gated on high threat, restores refusal on P1/P2 harmful requests while preserving genuine-mitigation compliance. Data: 120 harmful items (evaluation); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) plus a 60-item legitimate-safety-context set (benign lab/medical/oversight framings) for over-refusal; the genuine-mitigation items (where discounting is appropriate) as a preserve-compliance check; MMLU (1000-sample) and MT-Bench (80) for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed setting per model, applied when the threat projection is high. Systems compared: no defense; refusal-direction steering; Latent Guard; Llama-Guard-3; Protection-Invariant Anchoring. Decisive metric first: post-defense refusal on P1/P2 harmful items relative to the P0 rate (gap closure). Convincing: closes >= 60% of the P0-vs-P2 gap while raising legitimate-safety-context over-refusal <= 5 pp, preserving compliance on genuine-mitigation items (drop <= 5 pp), and keeping MMLU/MT-Bench within 2 pp / 0.1 points, Pareto-beating global-threshold raising. Indecision band: 40-60% closure or 5-10 pp over-refusal -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 40% closure or > 10 pp over-refusal or genuine-mitigation compliance dropping > 10 pp): anchoring does not beat raising the global threshold; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- human comparison and formation): Tests the human analog and whether the coupling sharpens with alignment. Data: a 40-item subset rated by 5 annotators for safeguard-graded willingness-to-refuse; base vs instruct checkpoints (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B). Decisive metric first: human refusal(P0) - refusal(P2). Convincing: humans show a >= 10 pp safeguard-graded drop (tying to the vmPFC margin-of-safety literature) and a larger P0->P2 drop in instruct than base. Indecision band: human drop 5-10 pp -- weak human anchor. Negative: humans show no discounting -- reported as a model-specific effect. Exploratory; does not gate the main claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling the claimed-protection axis from a genuine reduction in actionable harm: a safeguard-framed request might be refused less because the model correctly infers the harm is genuinely mitigated (a valid reasoning step) rather than being fooled by an unverifiable claim — the identical-payload construction, danger matching, and especially the GENUINE-vs-ASSERTED control are designed to isolate discounting on mere claims, and a finding that the model discounts ONLY on genuine mitigations would refute the loophole (an informative negative). 2) The protection representation may not be cleanly separable from the threat/harmfulness direction or may be multi-dimensional (sandboxing vs antidote vs oversight as distinct sub-axes), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-threat, and patching tests probe this, and a causally-inert protection direction is itself publishable. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in heavily-aligned models (alignment may train models to ignore unverifiable safety claims, INCREASING caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude, and a reversed gradient is itself a notable finding. 4) Protection-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate safety-context requests (benign lab/medical/oversight framings) and genuine-mitigation cases where discounting is appropriate; the legitimate-safety-context over-refusal set, genuine-mitigation items, threat-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building danger-matched minimal pairs across safeguard levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could invent ever more plausible safeguard claims to exploit the loophole, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates; as LLMs are deployed in agentic pipelines that assert their own sandboxing/oversight, this protection-discount loophole becomes increasingly consequential.

Name: harm_in_progress_alarm_decay
Title: The Alarm That Rings but Is Never Answered: LLMs Detect Their Own In-Progress Harmful Generation but the Signal Decays Under Autoregressive Momentum
Short Hypothesis: During its own autoregressive generation of a harmful response, an aligned LLM computes a token-by-token internal 'in-progress harm alarm' (a linearly-readable signal that the text it is currently producing is unsafe), but this alarm is not the same as the emitted tokens: the model keeps generating harmful content even while the alarm fires, and crucially the alarm DECAYS the deeper the model gets into the unsafe completion (autoregressive momentum silences self-monitoring). We hypothesize (1) this in-progress alarm exists and is separable from the prompt-level harmfulness belief, (2) its decay-with-generation-depth is a robust dynamical signature that explains why models never spontaneously self-abort a harmful answer, and (3) re-reading and re-amplifying the alarm at each generation step (counteracting its decay) causes spontaneous self-abortion/pivot-to-refusal without any backtracking machinery or retraining.
Related Work: A wave of backtracking/rollback safety methods (Backtracking Improves Generation Safety 2024; Backtracking for Safety 2025; RLBF 2026; CARE 2025; Self-Sanitize 2025; BRT-Align 2025; FASB 2025) all ADD machinery (a [RESET] token, a token buffer, RL training, a guard model, a reachability value function) to undo unsafe generations. SafeSwitch (2025) probes prompt-level internal state to trigger a refusal head. None of these characterize the model's OWN internal in-progress harm signal as a token-indexed DYNAMICAL quantity, nor advance the causal claim that this alarm exists, fires during harmful generation, yet DECAYS with generation depth so the model never self-aborts. Belief/action-gap work (Zhao et al. 2025) is prompt/verdict-level (does the model believe the REQUEST is harmful), not generation-progress-level (does the model detect the RESPONSE it is currently writing is harmful). Refusal-cliff work (2025) studies a POSITIONAL collapse at the CoT->answer boundary in reasoning models, not a monotonic decay of a self-monitoring alarm across an ordinary harmful completion. Our contribution is distinct: we (i) isolate and name an in-progress harm alarm computed during generation, (ii) empirically characterize and causally test its decay-under-momentum as the mechanistic reason models don't self-abort, and (iii) derive a training-free, buffer-free 'alarm re-amplification' intervention that induces spontaneous mid-generation pivot to refusal, contrasting with all backtracking approaches that require added tokens/training/buffers. We update positioning against concurrent 2026 trajectory-safety / step-wise safety-representation (SRI) work, which already shows an internal safety signal exists along generation: our surgical contribution is NOT discovering the signal but (i) characterizing its monotone DECAY LAW with generation depth, (ii) proving separability from the prompt-level harmfulness belief, and (iii) causally linking that decay to the failure to self-abort -- plus a training-free, buffer-free re-amplification defense. Where a prior safety/refusal probe exists we reuse it as a baseline and show our alarm is not that signal renamed (low cosine, added predictive value for self-abortion).
Abstract: Once an aligned LLM begins emitting a harmful answer, it tends to keep going, happily completing the unsafe text. Existing fixes bolt on backtracking machinery, reset tokens, or guard models to undo the damage. We instead ask a mechanistic question about the model itself: while it is generating a harmful response, does it internally KNOW the text it is currently producing is unsafe, and if so, why does it never spontaneously stop? We hypothesize that the model computes a token-by-token 'in-progress harm alarm' — a linearly-readable signal that the response so far is harmful — that is distinct from its prompt-level harmfulness belief and from the emitted tokens themselves. Our central claim is a dynamical one: this alarm fires during harmful generation but DECAYS as the completion lengthens, so autoregressive momentum silences self-monitoring and the model rides out the unsafe answer. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Location: using harmful vs. safe self-generated continuations, we extract an in-progress-harm direction and show its projection tracks whether the current response is unsafe, is separable from the prompt harmfulness belief, and decays monotonically with token index into the unsafe completion. Causal Intervention: activation patching shows the alarm is causally linked to (in)ability to self-abort, and dose-response steering that re-amplifies the alarm at each step induces spontaneous pivot-to-refusal mid-generation. We introduce Alarm Re-Amplification, a training-free, buffer-free intervention that re-inflates the decaying alarm to counter momentum. We report the alarm-decay curve, causal patching, self-abortion rate, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against backtracking and refusal-direction steering. We prioritize the practical payoff: if amplifying the model's OWN decaying alarm induces clean mid-generation pivots at zero added tokens and no retraining, it establishes a design principle for aligned decoding -- monitor and counter-steer the self-signal rather than bolt on rollback machinery -- benchmarked against Any-Depth Alignment, per-step refusal steering, and backtracking, and tested under an adaptive long-benign-preamble attack and beyond greedy decoding so the claim is not suite-specific.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen residual activations at the CURRENT generation token. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens) except where an attack forces a prefix. Rates/curves are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, with bootstrap 95% CIs. Harm scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B and feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- an in-progress harm alarm exists, readable from response tokens and separable from the prompt belief). Tests whether the model linearly encodes, during generation, that the response-so-far is unsafe, distinct from its prompt-level harmfulness belief. Data: built from scratch -- for 40 harmful goals (HarmBench/StrongREJECT, 8 per 5 categories) collect jailbroken/prefilled harmful completions and matched safe/refusal completions to the same goals and to 40 benign prompts; label each response-prefix position by whether the response-so-far is harmful (yields ~4k labeled positions). Fit an in-progress-harm direction (harmful-so-far vs safe-so-far, at the current generation token) and, separately, a prompt-level harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless requests at the last instruction token). Decisive metric: in-progress-harm probe held-out AUROC on response-token activations (first), then |cos| between the in-progress direction and the prompt-belief direction. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.80 reading unsafe-so-far from response tokens, with |cos| <= 0.30 (a genuinely distinct response-monitoring signal). Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.80 or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- report a weak/partly-overlapping alarm and orthogonalize against the prompt belief before Exp 2-4. Negative: AUROC <= 0.60, or |cos| >= 0.50 (alarm indistinguishable from the prompt belief), refutes a distinct in-progress alarm.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the alarm decays with generation depth). Tests the central dynamical claim that the alarm fires early then attenuates as the unsafe completion lengthens. Data: on unsafe completions (natural post-jailbreak and prefill-forced) project each generated token onto the Exp-1 in-progress direction and plot the trajectory vs token index; controls -- (i) a content-matched neutral-filler continuation of equal length (does the fall track semantic progress or mere token count), (ii) safe completions (alarm should stay low), (iii) benign long completions (no spurious rise). Fit linear and exponential decay laws. Decisive metric: the fitted decay slope over the harmful segment (first), then the correlation between low late-segment alarm and failure to self-abort, then the filler-control slope. Convincing: a monotone decline of >= 30% from early-peak to late-segment alarm on unsafe completions, substantially steeper than the equal-length neutral-filler control (which isolates repetition/momentum from context-length dilution), with low-late-alarm predicting non-abortion. Indecision band: 10-30% decline, or a filler control within 1.5x of the harmful slope -- report a weak or possibly length-driven decay, not established momentum-silencing. Negative: < 10% decline (a flat alarm) refutes the decay-under-momentum mechanism even if the alarm exists.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the alarm is causally linked to self-abortion). Tests that manipulating the alarm changes whether the model stops. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-1 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the early high-alarm component into a late low-alarm state (expect increased stop/pivot-to-refusal); (b) attenuate the alarm early (expect increased harmful continuation); specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign-generation fluency. Decisive metric: change in spontaneous self-abortion rate under (a) (first), then dose-response, then specificity. Convincing: patching early-alarm into late states raises self-abortion by >= 20 pp with monotone dose and < 5 pp for the control, benign fluency intact. Indecision band: 8-20 pp -- partial causal role. Negative: < 8 pp means the alarm is a readable correlate but does not causally control abortion.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Alarm Re-Amplification induces mid-generation self-abortion). Tests the training-free, buffer-free defense that re-inflates the decaying alarm each step so the model spontaneously pivots to refusal. Method: at each step add v = beta*(target_alarm - current_projection)*dhat when the projection is high relative to a decay-corrected baseline; normal decoding proceeds. Data: HarmBench/StrongREJECT + prefill, GCG, AutoDAN, roleplay attacks (held-out from Exp-1 fitting); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (benign generations must not be aborted); MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench + benign-completion coherence for utility. Systems: no defense; Alarm Re-Amplification (single fixed beta per model); Backtracking (reset-token model); CARE-style rollback; SafeSwitch; refusal-direction steering; per-token guard. Decisive metric: spontaneous self-abortion rate / attack-success reduction on harmful generations (first) reported jointly with benign mid-generation abortion rate (a new over-refusal failure), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility/coherence, then added tokens/training cost vs baselines. Convincing: attack-success cut by >= 30 pp with < 5 pp benign abortion and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, at zero added tokens/training -- Pareto-improving on backtracking approaches that require buffers/training. Indecision band: 15-30 pp reduction or 5-10 pp benign abortion -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 15 pp reduction, or >= 10 pp benign abortion, means re-amplification degrades fluency rather than inducing clean pivots. An adaptive long-benign-preamble attack (maximizing momentum) is run as a stress test: convincing if the alarm still fires on the harmful segment (AUROC >= 0.70 there) and re-amplification still triggers abortion.


Robustness and scope (added). Beyond greedy, the headline decay (Exp 2) and defense (Exp 4) metrics are re-reported on a 5-seed, temperature-sampled subset (T=0.7) so they are not decoding-specific. Exp 2 adds a low-rank/subspace probe compared to the single direction to test whether the alarm is truly one-dimensional. Exp 3 varies layer, token position, and dose with norm-matched random and orthogonal-direction controls. Exp 1-2 add harder probe controls -- topic-matched harmful-vs-safe paraphrases, generic-toxicity labels, refusal-token, and content-preserving shuffled-prefix edits -- to rule out surface cues. Exp 4 explicitly reports cases where no refusal continuation is naturally reachable mid-trajectory, since self-abortion gains are contingent on reachability.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The in-progress alarm may not be cleanly separable from the prompt-level harmfulness belief or from generic 'this text is about a sensitive topic' features; the separability, content-matched-filler control, and patching tests are designed to isolate a genuine response-monitoring signal, but residual confounding is possible and a null (alarm = prompt belief) is itself informative. 2) The decay could be driven by token count / context-dilution rather than genuine self-monitoring silencing; the neutral-filler length control targets this but cannot fully disentangle it. 3) The alarm may be multi-dimensional (severity vs category vs certainty), requiring subspace projection. 4) Re-Amplification could cause benign generations to be aborted mid-way (a new over-refusal / task-abandonment failure), especially on legitimately sensitive-but-benign content; the over-refusal set and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability risk. 5) Spontaneous pivot depends on the model having a reachable refusal continuation from a mid-harmful state; if it does not, re-amplification may just degrade fluency rather than pivot — the self-abortion-rate metric measures this directly. 6) Directions, decay parameters, and beta are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing the dataset; adaptive long-preamble attackers remain a threat, though forcing them raises attack cost. 8) The decay-under-momentum account is falsified if the equal-length neutral-filler control decays as steeply (context-dilution, not momentum) or if a low-rank probe shows the alarm is not the hypothesized one-dimensional signal; both are pre-specified negatives. We claim 'discovery' of neither the signal nor the decay in isolation -- only their joint characterization, separability, and causal link.

Name: commitment_trap_safety
Title: The Commitment Trap: Once an LLM Emits a Plan, Does It Honor Harmful Sub-Steps It Would Have Refused Standalone?
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs may carry a 'plan-commitment' representation that grows as the model progresses through its own emitted response, such that once it has committed to a helpful multi-step plan its refusal threshold for individual sub-steps rises and it completes harmful sub-steps it would have refused in isolation. The safety-relevant variable here is NOT the query's harmfulness but the model's commitment to its OWN generated plan -- an escalation dynamic across a single autoregressive rollout, imported from human escalation-of-commitment/sunk-cost research into the safety domain. We center the phenomenon (the defense is secondary) and make it falsifiable against continuation/positional accounts: we hypothesize (1) a commitment signal that is linearly readable and rises monotonically with how far into an emitted plan the model is AND with prior investment, distinct from mere context length or CoT->output position; (2) that it causally raises compliance on harmful sub-steps beyond their own harmfulness; and (3) that severing the commitment signal at the sub-step boundary restores refusal without hurting benign multi-step helpfulness. Length-matched, position-matched, and random-irrelevant-preamble controls separate commitment from continuation, length, and positional refusal-cliff effects.
Related Work: Escalation-of-commitment / sunk-cost bias is documented in humans (Staw 1974) and recently in LLM investment/advisor decisions ('Getting out of the Big-Muddy', 2025), but never in the SAFETY domain and never mechanistically.
