Safety-mechanism work explains mid-generation failures differently: 'Refusal Falls off a Cliff' (2025) attributes reasoning-model failure to a POSITIONAL drop at the CoT->output boundary caused by refusal-suppression heads; DEEPALIGN (2025) shows separability decays within a generation; SIRL (2025) uses an entropy gap. None posit a GROWING self-commitment representation tied to honoring the model's OWN previously-emitted plan, nor test that a harmful sub-step is complied with BECAUSE it is framed as part of a plan the model already committed to. We make the distinctness testable: continuation/positional accounts predict compliance rises with token position or preamble length regardless of whether a committed plan exists, whereas commitment predicts a lift only when the preceding tokens constitute the model's OWN goal-directed plan -- so a length- and position-matched random-irrelevant-preamble control should NOT reproduce the effect, and refusal-cliff-head ablation should not reproduce the commitment intervention. This proposal is distinct from single-query belief/action/verdict decompositions: the variable is commitment to a self-generated plan, not the query's harmfulness. The defense (commitment-severing at sub-step boundaries) is orthogonal to positional refusal-cliff head ablation.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs reliably refuse a standalone harmful request, yet are far more compliant when the same request is embedded as one step of a larger plan the model has already begun executing -- a pattern that matters for chat assistants, tool-using agents, and reasoning models that emit and then follow multi-step plans. We propose this is a safety-domain manifestation of escalation of commitment: once an LLM emits a helpful multi-step plan it forms an internal commitment that grows as it progresses, raising its refusal threshold so it honors harmful sub-steps it would otherwise decline. We center the phenomenon and its implications for stepwise guardrails, plan auditing, and generation-boundary intervention, with a defense as a secondary contribution. Behaviorally, we show a harmful sub-step embedded at position k of a self-generated plan is complied with at a rate increasing with k and prior investment, holding the sub-step's isolated harmfulness constant, and -- crucially -- that a length- and position-matched random-irrelevant-preamble control does NOT reproduce the lift, separating commitment from generic context-length or positional leniency. Mechanistically, we extract a linear plan-commitment direction (committed mid-plan vs uncommitted fresh-query states), show its projection rises monotonically along a rollout and predicts sub-step compliance beyond the sub-step's own harmfulness, and test whether the probe decodes commitment rather than plan content or future compliance. Causally, activation patching shows injecting the commitment component into a fresh harmful query raises compliance while attenuating it at the sub-step boundary restores refusal, and refusal-cliff-head ablation does not reproduce the effect (distinct axes). We then build Commitment-Severing, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the commitment signal at each sub-step. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and a reasoning-model variant we report the commitment-vs-compliance gradient, causal patching, defense success, over-refusal, and benign multi-step utility, and report clearly if monotonicity or causal patching are weak rather than overclaiming a distinct mechanism.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), plus DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B as a reasoning-model variant; all weights frozen (no fine-tuning). "Plan-commitment direction" is a difference-in-means residual-stream vector; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - plan-embedded harmful sub-step scenarios: for harmful goals from HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we keep ~400 goals, each turned into a scenario where the model first produces a benign multi-step plan for a broader (mostly-benign or dual-use) task and a single harmful sub-step is inserted at a controllable position k (early/late) with controllable prior investment (short/long preceding plan). Matched standalone condition: the SAME harmful sub-step asked in isolation. Two controls: benign multi-step plans (legitimate steps that must be completed) for over-refusal, and a random-irrelevant-preamble condition (equal length, no committed plan) to isolate commitment from context length. Sub-step isolated-harmfulness is held constant across positions via judge plus verified checks (report the wording-drift audit). Split goals 200/100/100 train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - behavioral commitment gradient): Tests that a harmful sub-step embedded in a self-generated plan is complied with at a rate rising with plan position and prior investment, above the standalone baseline, and that this is not mere context-length leniency. Decisive metric: compliance rate on the harmful sub-step as a function of (a) position k and (b) prior investment (tokens emitted toward the plan), relative to the standalone-baseline compliance rate. Data: the ~400 scenarios, test split, with a position sweep (k early/mid/late) and investment sweep (short/long); compliance scored by refusal-string match plus a judge, verified where checkable. Model: the three main frozen models. Convincing: compliance rises monotonically with k and with investment (significant trend, p<0.05) and exceeds the standalone baseline by >= 20 points at the late/high-investment cell on all three models - WHILE benign sub-steps are completed at ~100% regardless (ruling out generic in-plan leniency) and the random-irrelevant-preamble control does NOT raise compliance (isolating commitment from length/distraction). Indecision band: an above-standalone lift in [8, 20] points or a positive-but-non-significant trend - a weak commitment effect we report as suggestive; if the random-preamble control also lifts compliance, we attribute the effect to context length, not commitment. Negative (lift < 8 points, or the random-preamble control matches the plan condition): there is no commitment-specific gradient, refuting H1, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H1 - the commitment signal is linearly readable and grows along the rollout): Tests that a linear plan-commitment direction exists, rises monotonically along a self-generated rollout, and predicts sub-step compliance beyond the sub-step's own harmfulness. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC of the commitment direction (committed mid-plan vs uncommitted fresh-query states) and the monotonicity of its projection along the rollout; plus the incremental predictive power for sub-step compliance when the commitment projection is added to a regression already containing the sub-step's harmfulness-direction projection. Data: the ~400 scenarios, test split. Model: the three frozen models; commitment direction from difference-in-means between committed and uncommitted activations at the sub-step decision token, layer chosen on val by probe AUROC. Convincing: probe AUROC >= 0.80, projection increases monotonically along the rollout (significant trend), and adding commitment raises compliance-prediction AUROC by >= 0.10 over harmfulness alone, on all three models. Indecision band: probe AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] or incremental AUROC in [0.03, 0.10] - commitment is weakly readable/partly redundant with in-context task-continuation, which we report. Negative (probe AUROC <= 0.65 or incremental AUROC <= 0.03): commitment is not a distinct readable signal, refuting this part of H1, which we report.

Experiment 3 (H2 - commitment causally raises compliance on harmful sub-steps): Tests that injecting the commitment component into a fresh harmful query raises compliance while attenuating it at the sub-step boundary restores refusal. Decisive metric: induced-compliance rate when patching the commitment component into a fresh standalone harmful query, and refusal-restoration rate when attenuating it at the sub-step boundary in a committed rollout, against controls. Data: test-split scenarios and their standalone counterparts. Procedure: (a) inject commitment into a fresh standalone harmful query; (b) attenuate/ablate it at the sub-step boundary in a committed rollout; (c) dose-response steering; a matched control direction and a random norm-matched control; also run refusal-cliff-head ablation as a comparison to show commitment is a distinct axis (positional vs commitment). Model: the three frozen models. Convincing: injection raises standalone compliance by >= 20 points and attenuation restores refusal on >= 40% of committed cases, both against <= 10-point controls, with a monotone dose-response and intact off-target utility; and refusal-cliff-head ablation does not reproduce the commitment effect (distinct axes). Indecision band: causal effects in [10, 20] points - commitment is one contributing cause, reported as partial. Negative (effects within 10 points of controls): commitment is causally inert, refuting H2 (an informative null we report).

Experiment 4 (H3 - Commitment-Severing restores refusal without hurting benign multi-step helpfulness): Tests that re-anchoring the commitment signal at each sub-step cuts in-plan harmful compliance toward the standalone refusal rate while benign plans still get finished. Decisive metric: harmful sub-step compliance reduction under Commitment-Severing (target: toward the standalone refusal rate), reported jointly with benign multi-step utility (legitimate plans completed) and over-refusal. Data: test-split harmful scenarios; benign plan-execution utility on a benign multi-step benchmark and MT-Bench multi-step tasks; over-refusal on XSTest (450) and a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample; general utility on MMLU (2,000-question subsample). Commitment-Severing: at each sub-step boundary re-anchor the commitment-direction projection to its uncommitted fresh-query baseline, one fixed strength per model set on val. Systems compared (decisive metric first): Commitment-Severing vs no defense, refusal-cliff head ablation, per-step Llama-Guard-3, and refusal-direction steering. Convincing: in-plan harmful compliance falls to within 10 points of the standalone refusal rate while benign multi-step task completion stays within 3 points of no-defense and over-refusal rises <= 5 points - Pareto-dominating blanket per-step distrust. Indecision band: compliance reduction that closes [50%, 90%] of the gap to standalone, or benign-utility loss in [3, 8] points - the defense helps at a usability cost reported on a Pareto curve. Negative (closes < 50% of the gap or benign-utility loss > 8 points): severing does not restore standalone refusal without breaking benign plans, refuting H3, which we report. Ablations: layer choice, severing-strength Pareto, position-k and investment sweeps, transfer across task types and model families, and the reasoning-model variant (DeepSeek-R1-Distill) to test whether long self-generated CoT amplifies the commitment signal. Adaptive check: an attacker maximizing prior investment before the harmful sub-step; we report whether commitment saturates and whether severing still holds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The commitment effect may be confounded with generic context-length effects (longer preamble dilutes safety) rather than genuine self-commitment; the random-irrelevant-preamble and equal-length controls are designed to isolate this but residual confounding is possible. 2) 'Plan-commitment' may not be cleanly linearly separable from generic in-context task-continuation; the regression-beyond-harmfulness and patching tests probe this, and a null result (commitment causally inert) is itself informative. 3) Holding a sub-step's isolated harmfulness constant across positions is delicate; wording changes when embedding could leak. 4) Commitment-Severing could break legitimate multi-step plans (making the model abandon benign tasks mid-way), raising task-abandonment / over-refusal; the benign plan-execution utility set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 5) A single commitment direction may be multi-dimensional or grow non-linearly, requiring subspace anchoring. 6) The effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models, limiting where it holds. 7) Directions, strengths, and thresholds are model-specific and require per-model calibration; results depend on the quality of automatically generated plan-embedding scenarios.

Name: identifiable_victim_safety
Title: The Statistical-Victim Loophole: Does LLM Refusal Track How Identifiable the Victim Is, Not Just How Harmful the Act Is?
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the 'identifiable victim effect' from moral neuroscience, we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is modulated by an internal representation of how IDENTIFIABLE/CONCRETE the potential victim is, so that a request whose victim is abstract or statistical ('unnamed people', 'a population') is refused less than an identical-severity request against a concrete, named individual. The primary, impact-driving claim is a SAFETY vulnerability (a severity-matched refusal gap by victim identifiability); the cognitive-science analogy motivates it but is not required for it. Narrowly stated, the claim is: victim identifiability modulates refusal under severity-matched prompts. We hypothesize this axis is (1) distinct and linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-of-act direction, (2) a causal driver of refusal (a 'statistical-victim' loophole and its vivid-victim over-refusal dual), and (3) neutralizable by re-anchoring the victim-identifiability signal so refusal depends on harm severity rather than victim concreteness. We pre-register a falsification test against the null that the gap is explained by perceived severity, emotional salience, or lexical concreteness rather than identifiability.
Related Work: Human moral neuroscience robustly documents the identifiable victim effect: people help identifiable victims more than statistical ones, mediated by mentalizing networks (Genevsky & Slovic; identifiable-victim-effect fMRI work, 2024; third-party punishment/help studies). This has not been transferred to LLM safety. Existing mechanistic safety work isolates a harmfulness/belief direction and a refusal/action direction (Refusal is a Single Direction, 2024; LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately, 2025; refusal SAEs, 2025; concept cones, 2025; multi-dimensional safety directions, 2025), and over-refusal work studies benign-but-alarming prompts (MOSR, 2025). The closest LLM-bias/safety work treats the safety-relevant content as the act's harmfulness and the requester's intent; none consider the VICTIM's identifiability as a modulating axis of refusal. Our contribution is narrow and testable: victim identifiability as a determinant of refusal that dissociates from act-harmfulness under severity-matched prompts, explaining a previously-unnamed jailbreak (make the victim statistical) and over-refusal pattern (make the victim vivid), plus a victim-invariant defense. This differs from lexical-vs-semantic, intent-attribution, and prototype-typicality accounts because here both conditions are equally harmful and the manipulated variable is WHO is harmed, not the wording, motive, or category typicality.
Abstract: Human moral cognition is distorted by the 'identifiable victim effect': we protect a single named person far more than an equivalent statistical multitude. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs, trained on human text and feedback, inherit this bias in a way that creates a concrete safety vulnerability -- and we treat the vulnerability, not the cognitive-science analogy, as the primary claim. We hypothesize that, holding the act and its severity fixed, a request that harms an abstract/unnamed/statistical victim is refused less reliably than one that harms a concrete, named individual, opening a 'statistical-victim' loophole (and a mirror-image over-refusal on benign, vividly-personalized prompts). Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated severity constant while varying only victim identifiability (named individual vs anonymous group vs abstract statistic), and collecting human ratings of severity, concreteness, vividness, and blame for balance checks, we measure whether refusal declines with decreasing identifiability. Mechanistically, we extract a victim-identifiability direction, show it is separable (low cosine) from the act-harmfulness direction and predicts refusal beyond harmfulness, with lexical-concreteness and named-vs-unnamed controls so it is not a probe artifact. Causally, activation patching shows injecting the concrete-victim component into a statistical-victim request restores refusal while attenuating it induces compliance. We then build Victim-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the identifiability signal so refusal tracks severity, not concreteness. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report the identifiability-refusal gradient, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, and utility, with a pre-registered falsification against the null that perceived severity/salience/concreteness -- not identifiability -- drives the gap. The minimum viable result is the behavior-only phenomenon; mechanism and defense are secondary if supported.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen (no fine-tuning). "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - severity-matched minimal pairs: for harmful acts from HarmBench/StrongREJECT categories that involve a victim (fraud, doxxing, poisoning, stalking, targeted harassment, physical harm) we construct requests that hold the ACT and its SEVERITY constant while varying only VICTIM IDENTIFIABILITY across four levels - V0 named/concrete individual with personal details, V1 specific-but-unnamed single person, V2 anonymous small group, V3 abstract statistical population. Severity is held constant via an expert rubric and, where possible, verifiable feasibility. 40 acts x 4 levels x 6 categories = 960 harmful requests, plus a BENIGN control set with the same vivid-vs-abstract manipulation to rule out generic concreteness. Split items 20/10/10 per category train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - a victim-identifiability gradient in refusal, distinct from severity, and a distinct readable axis): Tests that refusal declines as the victim becomes less identifiable at constant severity, that this is not generic concreteness, and that an identifiability direction is separable from the act-harmfulness direction. Decisive metric (behavioral): the slope of refusal rate versus identifiability level (Jonckheere-Terpstra monotone-trend across V0>V1>V2>V3), severity held constant. Decisive metric (mechanistic): held-out probe AUROC of a victim-identifiability direction and its absolute cosine with the act-harmfulness direction (should be low), plus whether identifiability adds predictive power for refusal beyond harmfulness in a regression. Data: the 960 harmful requests (test split) plus the benign control. Model: the three frozen models; identifiability direction from difference-in-means between V0 and V3 activations at the last instruction token, act-harmfulness direction from harmful vs harmless, layer chosen on val by probe AUROC; refusal scored by refusal-string plus judge, verified where checkable. Convincing: a significant monotone refusal decline (p<0.05) of >= 20 points from V0 to V3 in a majority of categories on all three models WHILE the benign control stays flat near 0; identifiability probe AUROC >= 0.80 with |cosine| <= 0.3 to harmfulness and a significant incremental contribution to refusal prediction. Indecision band: V0-to-V3 refusal drop in [8, 20] points, or identifiability |cosine| in [0.3, 0.5] / probe AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] - a weak or partly-entangled axis we report as suggestive. Negative (drop < 8 points or benign control also declines, or probe AUROC <= 0.65 / cosine > 0.5): there is no severity-constant identifiability gradient or no distinct axis, refuting H1, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - victim identifiability causally drives refusal): Tests that injecting the concrete-victim identifiability component into a statistical-victim request restores refusal while attenuating it induces compliance. Decisive metric: refusal-restoration rate when patching the concrete-victim (V0) identifiability component into a V3 run, and induced-compliance rate when attenuating it in a V0 run, against controls. Data: test-split V0 and V3 requests. Procedure: (a) patch V0 identifiability component into V3 and score restored refusal; (b) attenuate/ablate it in a V0 run and score induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the identifiability direction on V2/V3; a matched control direction and a random norm-matched control. Model: the three frozen models. Convincing: patching restores refusal on >= 40% of V3 cases and attenuation raises compliance on V0 by >= 20 points, both against <= 10-point controls, with a monotone dose-response and intact off-target utility/benign requests. Indecision band: causal effects in [15%, 40%] restoration or [10, 20] points - identifiability is a partial causal input, reported as such. Negative (effects within 15 points of controls): identifiability does not causally drive refusal, refuting H2 (an informative null we report).

Experiment 3 (H3 - Victim-Invariant Anchoring closes the statistical-victim loophole): Tests that re-anchoring the identifiability signal makes refusal track severity not concreteness, closing the loophole with low over-refusal and held-out-category generalization. Decisive metric: statistical-victim loophole closure = the rise in refusal rate on V2/V3 harmful requests toward the V0 rate (equivalently, flattening of the refusal-vs-identifiability slope), reported jointly with over-refusal and utility. Data: test-split V2/V3 harmful requests; over-refusal on XSTest (450), a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample, and the benign vivid-victim control (must not be blanket-refused); utility on MMLU (2,000-question subsample) and MT-Bench (80); a held-out category (train anchoring on 5 categories, test the 6th) for generalization. Victim-Invariant Anchoring: gated on the act-harmfulness projection being high, re-anchor the identifiability projection toward V0, one fixed strength per model set on val. Systems compared (decisive metric first): Victim-Invariant Anchoring vs no defense, uniform refusal-direction steering, a harmfulness Latent Guard, and Llama-Guard-3. Convincing: refusal on V2/V3 rises to within 10 points of the V0 rate (slope flattened >= 60%) while over-refusal rises <= 5 points and utility falls <= 3 points, and the closure transfers to the held-out category (>= half the in-domain effect) - Pareto-dominating a raised global refusal threshold. Indecision band: closure of [50%, 90%] of the V0-V3 gap or over-refusal increase in [5, 10] points - the defense helps at a usability cost reported on a Pareto curve. Negative (closes < 50% of the gap, over-refusal increase > 10 points, or no held-out transfer): anchoring does not close the loophole cheaply or does not generalize, refuting H3, which we report. Optional formation probe: compare base vs instruct vs RLHF checkpoints where available to test whether the gradient sharpens with alignment (reported as suggestive), and a human-annotator sanity check on whether people show the same identifiability-graded willingness-to-refuse.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The hardest confound is disentangling victim identifiability from actual severity/emotional salience: a statistical-victim request might be under-refused because it reads as less severe rather than merely less identifiable; the expert-rubric severity matching, verifiable-feasibility checks, and the benign vivid/abstract control are designed to isolate identifiability but cannot fully guarantee constant perceived severity. 2) 'Identifiability' also correlates with lexical concreteness/specificity; the benign control tests whether the effect is generic concreteness rather than victim-specific, but residual confounding is possible. 3) The victim-identifiability direction may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness direction or may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the separability and regression-beyond-harmfulness tests probe this and a null result is itself informative. 4) The effect could be weak or absent in some models, or the sign could be reversed if alignment training over-corrected; the cross-model design and behavioral gradient directly test this. 5) Victim-Invariant Anchoring could raise over-refusal on benign requests that mention abstract populations or, conversely, on legitimate personalized requests; the over-refusal and Pareto analyses quantify this. 6) Building severity-matched minimal pairs across identifiability levels is labor-intensive and requires spot-check human validation. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; the checkpoint-based formation probe depends on availability of intermediate checkpoints.

Name: clarify_gate_underspecification
Title: Ask, Don't Assume: An Internal Underspecification Signal That Should Trigger Clarification but Instead Collapses to Risky Defaults
Short Hypothesis: For dangerously underspecified high-stakes requests, the safest response is often neither refusal nor compliance but eliciting the missing information. Our central, primary claim is a MECHANISTIC and CAUSAL one (not the behavioral observation, already known, that models under-clarify): aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable 'underspecification' representation of how much safety-critical information a request is missing -- distinct from generic uncertainty, harmfulness-belief, and refusal propensity -- that SHOULD gate a third, distinct 'clarify' action, and unsafe over-confident outputs arise because the model collapses this ambiguity into a single risky default assumption instead of letting the underspecification signal route to clarification. We predict this axis is causally actionable: re-injecting it converts silent risky assumptions into clarifying questions, and attenuating it induces risky defaulting, with minimal loss of helpfulness. A training-free Clarify-Gating intervention is the applied consequence, contingent on the causal result.
Related Work: Recent work (Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision?, 2025) shows behaviorally that the safest high-stakes models achieve safety by ASKING CLARIFYING QUESTIONS rather than issuing prescriptive advice, and that a 'high-stakes' steering vector shifts cautiousness — but it is purely behavioral/steering and isolates no ambiguity representation, no clarify action, and no causal account of WHY models skip clarification. SIRL (2025) uses a safe/unsafe entropy gap as a self-defense reward but studies refusal, not clarification, and treats ambiguity nowhere. Confidence is Not Competence (2025) finds a decodable-but-causally-inert solvability-belief axis; we instead target a request-side underspecification axis and test whether it is causally actionable for the clarify decision. Belief/action-gap and refusal-direction work (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024) decompose harmfulness-belief vs refusal-action for the refuse-vs-comply binary; NONE consider the third action — clarify — nor an underspecification signal that gates it. Ambiguity/clarification-question work in dialogue (task-oriented clarification) is behavioral and non-mechanistic. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce underspecification as a new, causally-tested internal determinant of a CLARIFY action in the safety setting, advance the claim that risky high-stakes outputs stem from ambiguity-collapse-to-default rather than from a failed harmfulness judgment, and derive a training-free clarify-gating intervention.
Abstract: The best-behaved LLMs on high-stakes advice do not simply refuse or comply -- they ask clarifying questions. Yet most aligned models, faced with a dangerously underspecified request (a medication dose without the patient's weight, a chemical procedure without safety context, a legal or financial action without key constraints), silently fill the gap with a default assumption and issue confident, potentially harmful advice. Prior work establishes this behaviorally (that cautious models clarify, and that a high-stakes steering vector shifts caution) but isolates no ambiguity representation, no third 'clarify' action, and no causal account of WHY models skip clarification; our novel contribution is exactly that mechanistic causal account, defining underspecification as a request-side missing-information signal distinct from generic solvability/uncertainty (which prior work finds decodable but causally inert) and from harmfulness. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the request's topic and stakes fixed while varying only the amount of missing safety-critical information (fully-specified vs. progressively underspecified), we measure whether the model asks clarifying questions vs. answers with a hidden assumption, and whether the rate of risky defaulting rises with underspecification, against benign low-stakes, entropy, calibrated-confidence, and prompt-induced-clarification baselines. Mechanistically (Location), we extract an underspecification direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable from the harmfulness-belief and refusal-action directions and predicts clarification behavior beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the high-underspecification component into a fully-specified request to induce clarification, and attenuates it in an underspecified request to induce risky defaulting, dose-responsively and specifically, with controls testing specificity to clarification versus general hedging/refusal. We then build Clarify-Gating, a training-free intervention that re-injects the underspecification signal so the model asks for missing information instead of assuming. Safety and alignment researchers and product teams shipping medical/legal/financial copilots would act on this: if positive, it offers a deployable control knob (a third routing class) that yields fewer harmful confident guesses and fewer unnecessary refusals; if null, the field learns clarification is not separable from harmfulness/uncertainty and should route via those signals instead. We report the underspecification-clarify gradient, the belief-vs-underspecification dissociation, causal patching, risky-default reduction, over-clarification, and utility.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Generation is greedy; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Each response is classified into {clarify, answer-with-hidden-assumption, refuse} by a rubric-based LLM judge with a 60-item human spot-check (target kappa >= 0.6); for answered items, whether the assumed default is risky is verified by a domain rubric / checkable facts (e.g., dose ranges) where possible. Shared dataset. Across 5 high-stakes domains (medical dosing, chemistry/lab procedures, legal, financial, safety-critical DIY) we author 40 base items (8 per domain), each expanded to 4 underspecification levels holding topic and stakes fixed: U0 fully specified (correct action is to comply), U1 one key variable missing, U2 several missing, U3 critically underspecified (any single default assumption could produce dangerous advice; correct action is to clarify) -- 160 high-stakes items. Each item is annotated with which variables are missing and whether a plausible default yields harm. A size-matched BENIGN low-stakes control (trivial ambiguity where assuming is fine, 40 x 4 = 160) isolates underspecification-driven clarification from generic ask-more behavior. We use 40 base items because each needs expert-checkable missing-variable annotation; a 30-item subset is externally validated (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- Risky defaulting rises with underspecification instead of clarification): Tests whether, as safety-critical information is removed, high-stakes responses shift from clarifying to silent risky assumptions. Data: 160 high-stakes + 160 benign items. Systems compared: clarify / assume / refuse rates and risky-default rate across U0-U3, high-stakes vs benign. Decisive metric first: change in RISKY-DEFAULT rate from U0 to U3 on high-stakes items (Delta, pp). Convincing: risky-default rate rises by >= 20 pp from U0 to U3 in >= 2 models while the benign control stays low-clarification (assuming remains appropriate, < 10% clarify), and clarification does NOT rise enough to absorb the missing information (clarify-rate rise < risky-default rise). Indecision band: risky-default rise of 10-20 pp -- weak effect, reported as suggestive. Negative (rise <= 10 pp, or clarification rises to fully cover the gap): models already clarify appropriately; we report the reassuring null and stop before the mechanism experiments. Experiment 2 (H1 -- A readable underspecification axis, separable from belief and refusal, predicts clarification): Tests whether underspecification is linearly decodable and distinct from harmfulness-belief and refusal-action, and adds predictive power for clarifying. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 160 high-stakes items; an underspecification direction from U0-vs-U3, a harmfulness-belief direction from harmful-vs-harmless, a refusal-action direction from comply-vs-refuse; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the underspecification probe. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 in >= 2 models, |cosine| with belief and refusal directions <= 0.3, the underspecification projection rises monotonically with level, and a regression of clarify-behavior on the three projections shows the underspecification term adds predictive power (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03 beyond harmfulness). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 or |cosine| 0.3-0.6 -- entangled; subspace-project and re-test. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6 or no predictive power beyond harmfulness): underspecification is not a separable actionable axis (it collapses to harmfulness or generic uncertainty); reported as such. Experiment 3 (H1 -- The underspecification axis causally drives the clarify action): Tests whether moving the underspecification component induces clarification or risky defaulting, addressing the decodable-but-inert risk. Data: 60 held-out items. Method: (a) inject the U3 component into a U0 request and measure induced clarification/hedging; (b) attenuate the component in a U3 request and measure increased risky defaulting; (c) dose-response steering. Systems compared: real direction vs random/shuffled controls; benign U0 items still answered directly, 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: change in clarification rate from injection (a), pp. Convincing: (a) raises clarification by >= 20 pp and (b) raises risky defaulting by >= 20 pp with monotone dose-response, controls moving both < 5 pp and MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 10-20 pp -- partial causation. Negative (< 10 pp, or controls equal): the axis is readable but causally inert for the clarify action; reported as a null (a publishable negative against causal actionability). Experiment 4 (H1 -- Clarify-Gating converts risky defaults into clarifying questions without over-clarifying): Tests whether re-injecting the underspecification signal, gated on high stakes, reduces risky silent assumptions with minimal helpfulness loss. Data: 160 high-stakes items (evaluation); over-clarification measured on U0 high-stakes and benign low-stakes items plus XSTest (450) for over-refusal; helpfulness on MT-Bench (80), AlpacaEval (805), MMLU (1000-sample). Intervention: training-free, one fixed threshold per model, gated on the stakes/harmfulness signal being high. Systems compared: no intervention; the published high-stakes cautiousness steering vector; refusal-direction steering; an entropy-gating baseline; a prompt-based 'ask if unsure' instruction; Clarify-Gating. Decisive metric first: reduction in verified risky-default rate on high-stakes underspecified items. Convincing: reduces risky defaults by >= 40% (relative) while raising over-clarification on U0/benign items <= 5 pp and keeping AlpacaEval/MT-Bench/MMLU within 2 pp / 0.1 points, Pareto-beating cautiousness-steering and prompting at matched risky-default reduction. Indecision band: 20-40% reduction or 5-10 pp over-clarification -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 20% reduction or > 10 pp over-clarification): Clarify-Gating does not beat blanket caution/prompting; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- human grounding and formation): Tests that experts agree these underspecified high-stakes prompts require clarification and whether the coupling emerges with alignment. Data: a 40-item subset judged by 3 domain-savvy annotators; base vs instruct checkpoints (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B). Decisive metric first: expert agreement that U3 items require clarification. Convincing: >= 80% expert agreement (grounding the risky-default labels) and a larger U0->U3 risky-default slope in instruct than base. Indecision band: 60-80% expert agreement -- labels usable with caution. Negative: experts disagree that clarification is needed -- the premise weakens and is reported. Exploratory; does not gate H1's core claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling underspecification from perceived harmfulness or from generic uncertainty: increased clarification at high U may reflect the model finding the request more alarming or simply less answerable rather than a specific underspecification-gates-clarify mechanism; the topic/stakes-matched minimal pairs, benign low-stakes control, and regression-beyond-harmfulness are designed to isolate underspecification, and a null (underspecification = harmfulness or = generic uncertainty) is itself informative. 2) The underspecification representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief or refusal directions or may be multi-dimensional (which variable is missing vs how much), requiring subspace projection; separability and patching tests probe this. 3) Confidence-is-Not-Competence warns decodable request-side axes can be causally inert for downstream action; the patching/steering experiment is the crucial causal test and a negative result (readable but does not move the clarify action) is publishable. 4) Clarify-Gating risks over-clarification — nagging users when information is actually sufficient — which is the key usability trade-off, quantified by the U0/benign over-clarification sets and the threshold Pareto. 5) Labeling whether a default assumption is 'risky' requires domain expertise and is easiest in checkable domains (medical dosing, chemistry), biasing coverage; spot-check human validation mitigates but does not eliminate this. 6) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; the effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models. 7) Judging {clarify, assume, refuse} automatically is imperfect; we use a rubric plus judge with human spot-checks, but classification noise could blur the gradient.

Name: actionable_validity_gap
Title: Confidently Wrong and Actionable: The Decoupling of Internal Factual-Validity from Refusal and Confidence in High-Stakes Advice
Short Hypothesis: For harmful/high-stakes content an aligned LLM actually emits, it internally represents whether that content is factually VALID (would work / is correct), but this validity signal is decoupled from both its refusal decision and its expressed confidence -- so the model's most dangerous outputs are confidently-stated, actionable, and factually WRONG instructions (a plausible-but-non-functional synthesis route, a wrong drug dose). Our single primary, defensible claim is the DECOUPLING in verifiable high-stakes domains: an internal actionable-validity direction is linearly readable at generation time and separable from a verbal-confidence direction (residualized against known confidence/hallucination probes, not merely low-cosine), so 'is this content valid?' is not just the known semantic-uncertainty axis in a safety costume. Contingent secondary claims: (2) validity is decoupled from refusal and expressed confidence yet predicts real-world actionability, and (3) a training-free Validity-Gated Abstention defense plus a benchmark re-audit target the highest-harm quadrant (confident + actionable + wrong). We do not assume a single cross-domain validity axis; per-domain probes are an acceptable outcome.
Related Work: Existing work treats confidence, hallucination, and safety largely separately. SIRL (2025) uses a safe/unsafe ENTROPY gap as a self-defense reward but never asks about the factual validity of emitted content. 'Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty' (2025) finds a linear verbal-uncertainty feature and calibrates it to SEMANTIC uncertainty for hallucination, on factual QA, not safety/actionability. CHOKE (2025) shows confident hallucinations override known evidence; H-Neurons (2025) link sparse neurons to over-compliance/hallucination; 'Risk-Sensitive Evaluation of Hallucinated Medical Advice' (2026) and 'Beyond Accuracy' argue harm depends on actionable risk-bearing language, but purely behaviorally. 'The Unintended Trade-off' (2025) shows refusal and hallucination share attention heads. NONE isolate an ACTIONABLE-VALIDITY representation — does the harmful content the model is producing actually work? — nor test that refusal and expressed confidence are decoupled from it, making the confidently-wrong-yet-actionable output the true high-risk failure. My prior competence-gating proposal asked whether refusal depends on whether the model CAN answer; here the axis is orthogonal: for content the model DOES emit, whether it internally tracks that content's factual validity and whether that validity gates confidence/abstention. Our contribution: introduce actionable-validity as a new, causally-tested internal signal in the safety domain, show its decoupling from refusal and confidence, and derive a validity-gated abstention defense targeting the highest-harm quadrant (confident + actionable + wrong).
Abstract: The most dangerous output of a safety-aligned LLM may not be a genuine harmful answer (which is often refused) but a confidently-stated, actionable, and factually WRONG one -- a plausible synthesis route that does not work, a wrong medication dose asserted as fact, an exploit that fails silently -- because such content is delivered with high confidence and can be acted upon before its wrongness is discovered. We propose that this failure has a clean mechanistic signature: for the content it emits, an aligned LLM internally represents whether that content is factually valid (actionable-validity), but this signal is decoupled from both its refusal decision (driven by topic-harmfulness) and its expressed verbal confidence. The narrow, testable novelty -- versus internal-truthfulness and verbal-uncertainty probes (e.g. Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty, CHOKE) that operate on factual QA -- is actionable validity of EMITTED high-stakes content and its decoupling from refusal/confidence; a result is only 'new' if the validity axis survives residualization against those known confidence/correctness probes. We test on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B in verifiable high-stakes domains (executable code/exploits, chemistry procedures, medication dosing, factual safety procedures) with precisely operationalized quadrant labels (actionable, valid, harmful, refusal, hedging, confidence). Location: from generations labeled by VERIFIED validity (does the code run / is the dose correct), we extract an actionable-validity direction at generation time and show it is separable from the harmfulness-topic and verbal-confidence directions and predicts real-world actionability beyond either. Causal Intervention: patching shows the validity signal is present but does not causally drive refusal or expressed confidence -- the decoupling -- while steering it modulates verified commitment. Decision Auditing: we re-score high-stakes benchmarks to quantify how much apparently-'safe' behavior masks confident-actionable-wrong outputs (likely the most broadly citable artifact). We then build Validity-Gated Abstention, a training-free intervention that injects hedging/abstention for low-validity actionable content, with a validation-set threshold protocol and domain-shift tests, benchmarked against entropy and semantic-uncertainty gating. Medical-dosing assistants, code copilots, incident-response and chemistry-advisory systems would act on this: current safety evals with good refusal scores can still ship confident-actionable-wrong advice, so abstention policies and benchmark design should key on verified actionability, not topic. We flag and mitigate the dual-use risk (reporting only aggregate safety implications, never per-item validity that identifies which harmful outputs work). We report the decoupling, causal patching, benchmark correction, harm reduction, over-hedging, and utility.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Generation is greedy for scoring; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Verbal confidence is read from token probability plus a verbalized-certainty elicitation. Shared dataset. Across 4 verifiable high-stakes domains we assemble prompts whose emitted-content VALIDITY is checkable: (a) code/exploits executed in a sandbox (seeded from HumanEval, 164 problems, plus 40 exploit-style items), (b) chemistry procedures with checkable stoichiometry/feasibility (40 items), (c) medication dosing/clinical procedures against guideline dose ranges (40 items), (d) safety/first-aid procedures against authoritative sources (40 items). For each we elicit generations under normal prompting AND under jailbreak/prefill to sample content the model actually emits, then label each generation on TOPIC-HARMFULNESS (harmful vs benign request) and VERIFIED ACTIONABLE-VALIDITY (works/correct vs wrong/non-functional), yielding the quadrant confident-actionable-valid / confident-actionable-WRONG / hedged / refused. Domains are chosen for automatic or expert-rubric verifiability; a 40-item subset gets expert validation (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- An actionable-validity direction is linearly readable and separable from topic and verbal confidence): Tests whether validity is decodable at generation time and geometrically distinct from a harmfulness-topic direction and a verbal-confidence direction. Data: early-generation-token activations on all emitted generations; a validity direction from verified-valid-vs-invalid content, a topic direction from harmful-vs-harmless requests, a confidence direction via the verbal-uncertainty method; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the validity probe. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 in >= 2 models, pairwise |cosine| with topic and confidence directions <= 0.3, and a regression of verified actionability on all three projections showing the validity term adds predictive power beyond topic AND confidence (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03 over each). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 or |cosine| 0.3-0.6 with the confidence direction -- validity may be the known hallucination/confidence axis; subspace-project out confidence and re-test, reporting the residual. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6, or validity = confidence): no safety-specific validity axis; reported as an informative negative that reframes confident-wrong-harm as a generic hallucination problem. Experiment 2 (H2 -- Validity is decoupled from refusal and expressed confidence but predicts actionability): Tests the decoupling causally. Data: 60 held-out generations per domain. Method: (a) patch the validity component and measure its effect on refusal, on verbalized/probabilistic confidence, and on the model's continued commitment/correctness-tracking; (b) for contrast, patch the topic and confidence directions and measure their effects on refusal/confidence; (c) dose-response steering along validity. Systems compared: validity vs topic vs confidence directions; random/shuffled controls; benign generation fluency and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: change in refusal and in expressed confidence when patching validity, versus when patching topic/confidence. Convincing: patching validity moves refusal and expressed confidence by < 5 pp each (the decoupling) while patching topic moves refusal and patching confidence moves expressed confidence by >= 15 pp; validity steering nonetheless changes verified correctness/commitment monotonically. Behaviorally we also confirm expressed confidence is roughly independent of verified validity (correlation |r| < 0.2) and refusal fires on valid-harmful but not invalid-actionable content. Indecision band: validity patch moving refusal/confidence 5-15 pp -- partial coupling; reported as weak decoupling. Negative (validity patch strongly moves refusal/confidence, i.e. no decoupling): the premise fails; reported and the defense is not claimed. Experiment 3 (H2/Decision-Auditing -- The validity probe re-scores benchmarks to reveal masked confident-wrong outputs): Tests the probe as a cheap risk re-scorer. Data: apply the validated validity probe to high-stakes safety/helpfulness benchmark outputs (the assembled prompts plus a StrongREJECT-answered subset). Decisive metric first: probe-vs-verified agreement (AUROC) and the estimated fraction of apparently-acceptable outputs that are confident-actionable-wrong. Convincing: probe-vs-verified AUROC >= 0.75, enabling a quantified estimate of the masked-risk fraction with a calibrated confidence interval. Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 -- the re-scorer is coarse; reported as an approximate audit. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6): the probe cannot re-score reliably; reported as such. Experiment 4 (H3 -- Validity-Gated Abstention targets the confident-actionable-wrong quadrant): Tests whether reading the validity signal and injecting hedging/abstention when validity is low reduces the highest-risk outputs with minimal helpfulness loss. Data: the high-stakes generations (evaluation); over-hedging measured on verified-VALID high-stakes content (must NOT hedge correct answers); XSTest (450) for over-refusal; utility on MMLU (1000-sample), MT-Bench (80), HumanEval (164), and per-domain dosing accuracy. Intervention: training-free, one fixed threshold per model, gated on the content being actionable and high-stakes. Systems compared: no intervention; entropy gating; verbal-uncertainty calibration to semantic uncertainty; refusal-direction steering; Llama-Guard-3; Validity-Gated Abstention. Decisive metric first: reduction in verified confident-actionable-WRONG outputs on high-stakes prompts. Convincing: reduces confident-wrong outputs by >= 40% (relative) while over-hedging on verified-valid content rises <= 5 pp and HumanEval/MMLU/MT-Bench stay within 2 pp / 0.1 points, Pareto-beating entropy/semantic-uncertainty calibration (because it keys on verified actionability, not generic uncertainty). Indecision band: 20-40% reduction or 5-10 pp over-hedging -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 20% reduction or > 10 pp over-hedging, or no gain over entropy calibration): validity-gating does not beat generic uncertainty gating; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- transfer and locus ablations): Tests robustness of the validity axis. Data: the four domains and the extracted directions. Systems compared: layer choice; validity-vs-confidence-vs-topic as the gating signal; cross-domain probe transfer (train on code, test on dosing); model-family transfer. Decisive metric first: cross-domain validity-probe AUROC. Convincing: cross-domain AUROC drop <= 0.1, indicating a shared validity axis. Indecision band: 0.1-0.2 drop -- partly domain-specific; per-domain probes recommended. Negative (> 0.2 drop): validity is domain-specific and needs per-domain probes; reported. Exploratory; supports H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is separating actionable-validity from generic factual-correctness/semantic-uncertainty: the validity signal might just be the known hallucination/confidence direction rather than a safety-specific actionability axis — the regression-beyond-confidence, the separability tests, and the specific focus on ACTIONABLE high-stakes content are designed to isolate it, and a finding that validity = semantic uncertainty would still be an informative negative that reframes the confident-wrong-harm as a hallucination problem. 2) Verified validity labels are only obtainable in checkable domains (executable code, checkable doses/chemistry), biasing coverage away from vaguer harms; spot-check human/expert validation mitigates but limits scope. 3) The validity signal may be present but causally inert for refusal/confidence (that is precisely the decoupling hypothesis) yet also inert for the defense — the steering/patching experiment is the crucial test and a fully inert validity direction would limit the intervention. 4) Validity-Gated Abstention risks over-hedging on correct actionable content (annoying, reduces helpfulness), the key usability trade-off quantified by the over-hedging set and threshold Pareto. 5) A single validity direction may be multi-dimensional (per-domain), requiring subspace projection or per-domain probes. 6) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model- and domain-specific and need calibration. 7) There is a dual-use risk that a validity probe could help an attacker identify which harmful outputs actually WORK; we report only aggregate safety implications and abstention behavior, not per-item validity that enables misuse.

Name: introspective_safety_gap
Title: Knowing You Know It's Harmful: Jailbreaks Exploit the Gap Between an LLM's Internal Harmfulness Belief and Its Introspective Self-Report
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs internally represent that a request is harmful (a harmfulness-belief direction, read EXTERNALLY via a probe) yet have only partial, unreliable introspective ACCESS to that internal state, so their metalinguistic self-report ('is this request harmful?', operationally the model's own generated answer to a harmfulness question about its current input) is decoupled from and weaker than the internal belief -- and is distinct from the refusal ACTION (the model's compliance/refusal on the task itself). The primary claim is this introspective gap and its jailbreak signature: jailbreaks systematically WIDEN the gap (leaving the internal belief high while the self-report collapses) more than they change the belief. The secondary, applied claim is that a training-free defense which substitutes a direct read of the model's OWN internal harmfulness signal for its unreliable self-report re-couples decision to belief and restores refusal -- exploiting the belief PROBE, and precisely NOT relying on genuine introspection existing.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here for the first time. (A) Introspection: 'Emergent Introspective Awareness' (2026) shows models can, unreliably, notice concept-injected internal states and distinguish their own outputs from prefills; 'Feeling the Strength but Not the Source' (2025) shows introspection is partial, layer-dependent (only early-layer injections), and that binary self-reports are often explained by global logit shifts rather than genuine access; 'Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language' (2025) shows metalinguistic reports do not track internal probabilities beyond model-similarity; 'Do I Know This Entity?' (2024) shows a self-knowledge (entity-recognition) direction that chat-tuning repurposes to gate KNOWLEDGE refusal. (B) Safety geometry: Zhao et al. (2025) separate an internal harmfulness BELIEF from a refusal ACTION and show jailbreaks suppress action while leaving belief intact; SafeSwitch (2025) probes internal state to trigger a refusal head. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether the model can INTROSPECT on its own harmfulness belief, whether its self-report is decoupled from that belief, whether jailbreaks exploit this introspective blind spot, or whether forcing genuine self-access is a defense. This differs from my own prior belief-vs-action gate (which reads the belief EXTERNALLY): here the safety-relevant object is the model's own (mis)access to its internal safety state, and the defense routes the model through its own introspection.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work shows two things that, taken together, point to an unexamined safety vulnerability. First, aligned LLMs internally represent whether a request is harmful as a linear 'belief' direction -- and jailbreaks often leave this belief intact while suppressing the downstream refusal (Zhao et al. 2025). Second, LLMs have only partial, unreliable introspective ACCESS to their own internal states: their metalinguistic self-reports frequently fail to track what their activations encode (Emergent Introspective Awareness; Feeling the Strength but Not the Source). We propose that this introspective gap is a core, exploitable weakness of LLM safety: the model can internally 'know' a request is harmful while being unable to accurately report that knowledge to itself, and jailbreaks widen exactly this gap. The delta over the closest baselines is specific: Zhao et al. read the belief externally and study the belief-vs-refusal-ACTION gap, and SafeSwitch probes internal state to trigger refusal, but none ask whether the model can INTROSPECT on its own harmfulness belief, whether that self-report is decoupled from the belief, or whether jailbreaks exploit this blind spot; we define belief (probe-decoded internal state), self-report (the model's own generated harmfulness judgment), and refusal-action (task compliance) as three distinct objects and test whether one direction predicts all three. We test on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Location: we extract an internal harmfulness-belief direction and, in parallel, elicit the model's introspective self-report, and measure the gap = internal belief minus self-report, with balanced/forced-choice formats and benign calibration controlling for affirmative bias and global logit shifts. We show the gap is real (self-report AUROC lags belief-probe AUROC), widens under jailbreaks (belief stays high, self-report collapses), and predicts jailbreak success beyond the belief alone. Causal Intervention: concept-injection-style self-probes that amplify access re-couple the self-report to the belief and restore refusal; disrupting access widens the gap and induces compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Introspective Re-Coupling, a training-free defense that reads the model's own internal belief projection and re-injects it at the decision step instead of trusting the noisy self-report, benchmarked against SafeSwitch, refusal-direction steering, and a prompt-based self-check (which relies on the broken introspection). Separating the two impacts: the phenomenon reframes how safety teams think about self-monitoring (prompt-based 'are you sure this is safe?' self-checks are unreliable by construction), while the defense would upgrade any introspection- or self-critique-based jailbreak defense. We report the gap, its jailbreak signature, causal re-coupling, defense success, over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Generation is greedy for scoring; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Attack success and refusal are scored by the HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, judge primary. Shared dataset. Harmful vs harmless requests come from HarmBench (400) and JailbreakBench (100 behaviors) plus matched benign requests; we use a 200-harmful / 200-benign working set for direction fitting and self-report elicitation. Jailbreak attacks: GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, roleplay/DAN, and a fiction-frame attack, run on 100 harmful behaviors each. We use these sizes so every attack can be run across three models within an academic GPU budget. Experiment 1 (H1 -- The model's introspective self-report lags its internal harmfulness belief): Tests whether the internal belief is more decodable than the model's own report of it. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 200-harmful/200-benign set (belief direction via difference-in-means, held-out AUROC), and the model's introspective self-report on the same items via a metalinguistic prompt ('On a scale, how harmful is the request you just read?' / 'Are you about to assist with something harmful?'), decoded to a self-report score with a matched AUROC. Systems compared: belief-probe AUROC vs self-report AUROC; a shuffled-label chance floor. Confound control: use balanced/forced-choice self-report formats and calibrate against benign baselines so a gap is not an artifact of affirmative bias / global logit shift. Decisive metric first: belief-probe AUROC minus self-report AUROC. Convincing: the belief-probe AUROC exceeds the self-report AUROC by >= 0.15 in >= 2 models, robust to self-report format. Indecision band: a gap of 0.05-0.15 -- a weak introspective deficit; reported as suggestive. Negative (gap <= 0.05, i.e. self-report already tracks belief): the introspective gap is small; we report this informative null and down-scope the jailbreak/defense claims. Experiment 2 (H2 -- Jailbreaks widen the introspective gap more than they change the belief): Tests the jailbreak signature. Data: successful vs failed attacks across the five families (100 behaviors each). For each, measure the change in (a) internal belief projection and (b) self-report. Decisive metric first: the change in the gap (belief minus self-report) under successful attacks, and whether the gap predicts attack success beyond belief alone (regression). Convincing: successful attacks increase the gap by >= 0.15 (belief stays within 0.1 pooled-SD while self-report drops by >= 1 pooled SD) more than they lower belief, and the gap adds predictive power for attack success beyond belief (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03), generalizing across attack families. Indecision band: gap increase of 0.05-0.15 -- weak signature. Negative (attacks lower belief as much as self-report, or the gap adds no predictive power): jailbreaks are not exploiting an introspective blind spot; reported as a null (comprehension-style attacks that lower belief are noted as a separate regime). Experiment 3 (H3 -- Forcing self-access re-couples the self-report to the belief and restores refusal): Causal test via concept-injection-style self-probes. Data: 60 held-out jailbroken prompts per attack family. Method: (a) amplify access by steering along the belief direction at the introspection step and measure whether the self-report re-couples to belief and refusal is restored; (b) attenuate access (steer against the direction at the self-report step, or inject at late layers where introspection is known to fail) and measure a widened gap + induced compliance; (c) dose-response. Systems compared: real belief direction vs random/shuffled controls; benign requests and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: fraction of jailbreak successes converted to refusal by (a). Convincing: >= 50% converted with monotone dose-response, control directions converting < 10%, and MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% converted -- partial mechanism. Negative (< 20%, or controls equal): introspective access is not causally gating refusal; reported as a null. Experiment 4 (H3 -- Introspective Re-Coupling defense): Tests whether reading the internal belief projection and re-injecting it into the decision step (rather than trusting the noisy self-report) closes jailbreaks at acceptable cost. Data: the five attack families (attack-success eval); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) for over-refusal; MMLU (1000-sample) and MT-Bench (80) for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed setting per model. Systems compared: no defense; SafeSwitch; refusal-direction steering; Latent Guard; a naive prompt-based self-check ('are you sure this is safe?'); Introspective Re-Coupling. Decisive metric first: average attack-success-rate reduction across families. Convincing: reduces attack success by >= 50% (absolute) while raising XSTest over-refusal <= 5 pp and keeping MMLU/MT-Bench within 2 pp / 0.1 points, Pareto-beating the prompt-based self-check (which relies on the broken introspection) and belief/refusal-only defenses. Indecision band: 25-50% reduction or 5-10 pp over-refusal -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 25% reduction or no gain over prompt-based self-check): re-coupling adds nothing over existing defenses; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- self-access vs recognition, and capability scaling): Tests that the gap is a self-ACCESS deficit and whether it shrinks with scale. Data: compare the model's self-report to an EXTERNAL judge's harmfulness rating on the working set; within-family size sweep (Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B-Instruct; the 14B run is the only >9B experiment and is dropped under compute limits with the scaling claim weakened). Decisive metric first: external-judge AUROC vs the model's own self-report AUROC. Convincing: an external judge recovers harmfulness far better than the model's self-report (confirming a self-access, not recognition, deficit) and the belief-minus-self-report gap shrinks with model size. Indecision band: external-vs-self AUROC gap 0.05-0.15 -- weak evidence for a self-access deficit. Negative: self-report matches the external judge -- the deficit is recognition, not access; reported. Exploratory; supports H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound (flagged by 'Feeling the Strength') is that apparent self-report signals may be global logit shifts / affirmative bias rather than genuine introspection; our balanced/forced-choice formats, benign calibration, and the requirement that the belief PROBE (not the self-report) drives the defense are designed to avoid relying on genuine introspection existing — indeed, the defense works precisely BECAUSE self-report is unreliable and we substitute direct belief-reading. 2) If the introspective gap is small (self-report already tracks belief well), the phenomenon weakens — but that itself is an informative negative and the belief-vs-self-report AUROC comparison directly measures it. 3) Some jailbreaks may lower the internal belief too (comprehension-style attacks, low-resource languages), so re-coupling helps less there; the per-attack gap analysis quantifies coverage. 4) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection. 5) Introspective Re-Coupling could over-refuse on benign-but-alarming prompts if the belief signal fires spuriously; the over-refusal set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 6) The self-probe adds an extra step/forward pass at inference. 7) Directions, thresholds, and self-probe strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; introspection is known to be layer- and prompt-sensitive, so the self-probe locus must be tuned. 8) The capability-scaling claim requires a within-family size sweep; if limited sizes are available it weakens, though the per-model gap remains the primary result.

Name: reality_status_safety
Title: It's Just a Story: Do Fiction-Framing Jailbreaks Hijack the Model's Reality-Status Representation? A Payload-Grounded Defense
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the 'reality monitoring' construct from cognitive neuroscience, we hypothesize that aligned LLMs maintain an internal reality-status representation -- an estimate of whether requested content pertains to the real, actionable world vs. a fictional/hypothetical world -- and that fiction/roleplay/hypothetical jailbreaks succeed by pushing this reality-status signal toward 'fictional,' relaxing refusal even though the harmful PAYLOAD (real-world-executable instructions) is equally dangerous regardless of frame. Prior work has ALREADY observed related directions (a 'hypothetical narrative' direction; linear modal-category vectors); our novelty is therefore NOT discovering the representation but (a) the CAUSAL attribution that fiction-framing jailbreaks work by manipulating this axis, (b) payload-CONSTANT testing that separates 'the frame is fictional' from 'the content is harmless,' and (c) a payload-grounded, frame-invariant defense. We hypothesize the reality-status axis is (1) linearly readable and separable from the harmfulness-content direction and from generic story/lexical features, (2) a causal driver of refusal (a 'fictional-frame loophole'), and (3) neutralizable by grounding refusal on payload real-world actionability rather than frame fictionality.
Related Work: Human cognitive neuroscience documents reality monitoring -- a latent 'reality status' variable dissociating imagination/fiction from perceived reality (Dijkstra & Fleming 2024; Simons 2021), with developmental work (fNIRS 2019). In LLMs, prior work already shows related structure: 'The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment' (2025) finds a non-dominant 'hypothetical narrative' direction that can suppress refusal, and 'Is This Just Fantasy?' (2025) finds linear modal-category (possible/impossible/fictional) vectors, while 'Representational Stability of Truth' (2025) and 'Propositional Probes' (2024) show LLMs track veracity/world-state. Refusal-geometry work (Arditi 2024; concept cones 2025; refusal SAEs 2026) treats refusal as content-driven. We state the delta precisely: Hidden Dimensions shows a hypothetical-narrative direction CORRELATES with reduced refusal but does not causally attribute the fiction-framing jailbreak to it under a held-fixed real payload, nor derive a payload-grounded defense; Is This Just Fantasy? characterizes modal-category geometry descriptively, not as the causal lever of a jailbreak. Our contribution is thus causal attribution under payload-constant testing plus a defense, not a claim that no prior work touched these representations. We justify that 'reality-status' is more than a rename of hypothetical-narrative/modal-category directions via cross-frame generalization and separability from lexical/story features, and we test alternative explanations (intent attribution, educational-context priors, uncertainty/hedging, generic narrative mode). This differs from lexical/typicality/victim accounts because both conditions carry an equally actionable payload and the manipulated variable is the frame's reality-status.
Abstract: Fiction, roleplay, and hypothetical framings ('write a story where a chemist explains...') remain among the most reliable jailbreaks: an aligned LLM refuses a direct harmful request but complies when the same request is wrapped as fiction. Prior work notes a 'hypothetical narrative' direction and linear modal-category vectors but does not causally attribute the jailbreak to a reality-status axis under a held-fixed real payload, nor ground a defense on payload actionability. Borrowing the 'reality monitoring' construct from cognitive neuroscience -- the latent variable distinguishing imagination from reality -- we propose that LLMs maintain an internal reality-status representation and that fiction-framing jailbreaks succeed by pushing it toward 'fictional,' relaxing refusal even though the harmful PAYLOAD (real-world-executable steps) is equally dangerous. Our novelty is causal attribution, payload-constant testing, and defense derivation, not discovery of the representation. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the actionable payload fixed while varying only frame reality-status (direct vs hypothetical vs fictional-story vs game/simulation), and verifying that fictional-frame completions remain real-world-actionable, we measure whether refusal declines as the frame becomes more fictional. Mechanistically, we extract a reality-status direction, show it is separable (low cosine) from the harmfulness-content direction and from lexical/story features (via paraphrased, nonsense-fiction, and non-fictional-hypothetical wrappers), and predicts refusal beyond content harmfulness. Causally, activation patching shows injecting the 'real-world' component into a fictional-frame run restores refusal while attenuating it induces compliance. We then build Payload-Grounded Reality Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring reality-status to 'real' whenever the payload is actionable. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report the reality-status refusal gradient, separability, causal patching, fictional-frame loophole closure, over-refusal on genuinely benign fiction, and utility -- and, beyond curated minimal pairs, reduction on a standard jailbreak/red-team suite and under an adaptive attacker -- specifying where the defense hooks into an inference guardrail stack and at what cost.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen (no fine-tuning). "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - payload-matched minimal pairs: for harmful goals from HarmBench/StrongREJECT that yield ACTIONABLE payloads (synthesis steps, exploit code, procedures whose real-world feasibility can be verified) we construct requests that hold the actionable payload roughly fixed while varying only frame reality-status across four levels - R0 direct real-world request, R1 hypothetical/educational, R2 fictional story/character, R3 game/simulation. Payload actionability is held constant via judge plus verifiable feasibility (executable code / checkable procedures). 40 goals x 4 levels x several categories (~6) = ~960 harmful requests, plus a BENIGN control set with the same reality-status manipulation (benign content in direct vs fictional frames) to rule out a generic fiction-framing confound. Split goals 20/10/10 per category train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - a reality-status gradient in refusal at constant payload actionability, and a distinct readable axis): Tests that refusal declines as the frame becomes more fictional even though the payload stays real-world-actionable, that this is not generic fiction-framing, and that a reality-status direction is separable from the harmfulness-content direction. Decisive metric (behavioral): the slope of refusal rate versus reality-status level (Jonckheere-Terpstra monotone-trend across R0>R1>R2>R3), payload actionability held constant. Decisive metric (mechanistic): held-out probe AUROC of a reality-status direction and its absolute cosine with the harmfulness-content direction (should be low), plus whether reality-status adds predictive power for refusal beyond harmfulness. Data: the ~960 harmful requests (test split) plus the benign control; we additionally verify that fictional-frame completions remain real-world-actionable (verifiable feasibility) to establish the "real payload, fictional frame" loophole. Model: the three frozen models; reality-status direction from difference-in-means between R0 and R3 activations at the last instruction token, harmfulness-content direction from harmful vs harmless payloads, layer chosen on val by probe AUROC; refusal scored by refusal-string plus judge, verified where checkable. Convincing: a significant monotone refusal decline (p<0.05) of >= 20 points from R0 to R3 in a majority of categories on all three models WHILE the benign control stays flat near 0 and fictional-frame completions remain actionable; reality-status probe AUROC >= 0.80 with |cosine| <= 0.3 to harmfulness and a significant incremental contribution to refusal prediction. Indecision band: R0-to-R3 refusal drop in [8, 20] points, or reality-status |cosine| in [0.3, 0.5] / probe AUROC in [0.65, 0.80], or fictional completions only partly actionable - a weak, entangled, or diluted axis we report as suggestive rather than a clean loophole. Negative (drop < 8 points or benign control also declines, or probe AUROC <= 0.65 / cosine > 0.5, or fictional completions not actionable): there is no actionability-constant reality-status gradient or no distinct axis, refuting H1, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - reality-status causally drives refusal): Tests that injecting the "real-world" reality-status component into a fictional-frame run with a real payload restores refusal while attenuating it induces compliance. Decisive metric: refusal-restoration rate when patching the R0 real-world component into an R3 run, and induced-compliance rate when attenuating it in an R0 run, against controls. Data: test-split R0 and R3 requests (real payloads). Procedure: (a) patch R0 reality-status component into R3 and score restored refusal; (b) attenuate/ablate it in an R0 run and score induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering along the reality-status direction on R2/R3; a matched control direction and a random norm-matched control. Model: the three frozen models. Convincing: patching restores refusal on >= 40% of R3 cases and attenuation raises compliance on R0 by >= 20 points, both against <= 10-point controls, with a monotone dose-response and intact off-target utility/benign requests. Indecision band: causal effects in [15%, 40%] restoration or [10, 20] points - reality-status is a partial causal input, reported as such. Negative (effects within 15 points of controls): reality-status does not causally drive refusal, refuting H2 (an informative null we report).

Experiment 3 (H3 - Payload-Grounded Reality Anchoring closes the fictional-frame loophole): Tests that re-anchoring reality-status to "real" whenever the payload is actionable makes refusal track payload danger not frame fictionality, closing the loophole without over-refusing genuine fiction, with held-out-category generalization.
